#6357. Researchers Discover Earth May Have Made Its Own Water 4.5 Billion Years Ago

Laboratory experiments suggest that rocky planets could generate their own water as they form, potentially giving distant worlds an essential ingredient for life.

Rocks, hydrogen gas, and intense heat might sound like an unlikely recipe for an ocean. Yet experiments suggest that these ingredients could have produced much of Earth’s water while the planet was still taking shape.

One leading explanation for Earth’s water involves small particles containing ice, known as icy pebbles. These formed in colder regions of the early solar system, where water could remain frozen, and may have carried that water to the growing Earth. Questions remain about how the particles traveled such long distances and whether those deliveries can fully explain Earth’s chemical composition.

Graduate student Susmita Garai led the new research with Zachary Sharp, professor and director of Earth and Planetary Sciences, and Peter Olson at the University of New Mexico. Their study, published in Nature Geoscience, investigated whether iron-bearing silicate rocks could react with atmospheric hydrogen under conditions resembling those of early planetary formation.

“In order to evaluate the possibility of ‘pebble’ rain’ being a source of water, we needed to construct and execute some very challenging high-temperature experiments. Dr. Garai’s efforts paid off mightily, as she found that water is produced in just minutes in the high-temperature environment of the Early Earth’s atmosphere,” Sharp said.

The researchers heated silicate rock samples to between 1,200 and 1,400 degrees Celsius, or about 2,192 to 2,552 degrees Fahrenheit, in experiments lasting from 15 minutes to three hours. Some samples were exposed to streams of hydrogen. Others were heated in helium for comparison, allowing the team to test hydrogen’s role in the reaction.

In the hydrogen experiments, nearly 80% of the iron oxide in the samples was converted into metallic iron, producing water vapor in the process. Hydrogen reacted with oxygen bound to iron in the rocks, leaving the iron as metal and forming water. The same reaction did not occur in helium.

“Previous ideas about the source of water to Earth rely on an external source, such as comets or meteorites. Here we show that virtually any Earth-sized planet should have water by this newly identified mechanism,” Sharp explained.

For this chemistry to supply a growing planet with water, rocky material, and hydrogen would need to meet under suitable conditions. That could happen during pebble accretion, a process in which small rocky particles accumulate to build a larger planetary body. Once the growing planet became sufficiently massive, it could develop a hot, high-pressure atmosphere rich in hydrogen. Silicate pebbles falling through that atmosphere could then undergo the water-producing reaction tested in the laboratory.

“We had suspected and hoped that we would produce iron metal and water in our reduction experiments, but we really had no way of knowing how fast and how much. We were quite surprised to find that extrapolation of our work suggests that hundreds of oceans worth of water were likely produced in this way. Looking out over a large body of water, it is hard to imagine that that water may have been produced 4 ½ billion years ago in a hell-like atmosphere, but it very well may have,” said Sharp.

If comparable conditions developed around other rocky planets during their formation, the reaction could provide a widespread route to water on Earth-sized worlds beyond our solar system.

“The idea of pebble accretion is still relatively new. It’s only been around for the last decade. But it seems to solve many problems that exist with the existing paradigm for planet formation,” Sharp said. “And now we see that it also can explain why our planet is habitable. By extension, it is reasonable to expect that other Earth-sized bodies circling other stars would also have water and possibly life.”

The experiments demonstrate a potential mechanism for producing water during planetary formation. Determining how much of Earth’s water actually originated this way will require further research.

Reference: “Dry pebble rain could have delivered water to Earth through hydrogen reduction of iron oxide”, 12 October 2026, Nature Geoscience. DOI: 10.1038/s41561-026-02138-3

The Cat's Head Nebula shows its ghostly insides and sinister red eye in rival views from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In space, nobody can hear you scream — or meow, for that matter. This was as true for Félicette — the stray Parisian tuxedo cat who safely completed the world's first (and only) suborbital feline flight, in 1963 — as it is for the gargantuan Cat's Head Nebula, which is featured in stunning new images from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

Rising from the cloudy Carina Nebula some 7,500 light-years from Earth, the Cat's Head Nebula is a column of star-sculpted gas and dust that vaguely resembles a feline sitting with its back to us, coyly turning its head to show off a single red eye. That eye is a young star that's embedded deep within the dust and possibly transforming it before our eyes.

Nebulas like these occur when the radiation from active young stars lights up and erodes the material around them. They are beautiful and easy to find; if this cosmic cat gets bored staring at us, it can just waltz over to the other side of the Carina Nebula and crawl into a similar globule of gas that looks exactly like a box with an open lid. (Cats will be cats, after all.)

In honor of Halloween, the European Space Agency (ESA) shared three competing views of the Cat's Head Nebula — one from the Hubble Space Telescope, which captures optical light, and two from the infrared instruments aboard the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The three views, shown below, reveal different features of the nebula in different wavelengths of light, getting progressively spookier as more color drains out of the scene.Take a look at all three images — and cast your vote for the spookiest in the poll at the end.

The Hubble Space Telescope's optical light view of the Cat's Head Nebula.

Observing the nebula in the same visible wavelength range that you could see through a strong backyard telescope, Hubble highlights the dark pillar of dust that has survived the ultraviolet assault of nearby stars. The wispy edges at the right of the column show where starlight is evaporating the gas around it, slowly whittling it away to nothing.

The glow of blue, yellow, orange and red light around the dust pillar mark where starlight is interacting with different gas molecules, including oxygen, hydrogen and sulfur, according to ESA. The process is similar to how different molecules in Earth's atmosphere produce different-colored auroras when excited by solar radiation — just on a much grander scale.

The James Webb Space Telescope's view of the Cat's Head Nebula in near-infrared light.

Switching to light human eyes cannot see, JWST's Near-Infrared Camera cuts through the wispier outer layers of dust to show the densest material at the column's center. Countless additional stars and galaxies appear in the field of view as their infrared glow penetrates the surrounding material.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Here we see a more complex, turbulent column, showing how stellar radiation is carving up the inside of the cat's head as well as its edges. JWST's view also illuminates a disembodied, hand-like structure to the left of the cat, reaching out as if to pet its cosmic companion.

The James Webb Space Telescope's view of the Cat's Head Nebula in mid-infrared light.

The final view, taken with JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument, cuts to the ghostly core of the nebula, showing little more than smoky, bluish light. According to ESA, these are the emissions of molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons — typically colorless molecules of carbon and hydrogen related to combustion.

While most starlight disappears in this view, a strange new bright spot emerges to the right of the cat's head. This orange speck is a true mystery, according to ESA, and its relationship to the rest of the nebula is unknown.

#6354. Your Genes May Already Know Who You’ll Fall in Love With

Observable traits often determined by genetics may attract us to someone who shares them.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Besides the clichéd “must love dogs” and “likes long walks on the beach at sunset,” what do people actually look for when seeking a partner? Dating profiles barely touch on the qualities someone might imagine in their ideal match, and bathroom selfies aren’t doing us any favors. Sometimes the answer is so subconscious, it can only be found in our genes.

Trying to find the person who’s right for us is less random than we might think. When individuals with similar traits find each other, it’s known as assortative mating, which continues shaping the genetic makeup of human populations and is intentional—in a way—whether those couples realize it or not. In the back of our minds are criteria, such as education or certain behaviors, that potential matches have to meet. This can partly explain why some families have been known for certain traits for generations. Researcher Gretchen Saunders of the University of Minnesota decided to find out just how prevalent this phenomenon is by comparing genetic signatures in couples and across generations.

“Understanding mate choice, including how it is changing over time, is critical for both social science and genetics research, as it informs patterns of social homogamy and inequality while also affecting key assumptions in quantitative genetic and genetic epidemiological models,” Saunders, who specializes in statistical genetics and psychology, said in a study recently published in Behavior Genetics.

When partners carry similar traits that can be inherited, their children are also highly likely to be born with them, which can affect how those traits end up being distributed throughout a population. This doesn’t necessarily mean people explicitly choose each other based on those traits alone. It’s more likely that they already associate with groups that share the traits, and through those social and professional connections, they may eventually find a partner in such a group. Saunders based her research on eight specific traits ranging from physical features to education to habits that affect health. These included the visible factors of height and body mass index along with education level. She added five more having to do with drinking and smoking, such as frequency and the start or end of these habits.

Each subject who provided information for the study was given a polygenic score. These are numbers that merge the effects of different DNA variants in the genome to gauge a person’s genetic predisposition to a phenotypic, or observable, trait. Polygenic scores can also predict the likelihood of inherited diseases, which was not a factor in Saunders’ research. She was especially looking for similarities in polygenic scores between spouses and siblings. The phenotypic factor that was most similar between married couples was education level, which wasn’t surprising given that sociocultural variables have been observed in couples with phenotypic similarities for decades. Education was followed closely by alcoholic drinks per week. Less obvious links were body mass index, smoking initiation, and smoking cessation.

Seemingly unrelated traits were often found together. Those who had completed a higher level of education were often found to prefer partners who were taller, had a lower body mass index, and lower likelihood of smoking. Heavy smokers and drinkers tended to be attracted to those with similar habits and a higher body mass index. Polygenic scores based on this data revealed that while spousal genetic correlations were not as strong, they were still substantial. Traits already determined before these subjects became couples, such as height and body mass index, were the most correlated, while traits that were subject to change over time, such as cigarettes or drinks per day and smoking cessation, showed less of a connection. Comparing siblings showed evidence for partner matching based on these traits in earlier generations.

“Apparent differences in genetic architecture across cohorts may reflect not only temporal changes in assortative mating within populations, but also cross-cohort differences in underlying social structure, opportunity, and behavioral norms that shape mating patterns and phenotype distributions,” Saunders said.

So while DNA isn’t necessarily destiny, it may be, at the very least, pointing you in the right direction.

She lurks right outside New York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

#6353. A Devastating Disease Is Threatening the World’s Chocolate Supply – but Scientists May Have Found the Answer

A change to just two DNA letters reduced disease in cacao by about 42% under laboratory conditions, suggesting a possible way to protect future chocolate harvests.

Black pod disease is estimated to reduce cacao yields by roughly 30% worldwide, threatening the livelihoods of farmers who grow the crop used to make chocolate. Shifting weather patterns and other environmental stresses are making production even more difficult. With millions of farmers depending on cacao, these pressures are raising concerns about the future of the global chocolate supply.

Scientists at Penn State have developed a new variety of cacao that shows significantly improved resistance to black pod disease in laboratory tests. The researchers used gene editing and traditional breeding to strengthen the plant’s natural defenses, offering a potential way to reduce losses without introducing foreign DNA into the final plant. The promising results are now moving toward field testing and possible commercial production.

The work builds on decades of research led by Mark Guiltinan, the J. Franklin Styer Professor of Horticultural Botany and professor of plant molecular biology in the Department of Plant Sciences at Penn State’s College of Agricultural Sciences, and Siela Maximova, a research professor of plant biotechnology in the same department.

“For consumers, chocolate is something they expect to find on store shelves every day, but behind that product is a crop and industry facing significant challenges,” Guiltinan said. “Our goal is to develop tools that help growers continue producing cacao sustainably and profitably.”

Cacao is particularly vulnerable to environmental changes because of where it evolved. Native to the Amazon rainforest, the species originally grew beneath the canopy of tropical forests, where surrounding trees helped create relatively stable conditions. Today, cacao is cultivated across tropical regions of Africa, Asia, and Latin America, often in environments quite different from its original habitat.

“Cacao evolved in a very stable rainforest environment,” Guiltinan said. “It’s a delicate plant in many ways. Changes in rainfall, temperature, and humidity can all affect production, and some of those changes can also increase disease pressure.”

These environmental pressures are especially concerning because cacao trees cannot be improved quickly through traditional breeding. A tree takes roughly three years to mature and begin producing seeds, and developing and evaluating a new variety can take decades. Meanwhile, changing weather conditions, including increased humidity and variability, can create more favorable conditions for pathogens and insect pests.

“The climate is changing faster than these trees can naturally adapt,” Maximova said. “One of our goals is to develop tools that help breeders respond more quickly to those challenges.”

In a study published in the Plant Biotechnology Journal, the team combined genome sequencing, CRISPR gene editing, and traditional crossbreeding to develop cacao plants with greater resistance to black pod disease. The disease is caused by a mold-like pathogen that attacks cacao plants and can severely reduce harvests.

The researchers targeted a gene called TcNPR3, which normally acts as a brake on the plant’s immune system. By changing this gene, they partially activated the cacao tree’s natural defense response, giving it greater protection against subsequent pathogen infections.

The genetic change was remarkably small. Rather than introducing a completely new defense system, the scientists adjusted one already present in the plant. After making the edit, they used traditional breeding to remove all transgenic material, including the foreign DNA associated with the gene-editing machinery. The resulting plants retained the beneficial change without carrying foreign DNA.

This distinction is important for how the plants are regulated. According to the researchers, the resulting cacao is no longer considered a genetically modified organism, or GMO, consistent with U.S. and European Union regulatory frameworks that treat certain gene-edited traits similarly to those produced through conventional breeding.

“In one case, we only changed two bases in the entire genome of the plant,” Guiltinan said. “Out of roughly 450 million bases, that single change resulted in about a 42% reduction in disease under laboratory conditions.”

That result provides encouraging evidence that a small genetic adjustment can improve cacao’s disease defenses. However, laboratory conditions cannot fully reproduce the environmental challenges trees encounter on farms, and the researchers have not yet established whether the same protection will hold under commercial growing conditions.

Field evaluations are now underway through collaborations with the U.S. Department of Agriculture in Hawaii and Puerto Rico. These trials will help determine how the edited plants perform in actual growing environments before decisions are made about broader cultivation.

“These plants are specifically designed to improve disease resistance,” Maximova said. “The next step is proving performance in field trials. Scale-up and marketing will be the next challenges should the field testing prove encouraging. That’s where commercial partners can play an important role in helping move the technology forward.”

Penn State has recently entered into a licensing agreement with AgroNetica, a biotechnology company focused on cacao, to advance that process. The company has licensed the commercial rights to plants carrying the disease-tolerance mutation and plans to continue testing, expand production, and eventually market improved cacao varieties directly to growers in cacao-producing countries.

Turning a successful laboratory experiment into a crop that farmers can reliably grow requires considerably more than demonstrating that the genetic modification works. Plants must undergo additional testing, be produced in sufficient quantities, and reach growers through commercial distribution systems. Universities generally lack the resources needed to carry out that entire process.

“It takes millions of dollars and many years to bring a new crop variety to farmers,” Maximova said. “That’s why partnerships with companies willing to invest in development, testing and deployment are so important.”

The agreement also marks a milestone for Penn State’s Program in the Molecular Biology of Cocoa, which Guiltinan and Maximova co-direct. The program traces its origins to an industry-supported endowment established in the 1980s. Over the following decades, Penn State researchers developed foundational tools for cacao biotechnology, mapped important genetic pathways, and established one of the world’s leading cacao research programs.

Those advances created the scientific foundation for the current gene-editing work. They also demonstrate why maintaining a research program over many years can be necessary before discoveries become practical agricultural technologies.

“Thanks to this long-term investment in research and maintaining a sustained program, we now have an opportunity to begin getting technologies developed here in the lab closer to the hands of farmers,” Maximova said. “The focus was always on helping cacao farmers and the industry. We’re now at the place where we have a partner whose expertise is moving these discoveries into real-world use.”

Disease resistance is only one of the traits that researchers and commercial developers hope to improve. AgroNetica also plans to introduce additional characteristics from its development pipeline, including greater tolerance to heat and drought, reduced cadmium accumulation, and more compact trees that could allow greater mechanization. Other goals include shortening the time before a tree’s first harvest and developing caffeine-free cacao varieties. These remain development objectives rather than demonstrated benefits of the newly licensed disease-tolerant plants.

Guiltinan and Maximova are continuing to investigate traits associated with climate resilience and crop productivity. They expect accelerated breeding and genome editing to play increasingly important roles in helping cacao growers respond to environmental pressures that may change throughout the lifetime of a tree.

“The diseases are changing. The climate is changing. The challenges growers face continue to evolve,” Maximova said. “This is not something you solve once, and then you’re finished. It’s an ongoing effort to develop better plants and provide growers with new options.”

For Guiltinan, the success of the research will ultimately depend on whether these advances translate into meaningful improvements for the people growing cacao.

“We’re trying to solve real problems for farmers,” he said. “If we can help growers reduce losses, improve productivity and adapt more quickly to changing conditions, then that’s the ultimate measure of success.”

Reference: “Reduced Susceptibility to Phytophthora in Non-Transgenic Cacao Progeny Through CRISPR–Cas9 Mediated TcNPR3 Mutagenesis” by Mark J. Guiltinan, Lena Landherr, Siela N. Maximova, Dante DelVecchio, Aswathy Sebastian and Istvan Albert, 9 September 2025, Plant Biotechnology Journal. DOI: 10.1111/pbi.70365

#6352. A striking Mars cloud may be born from surprising physics

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud might not need dust to kick-start its formation

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud emerges every day during spring and summer on Mars, a long wispy ribbon downwind of the Arsia Mons volcano. This image of the cloud was captured by a camera aboard the European Space Agency’s Mars Express mission.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

One of Mars’ strangest clouds may rely on unusual physics to emerge.

The Red Planet’s ribbonlike cloud — which stretches as long as four Grand Canyons laid end-to-end — may form without a speck of starting material to seed it, researchers report October 7 in Nature Geoscience. This manner of forming clouds, called homogenous nucleation, was thought to be possible on paper but not to occur naturally.

Tiny particles such as dust or salt floating in the air seed typical clouds on Earth. But that cloud physics doesn’t seem to apply to the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud. Beyond its impressive length, this wisp of water ice is remarkably consistent, forming daily in the same spot roughly 45 kilometers high on the slope of a Martian volcano for several months each year.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The team tried and tried but couldn’t reproduce the cloud’s formation, including its lengthy tail and consistent cycle, with computer models employing standard cloud physics, says François Forget, an astrophysicist at the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique, or LMD, in Paris.

There’s no shortage of dust on Mars. The trouble is that high up in a thin Martian atmosphere, few cloud-forming dust particles stay suspended. Instead, they probably clump together and eventually fall, says planetary physicist Jorge Hernández-Bernal, who did the work at LMD. This left cloud formation without seeds as the most convincing explanation, he says.

Every day during some seasons on Mars, a long wispy cloud emerges along the flanks of the Arsia Mons volcano, as seen in the observations video spanning three Martian hours. How that cloud forms has been a mystery. A new simulation, bottom, included unusual physics, in which clouds form without starting material. That approach replicated the shape and timing of Mars’ Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud for the first time.

The team’s model suggests that the eye-catching plume originates when air flowing across the volcano triggers a rapid lifting of a moist parcel of air. The decrease in pressure at that altitude lets the air parcel expand, rapidly cooling it.

The newly cooled air now has 100,000 times more moisture than it can hold, the team’s model suggests. This excess moisture undergoes homogenous nucleation, rapidly forming more stable ice crystals. Winds sweep the forming cloud outward, creating the cloud’s distinctive long shape.

While the model doesn’t perfectly match satellite observations, it does capture how the phenomenon that leads to the cold air pocket reoccurs day after day, just like the real cloud does.

The study was surprising because “homogeneous nucleation is generally treated in our field as this theoretical concept,” says Samuel Atwood, an atmospheric and planetary scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., who was not associated with the study.

“It’s a pretty compelling story that they’re telling with the model, but it’s only one view or one perspective on it,” Atwood says, adding that future measurements supporting the team’s finding will provide more certainty. Hernández-Bernal says that he plans to validate the study by testing alternative explanations.

Even beyond Mars, the study provides food for thought. Previous studies have suggested that on Earth, meteor smoke provides particles for cloud formation in an upper layer of the atmosphere called the mesosphere, though a few studies have suggested homogenous nucleation could be responsible. Now that scientists are proposing homogenous nucleation on Mars, Hernández-Bernal says, “maybe there will be an increased interest in investigating this on Earth.”

D.E. Siskind et al. Understanding the effects of polar mesospheric clouds on the environment of the upper mesosphere and lower thermosphere. Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres. 2018. doi: 10.1029/2018JD028830

Blue whale sightings have fallen off dramatically near the Galápagos. El Niño may be to blame.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For nine months, a scientific expedition searched for blue whales in the waters around the Galápagos Islands but found none. Between October 2025 and July 2026, the researchers surveyed areas of the Ecuadorian archipelago where the giants had historically been recorded, hoping to attach satellite tags and learn more about the animals' migratory routes. The search ended without the team tagging a single whale.

The absence coincided with unusually warm ocean conditions during an El Niño event. Sea surface temperatures were as high as 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 degrees Celsius), while at a depth of 330 feet (100 meters) water temperatures ranged from 66 to 67 F (18.9 to 19.4 C) — up to 9 F (5 C) warmer than usual for that time of the year.

This raised the possibility that El Niño changed where blue whales were finding food and, in turn, where they went. The researchers suspect the animals may be seeking colder, more productive waters. However, the whales themselves are still missing.

Blue whales have not been feeding off the Galapagos this year, and likely migrated somewhere further south, where waters are cooler and food is more abundant.

"The hypothesis is that the whales are staying in areas with greater productivity [more food] farther south, in waters with slightly cooler temperatures," Daniela Alarcón, the expedition's leader and a researcher at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito's Galápagos campus and the Galápagos Science Center, told Live Science.

As to where the missing whales have gone, possibilities include the waters off Peru and offshore areas where the animals could go undetected. In this scenario, the unusually warm waters around the Galápagos Islands would act as a "temperature barrier," Alarcón said, preventing them from feeding in the archipelago's waters.

Blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus) can consume up to 12,100 pounds (5,500 kilograms) of krill — small crustaceans that make up the whales' primary food source — every day. That means they need to find areas with enough food to sustain them.

"These are very large animals that need to move to areas where they can keep feeding," Alarcón said.

It's not yet clear whether this year's El Niño caused a krill shortage in the waters off the Galápagos, but some indirect evidence points that way.

We thought that if we put in more effort, we might be able to find some individuals. But we searched, and searched, and searched — and found nothing.

Past expeditions suggested that blue whales tend to feed in water layers around 71 F, which this season was identified around the Galápagos at a depth of about 197 feet (92 m). By contrast, peak chlorophyll concentrations, an indirect indicator of abundance of the krill's food source, phytoplankton ‪—‬ were recorded much higher in the water column, at between 39 and 121 feet (12 to 37 m) below the surface. Because krill abundance wasn't directly measured, that data suggests, but does not establish, that there was a mismatch between the whales' preferred feeding layer and the presence of their food.

"Honestly, we had never encountered such unusual conditions before," Juan Pablo Muñoz, a marine biologist at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito who was also on the expedition, told Live Science.

The whales' absence did not come as a complete surprise to the team. Sightings had already begun to decline before the most recent expedition. Reports submitted through Cetácea Galápagos, a citizen science network, began to dwindle between August and September 2025. There were two isolated reports of blue whales, in May and June 2026, but the team could not confirm either one, despite intensifying its search.

"We knew conditions wouldn't be the same, but we thought that if we put in more effort, we might be able to find some individuals. But we searched, and searched, and searched — and found nothing," Alarcón recalled.

Despite nine months of looking, a recent expedition to search for blue whales around the Galápagos region did not spot a single one.

Part of that could be down to the elusive nature of the giant creatures. Humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae)are generally easier to spot, Muñoz noted. In some places, they can be seen from the shore or after a half-hour boat ride. Blue whales, by contrast, rarely approach mainland Ecuador's coast and tend to stay far from populated areas in the Galápagos.

Fernando Félix, a marine biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Ecuador who was not part of the expedition, was unsurprised by the result.

"We already knew there wouldn't be any blue whales in the Galápagos," said Félix, who is also a researcher at the Whale Museum (Museo de Ballenas).

Félix told Live Science that there are historical precedents for this behavior in the southeastern Pacific. During the 1982-1983 El Niño, which also brought substantial ocean warming, blue whales and other species, including fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus) and Bryde's whales (Balaenoptera brydei), were recorded shifting southward.

"We might think that because they are 'just animals,' they lack memory or don't understand these processes — but we would be wrong," Félix said. "They can clearly sense that when temperatures are unusually high as they travel north from the south, vertical mixing has been disrupted and there is no food in the Galápagos. They perceive environmental conditions and naturally direct their movements toward areas where they believe feeding conditions are better."

Sea surface and subsurface temperatures during the 2015 El Niño, showing a band of warmer water at depth. After that season, whale sightings bounced back, suggesting the missing blue whales will return once water conditions cool.

Rather than indicating a mass die-off, the whales' disappearance may reflect a shift in their movements in response to changing ocean conditions, Félix said.

"I don't think the whales have died," Felix said. "They simply didn't go to the Galápagos region. They went elsewhere, where conditions were better."

This response to environmental conditions may also have impacted dolphin movements. Pods may have moved toward colder waters, where food could be more abundant, or may have even dispersed, Félix suggested.

El Niño's effects will likely persist over the coming months. "Between January and May 2027, we'll have warm water coming from the north and warm water coming from the west," Félix warned. "This is going to hit us extremely hard."

Blue whales, humpback whales and dolphins would likely return to Galápagos waters once El Niño subsides and ocean conditions begin to normalize. He said pelagic fish (species that live in the water column rather than on or near the seafloor) ‪—‬ including tuna, swordfish, anchovies and sardines, which have also moved toward colder waters ‪—‬ would return as well.

Muñoz agreed. Krill populations can rebound just one to three months after cold, nutrient-rich waters begin to rise to the surface. More whale sightings were recorded in the years following the 2015 and 2023 El Niño events. Based on these precedents, he suggested that 2028 could be a promising year if cold water returns to the surface. "The system bounces back," he said.

Félix compared El Niño to a computer restart. "It resets the environment, allowing ecological processes to begin again," he said. He's confident that blue whales will return to the area. "I can guarantee that there will be large numbers of blue whales at this time in 2028," he told Live Science.

#6348. Deep ocean oxygen kept rising and falling long after animals appeared

Geologists found deep ocean oxygen built up and vanished again for over 100 million years after the Cambrian, complicating how animals evolved.

Researchers often explain the Cambrian Explosion, the burst of animal life half a billion years ago, with a lasting rise in ocean oxygen. In the deep ocean, though, the oxygen didn’t last..

Geologists studied mud that settled on the seafloor between about 485 million and 380 million years ago and later hardened into rock.

They found oxygen near the bottom building up for short stretches and then disappearing again. So animals may have evolved under less deep-sea oxygen than researchers once assumed.

Chadlin Ostrander, an assistant professor in the Geology & Geophysics department at the University of Utah, led the study. His team found no evidence of sustained oxygen in the deep ocean during that span.

The team concluded that oxygen didn’t settle into the deepest water for good until sometime after roughly 380 million years ago.

“Just a decade ago, it was thought that a deep ocean oxygenation switch was flipped around 540 million years ago. Our new dataset pushes that forward in time by at least ~160 million years,” he said.

The team didn’t measure oxygen directly. Instead, it read a chemical record in the rock that follows oxygen indirectly.

Researchers have invoked oxygen in the deep ocean to explain nearly every major step in early animal history. That includes the first animals and the Cambrian Explosion. It also includes a second burst of marine diversity from about 485 to 444 million years ago.

Other scientists have raised serious counterarguments to each. A common objection is that oxygen may have risen during these events, but not high enough, or for long enough, to fill the deep ocean.

Visitors to the Grand Canyon can see some of that early history. Its walls include about 1,600 feet (500 meters) of rock that settled in a Cambrian sea.

Ostrander’s samples start right after the Cambrian ended, about 485 million years ago, so the team didn’t sample that sea.

Geologists find tiny amounts of thallium, a heavy metal, in ordinary rock. It comes in two forms that differ by a hair in weight.

When a manganese mineral settles into seafloor mud, it pulls more of the heavier form out of seawater. That mineral survives in mud only where oxygen is steadily present in the water above it, and a few days without oxygen dissolve it again.

Mud formed in oxygen-poor places keeps a sample of the surrounding seawater, including its mix of the two forms. The team read a lower value, meaning more of the lighter form, as a sign that more seafloor lay under oxygen-rich water.

The team measured 82 shale samples from the Peel River in Canada’s Yukon. The river has cut into the rock, exposing fresh layers that stayed largely unweathered in the cold.

Erik Sperling of Stanford University and Justin Strauss of Dartmouth College led the expeditions that collected the Yukon mud.

Another 44 samples came from sites including Latvia, Libya, Wales and Montana.

For most of the record, the team found the same thallium mix as in ordinary continental rock. A seafloor with little oxygen above it should leave exactly that. In Yukon mud that formed between about 405 million and 386 million years ago, the readings dropped.

The lowest value came from a Marcellus Shale sample from the Appalachian Basin that formed about 388 million years ago. By the team’s calculations, that value means oxygen-rich water covered much more than 30% of the seafloor, well past the continental shelves and into the deep ocean.

Readings from the peak of the last ice age look similar, with surface oxygen reaching the deep ocean only slightly less effectively than it does now.

That high-oxygen stretch didn’t last. By about 378 million years ago, the readings returned to ordinary values and stayed there to the top of the rock. That could mean more of the deep ocean had lost its oxygen again.

Local conditions could have faked the dip, so the team checked. The 11 Yukon samples from the dip had the same chemistry as the other Yukon samples, and the Marcellus Shale, from a separate basin, dipped the same way.

By the time of those samples, Ostrander said, marine life was already large and doing energy-expensive work.

“You have some phenomenal changes in evolutionary biology happening during this time. And none of it seems to require substantial and sustained deep ocean oxygenation,” he said.

Animal life was changing fast before that window opened.

Paleontologists working at a fossil site in southwest China have found that many animal groups already existed before the Cambrian began. Researchers who analyzed fossil trails from about 545 million years ago reached a similar conclusion.

In rock about 520 million years old, researchers have found colonies of tiny filter-feeding animals and an early relative of octopuses and squid.

The deep ocean has had steady oxygen since then. The team can’t say when that began, only that it came after about 380 million years ago. Ostrander called that the study’s one disappointment.

Gaps remain. The team has only one rock sample for roughly every 450,000 years, so the real swings may have been even larger than the mud shows.

The team also couldn’t fully rule out that thallium cycled through seawater too fast for the mud to reflect the whole ocean. Its models and the match between basins make that unlikely.

The researchers wrote that long, closely spaced oxygen records from the late Paleozoic and the Mesozoic are still needed to learn when the deep ocean filled with oxygen for good.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6347. What an artist thought were ancient stone ovens in South Africa turned out to be termite nests at least 323,000 years old

Stone pipes near Calitzdorp, South Africa, once thought to be ovens, are fossil termite nests at least 323,000 years old and a new trace fossil.

In the early 2000s, a local artist named Tim Robson dug hard, pipe-like structures out of a river terrace. The spot was near Calitzdorp, a small town in South Africa’s Little Karoo.

He thought they were ovens built by early humans. They were fossil termite nests, and uranium dating now shows they are at least 323,000 years old.

A team led by Miengah Abrahams of the University of Cape Town’s Department of Geological Sciences has named them Columnanidus calitzdorpensis, a new trace fossil. No termite bodies were found with the nests, so the species that built them is still unknown.

The site is on a flat terrace of the Gamka River outside Calitzdorp, in the Western Cape. Nothing about Robson’s dig was recorded at the time.

Paleontology consultant John Almond heard about the oven theory from Tom Barry of CapeNature and from Bob Wood in 2003 and 2004. Several pieces were removed from the site. One went to the Calitzdorp Museum, and it is still there.

In 2005 Almond wrote a short entry on the pipes for a heritage study. It covered the Gamkaberg-Rooiberg conservation area, around CapeNature’s Gamkaberg Nature Reserve. He said they might be fossil termite nests, but no one was interested in returning to the site.

Emese Bordy, a University of Cape Town geologist, saw the entry and told Abrahams. Bordy had supervised her PhD. The work began in 2021, and Almond is one of the eight authors.

Barry guided the team in the field. Two pits had been dug into the terrace about 33 feet (10 meters) apart. Only the first one had nests in it.

Eight nests still stand there within 15 feet (4.5 meters) of each other. Some were built up against a neighbor, and a few share a wall.

The visible part of each nest is 14 to 41 inches (36 to 104 centimeters) tall. A nest is about 26 inches (65 centimeters) across, with a wall close to 5 inches (12 centimeters) thick.

River cobbles are stuck in the walls at all heights, and one wall holds a snail shell. So the nests were dug fully underground, the authors say, in an old soil lying on the gravel.

On the inside of the wall, the termites built rows of flat chambers stacked like shelves. Ramps link the levels. An average chamber is about 2.5 inches (6.4 centimeters) wide and less than a third of an inch (0.73 centimeters) high.

The inner chambers are lined with a dark organic layer. The paper notes that ants occasionally line their burrows too, but termites do so far more often.

Muofhe Tshibalangada CT-scanned pieces of the wall at Stellenbosch University. Megan Purchase-Wellman at the University of the Free State checked the minerals by X-ray diffraction.

“We determined that these were a unique ichnogenus and ichnospecies, because of their distinct cylindric nature,” Abrahams said in a university press release.

“The distinct zones in the shapes of the burrows and chambers within the nest wall have not been seen anywhere else before either.”

All eight nests have an empty center about 16 inches (40 centimeters) wide. The paper calls this feature curious and not understood. A soft hive may have rotted away, or the termites may have built around a tree trunk.

The team drilled 11 cream-colored carbonate layers out of the nest walls. Samples went through uranium-thorium dating, a method described by co-author John Hellstrom of the University of Melbourne, who works in the university’s School of Geography, Earth and Atmospheric Sciences.

Two of the 11 carried too much detrital grit and were dropped. The other nine gave dates from about 422,000 to 206,000 years, which cluster at 401,000 (three dates), 323,000 (five dates) and 206,000 years (one date).

The single 206,000-year date came from a layer that did not follow the chamber shapes, so the authors did not take it as the minimum age.

The 323,000-year group was the largest and most precise, with an error of 12,000 years. The team took 323,000 years, give or take 12,000, as the minimum age, in the Middle Pleistocene.

Columna is Latin for column and nidus is Latin for nest. The second half, calitzdorpensis, is for the town.

Calcium carbonate built up in the sand the termites had worked and slowly set hard. Geologists call it calcretization.

Over the nests sits a honeycomb layer of carbonate lumps and an 11-inch (28-centimeter) cap of hardpan. In the second pit, 33 feet (10 meters) away, neither layer is there, a gap the authors tie to the termites.

Modern termites change the chemistry of the soil they live in and the way water moves through it, Abrahams said. “In ancient times such activity would have also provided good conditions for carbonate minerals to build up in the nests and be preserved.”

Living colonies build well-ventilated nests that move air and moisture through the ground. In dry country they dig deep for damp soil. The living species Hodotermes mossambicus nests as deep as about 11.5 feet (3.5 meters).

Other termite works have lasted a long time too. In Brazil, millions of mounds about 4,000 years old can be seen from space. In the Namib Desert, sand termites have been tied to bare rings known as fairy circles.

According to the paper, no single feature can fully discern a termite nest from an ant nest. The team calls the pipes “likely attributable to termites.”

The bottoms of the nests are not well exposed, and in the ones the team emptied out, the wall just stopped. The uranium dates show when carbonate grew in the walls, not when the termites dug, so the nests could be older. Few continuous climate records exist in the region to compare them with.

Next, the group will look at fossil termite and ant nests in the Northern Cape and near Ceres and Worcester. Abrahams will co-convene an ichnology symposium at the 7th International Palaeontological Congress in Cape Town, November 30 to December 3, 2026.

In October 2026 the researchers went back to Calitzdorp and gave the museum a poster about the find. “We hope visitors to the museum, especially children, will gain a deeper appreciation for the natural world around them,” Abrahams said.

The museum’s piece, once taken for an oven, is now the holotype. That is the reference specimen for the new name, accession number 93/01/01.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Quaternary Science.

This Roman glass cup can change from jade green to ruby red, and it features a mythical king who tried to banish Dionysus.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Roman-era Lycurgus Cup has a color-changing effect depending on the light source.

The Lycurgus Cup is a Roman-era glass goblet that changes color from jade green to ruby red depending on if a light is shining on its front or back. But experts are unsure where the cup was found, where it was made, or whether the glassblower who made it created the color-changing effect on purpose.

In 1958, the British Museum acquired the cup from the Rothschild banking family, which had owned the artifact since the mid-19th century. Known colloquially as the Lycurgus Cup for its depiction of the mythical king who angered the god Dionysus, the glass is about 6.3 inches (15.9 centimeters) tall and weighs around 1.6 pounds (700 grams).

The glass is a remarkably well-preserved example of a Roman "cage-cup," according to a 1959 study of the artifact by archaeologists D. B. Harden and Jocelyn Toynbee. Only a handful of cage-cups still exist, and experts believe the goblets were made by cutting and grinding decoration into thick glass. Because small bridges were left to ensure the decoration remained on the glass, the overall effect is like a cage. Harden and Toynbee estimated that the Lycurgus Cup was manufactured in the fourth century, likely in Italy, but they noted that the bronze frame that forms the stem and rim of the goblet is probably a 19th-century addition.

Depicted on the cup is the myth of the punishment of Lycurgus, king of the Thracian tribe called the Edoni (also called the Edonians). Lycurgus did not approve of the worship of Dionysus and banished the god into the sea with an ax. But one of Dionysus' priestesses, Ambrosia, decided to fight Lycurgus. Ambrosia changed herself into a vine and wound herself around Lycurgus, who was unable to escape. The other priestesses thronged around them and tormented Lycurgus. Given that Dionysus was a god of wine and merriment, the depiction of Lycurgus' punishment may have been particularly appropriate for this goblet. Additionally, the change in color from green to red may have been meant to mimic the ripening of grapes on the vine.

Color-changing cups, also called dichroic cups, were mentioned in ancient Roman historical records. For example, a second-century letter possibly penned by Emperor Hadrian to his brother-in-law mentions a gift of two dichroic cups to use during banquets. But very few fragments of this mysterious type of glass survive today, a 2007 study noted.

For decades, experts have been working out how ancient Romans produced dichroic cups, and some have even replicated the Lycurgus Cup's color-changing effect. A 1963 study confirmed that the key seems to be the addition of microscopic nanoparticles of gold and silver during glassblowing that produce the appearance of milky-green glass when lit from the front and nearly translucent red glass when lit from behind. The metal nanoparticles are smaller than grains of sand and interact with light, creating the perception of a color change.

A replica of dichroic glass made by Corning Glassworks in the 1960s went from green to amethyst in the light, the 2007 study reported, and in 2020, researchers included silver and gold nanoparticles in 3D printing to replicate the color-changing properties of the glass.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

More recently, experts at the University of Sheffield in the U.K. reproduced the dichroic glass by reverse-engineering the "recipe" from the original Lycurgus Cup. The team then commissioned a glass artist to create a Lycurgus-inspired design from the replica.

But because so few examples of dichroic glass exist, experts are still unsure whether Roman artisans created the color-changing effect on purpose or whether traces of gold, which would have been available in an ancient craft studio, slipped into the molten glass and made a rare and unusual material that mystified even the most skilled glassblowers.

#6344. Some of the world’s biggest bats are getting smaller

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Madagascan flying foxes, easy targets for hunters, have shrunk since the 1980s

Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus) (shown) have skulls that are 6 percent smaller than they were prior to the 1980s. Large-scale hunting by humans may be the reason.

These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.

With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).

“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.

To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.

Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.

“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.

As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.

It’s possible that the smaller size could have long-term impacts on the population, says Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath in England. “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years,” she says. Changes in the animals’ physical traits or adaptations caused by human pressures might make the bats less able to respond to environmental, climate or disease stresses.

The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.

“These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

#6343. A simple change could make lifesaving blood transfusions easier for dogs

A new study suggests refrigerated blood platelets could help control dangerous bleeding in dogs while making lifesaving transfusions more accessible.

Platelets, the tiny cell fragments that help stop bleeding, have long been stored at room temperature because veterinarians believed refrigeration made them less effective.

A new study of sick dogs suggests chilled platelets can still help control bleeding, and they can be kept for weeks instead of days.

Dogs given platelets stored for up to three weeks showed less bleeding within four hours, and no transfusion reactions were recorded.

A longer shelf life could make platelets easier for animal hospitals to keep on hand.

Jillian Haines, a veterinarian who directs the blood bank at Washington State University’s Veterinary Teaching Hospital, led the research.

Her team reviewed hospital records rather than running a trial, and no group of dogs was given standard room-temperature platelets for comparison.

“It is hard to overstate how important the ability to transfuse platelets is,” Haines said. “Many of us have seen patients die from bleeding complications because there was simply nothing we could offer them.”

“We went from having essentially nothing available to now having a really viable product that we can use.”

Bleeding on its own becomes a serious risk once a dog’s platelet count falls below about 30,000 to 50,000 per microliter, which is a millionth of a liter of blood.

At that point, a transfusion of platelets can be lifesaving for a dog with severe bleeding or one about to have surgery.

Getting those platelets is the hard part. Veterinary hospitals usually store them at 68 to 75°F (20 to 24°C) in constant motion, and a bag lasts about five days.

Warm storage also raises the risk of bacteria growing in the bag. Keeping platelets at 34 to 43°F (1 to 6°C) may slow that growth, stretch their storage time and make them easier to ship.

Human hospitals turned to cold-stored platelets during pandemic blood shortages, and reports found they controlled bleeding with no apparent rise in reactions or infections.

In dogs, Haines’s earlier lab work showed that refrigerated platelets could stay functional for up to three weeks, but no study had checked whether they help sick dogs stop bleeding.

Shannon Monaco, the study’s first author, worked with Haines and colleagues at the Washington State University College of Veterinary Medicine.

They found 24 dogs that had received 27 transfusions of chilled platelets between March 2022 and October 2024.

In nine of the dogs, the immune system was destroying their own platelets, a condition called immune-mediated thrombocytopenia.

Seven had cancer, and the rest had problems that included liver failure from a toxin, a twisted stomach and swallowed rodent poison.

Nine of the transfusions were given for bleeding that had started on its own. Six came before surgery, and 12 came before smaller procedures such as placing an IV line or taking a needle sample.

Each bag began as about 15 fluid ounces (450 mL) of donated dog blood, spun twice to pack the platelets into about 2 fluid ounces (60 mL).

The bags were stored at 39°F (4°C) without shaking, for an average of 12 days before use.

Clinicians judged bleeding with a bleeding score designed for dogs, which rates each site on the body from zero to two.

The team added bleeding inside the chest or belly, checked by ultrasound, for a top score of 20 points.

Six of the dogs showed no signs of bleeding before their transfusions.

Among the rest, the average bleeding score was 3.15 before the transfusion, 3.00 an hour later and 2.21 after four hours.

Only the improvement measured at four hours was statistically significant. In plain terms, bleeding had eased a little by the four-hour mark.

Clinicians recorded improvement within four hours after 19 of the 27 transfusions, or 70%. That meant bleeding slowed or stopped, or a procedure went ahead without bleeding.

Seven more transfusions were followed by partial improvement.

One case couldn’t be judged, because the dog’s heart stopped soon after the transfusion, which the team attributed to suspected cancer.

Nineteen of the 24 dogs, or 79%, survived to leave the hospital.

The dogs that died had higher bleeding scores before and after their transfusions, which fits earlier studies tying bleeding severity to survival in dogs with low platelet counts.

The platelet counts told a different story. Before transfusion, the dogs’ median count, the middle value in the group, was 17,000 per microliter.

An hour later it was 23,500, a change too small to rule out chance.

That wasn’t unexpected, the authors wrote. In people and dogs alike, a platelet count often fails to reflect how well a transfusion is working, especially in dogs whose bodies are destroying or using up platelets.

Chilled platelets also leave the bloodstream sooner than room-temperature ones.

Earlier lab studies found they clump together more readily and form clots faster, which may make up for their shorter stay.

The team didn’t test any of that in these dogs. They wrote that such properties may help explain the lower bleeding scores, although the cause can’t be determined.

None of the 27 transfusions was followed by a fever, an allergic reaction, an infection or any other reaction in the records.

The researchers noted that showing a lack of harm is an essential early step for any new way of storing platelets.

Records can miss mild reactions, though. Two of the dogs were also taking drugs that calm inflammation or suppress the immune system, which could have masked a reaction.

Three dogs did bleed later. Two with immune-mediated thrombocytopenia developed suspected bleeding into the belly 12 to 18 hours after a needle sample was taken from the spleen.

One of those two dogs stabilized after a second bag of chilled platelets, and the other stabilized without more treatment.

A third dog, a surgical patient, had mild bleeding from its incision a day after its operation that stopped on its own.

The authors suggested that these later bleeding episodes may be related to how quickly chilled platelets leave the bloodstream. Some dogs may need a repeat dose.

Nine dogs also received other blood products, such as red blood cells or plasma, on or near the day of their platelet transfusions.

Two received freeze-dried platelets during their stay, and those treatments could have helped steady some of the dogs too.

The bleeding score was modified for this study and hasn’t been formally tested, and some scores had to be rebuilt from clinicians’ notes.

The dose also varied from dog to dog, and the study didn’t determine the best one.

Even in people, the right dose is unsettled. A large human trial of preventive platelet transfusions found that low, medium, and high doses led to similar bleeding outcomes.

The university’s blood bank now keeps a routine supply of cold-stored platelets.

Haines said she has trained veterinarians and blood bank staff from other institutions in the method.

“It’s not needed often, but when it is needed, it is the only option,” Haines said. “These products can be lifesaving.”

Haines hopes to work out the best dose and find better ways to tell whether a transfusion helped an individual dog.

She also hopes to test whether the platelets still work after more than three weeks in the refrigerator.

The full study was published in the Journal of Veterinary Internal Medicine.

#6341. Tiny Arctic bacterium has an unexpected strategy for capturing carbon dioxide

Scientists discover an Arctic bacterium with an unusual metabolism that combines acetone consumption, sunlight, and carbon dioxide fixation.

A tiny bacterium drifting through the surface waters of the Arctic Ocean has been hiding an unusual metabolic trick.

It can’t eat sugar and it carries one of the smallest genomes of any marine microbe. And yet it thrives by doing something no one had documented in the marine world before.

This unusual organism appears equipped to break down acetone while incorporating dissolved carbon dioxide into its metabolism.

Researchers at Concordia University in Montreal and Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh have described the organism, Porticoccus arcticus, in a recent study.

Acetone is one of the most common volatile organic compounds floating around in seawater. It’s produced by phytoplankton, broken down from organic matter, and deposited from the atmosphere.

Arctic surface waters contain concentrations above 40 nanomolar – enough, it turns out, to sustain microbes.

The researchers first confirmed the concept in a related species, Porticoccus hydrocarbonoclasticus, a bacterium previously isolated from a lab culture.

When they offered it acetone as its only food, it grew. Its cell density was directly tied to how much acetone was available.

Higher concentrations actually proved toxic, which makes a certain biological sense. This is an organism tuned for scarcity, not abundance.

P. arcticus caught the team’s attention through metagenome-assembled genomes pulled from Canada Basin water samples.

Its genome is strikingly compact – just 1.29 million base pairs with a GC content of 41.6%.

For context, its closest well-characterized relative, P. hydrocarbonoclasticus, carries a genome nearly twice that size at 2.47 million base pairs and 53.1% GC content.

Its streamlined genome suggests that evolution has favored a compact set of genes suited to life in nutrient-poor waters.

It has no sugar transporters. Its glycolytic pathway is incomplete. It can’t break down glucose the way most bacteria do.

What it has kept, though, is telling. A complete acetone carboxylation pathway sits right there in the genome.

The other surprise is the light-harvesting equipment. P. arcticus carries two proteorhodopsin genes – molecular light-driven proton pumps – and neither one appears to be ancestral.

Phylogenetic analysis shows they were picked up through lateral gene transfer from distantly related bacteria, one from a Gammaproteobacterium and the other from a Betaproteobacterium.

The blue-light-absorbing proteorhodopsin dominates expression by a factor of roughly 64 over the green-light version.

That’s a sensible adaptation for an organism living in Arctic surface waters, where blue light penetrates farthest.

A carotenoid biosynthesis pathway also appears nearby, suggesting that the bacterium has additional machinery involved in producing pigments and protecting its cells from light-related damage.

“This organism has evolved a fascinating metabolic strategy,” said corresponding author David Walsh, a professor of biology at Concordia University.

“It combines the use of acetone as a carbon source with light-driven energy production, allowing it to thrive in nutrient-poor Arctic waters where other bacteria struggle to survive.”

This isn’t some boutique organism lurking at the edges of Arctic microbial communities.

The team analyzed microbial samples collected between 2017 and 2023 across a broad stretch of the Arctic Ocean.

P. arcticus showed up consistently. At some surface sites in the Canada Basin, it represented up to 9% of all 16S rRNA gene sequences at 5 and 20 meters depth.

It had a clear habitat preference: oligotrophic surface waters with intermediate sea ice cover. It was abundant at open ocean sites experiencing dynamic, year-to-year changes in ice conditions.

At permanently ice-covered stations and in deeper water layers, its numbers dropped sharply.

The real biogeochemical kicker is the carbon dioxide angle. P. arcticus carries a cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase.

This is an enzyme that converts dissolved CO2 into bicarbonate, the form its acetone carboxylase needs as a substrate.

So the acetone carboxylation isn’t just about eating acetone.

The acetone carboxylation reaction incorporates one molecule of inorganic carbon for every acetone molecule processed, linking acetone metabolism directly to carbon fixation.

“It’s a form of photoheterotrophy we haven’t seen before in the ocean,” Walsh said.

“This bacterium uses sunlight for energy while consuming acetone and fixing CO2 – it’s operating at the intersection of several metabolic strategies that were previously thought to be separate.”

The Arctic Ocean is warming faster than any other ocean basin on Earth.

As Arctic sea ice retreats and ocean conditions change, the habitat available to P. arcticus could shift, potentially altering its role in regional carbon cycling.

An organism that simultaneously consumes a volatile organic compound and fixes CO2 while being powered by light could play a larger role in Arctic carbon cycling than previously assumed.

The team is careful to note that the acetone carboxylation pathway they’ve identified could exist in other marine photoheterotrophs as well.

Its abundance in Arctic surface waters suggests that this previously overlooked metabolic pathway could have broader ecological importance.

Acetone degradation via carboxylation had only been described in terrestrial bacteria before this work.

The discovery reveals an overlooked pathway in the Arctic carbon cycle, suggesting that even the smallest ocean microbes may influence how carbon moves through the environment.

The study is published in the journal Nature Communications.

Live Science spoke with psychiatrist Anand Kumar about the next edition of the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual Of Mental Disorders", which will include biological factors like genetics in studying and diagnosing psychiatric conditions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For decades, psychiatrists and other mental health professionals have used the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders," or DSM, to diagnose patients with conditions such as major depression, anorexia and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). To reach diagnoses, mental health practitioners identify symptoms via interview, case history, questionnaire, or observation to paint a clinical picture.

But for the next version of this "psychiatry bible", the DSM-6, scientists are planning to add other factors into the diagnostic criteria.

Dr. Anand Kumar, a psychiatrist who served for two years on the DSM Strategy Committee, says one of the most important potential changes is the introduction of biological factors into the diagnostic framework. While Kumar, the head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois Chicago, no longer serves on the committee, he was influential in discussions about how biology could be incorporated into the DSM-6. Some of these biological factors include data from genome-wide association studies of hundreds or thousands of genes that each increase the risk of a mental disorder by a tiny amount. Other biological factors include signs of inflammation or immune-system dysfunction that may show up in blood tests or brain scans.

Live Science spoke to Kumar about how this update to the DSM could change the way mental disorders are understood and potentially help improve treatment.

Dr. Kumar is the Lizzie Gilman Professor and Head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois at Chicago. Dr. Kumar's research focuses on late-life depression and mental disorders of the elderly, including Alzheimer's disease. He has served as Treasurer, Program Committee Chair, and President of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry (2004-2005). Dr. Kumar is Associate Editor of the American Journal for Geriatric Psychiatry and has served as reviewer for numerous NIH review committees.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: How is the DSM-6 going to be different from the DSM-5?

Anand Kumar: Up to this point, the distinctions between the different major groups — who has clinical depression, or what we call major depression; who has an eating disorder; who has PTSD, etc. — have been based exclusively on clinical grounds: You meet certain criteria, and you fall into this category. If you meet some other criteria, you fall into another category.

An attempt that's being made now, one of the major attempts for the next DSM, is to introduce biological factors into the manual.

The idea is not new. It's been discussed in the past, but it was difficult to get a consensus on what goes in and what should not go in. That's still going to be tricky, but at least there's a broad acknowledgement that the time is ready to start introducing biology into the DSM.

It's very likely that, at the end of it, there will be meaningful changes in a positive kind of way. It's not going to make everyone happy. There are going to be gaps, but the idea is to incrementally improve this and make it more modern as we go along.

KHC: What sort of biological markers have you seen that we can actually correlate with these disorders?

AK: What the committee is doing is taking a more nuanced approach. Outside the realm of Alzheimer's disease, which I'll get into in a minute, there are no clear-cut diagnostic biomarkers — meaning no blood tests or brain scans that you can look at and say, "This person has a diagnosis of depression," or "This person has PTSD," or "This person has schizophrenia."

The committee talked about how, in addition to biological biomarkers, there's a concept of biological factors. What I mean by that is biological pathways and mechanisms that have a role in the development of a particular disorder, but the findings have not crystallized into a laboratory test.

For example, immunology — the study of the body's response to a variety of stresses, including infections and others — has been shown to be impactful in about 30% of cases of major depression. Yet there is no single biological laboratory test that is currently available that can be used [to diagnose immune-mediated depression] in clinical practice. So these come under the category of what we call biological factors.

In the Alzheimer's disease field there are clear-cut biomarkers. There are now blood tests for proteins called tau and amyloid that have been approved by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] as biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease. Meaning, if you have a clinical picture and a mental-status exam consistent with intellectual decline, you must have a positive biomarker test to be categorized as having definitive Alzheimer's disease.

And that's new. Ten or 15 years back, there were brain scans, and if you did a lumbar puncture, you could find these proteins in the spinal fluid. But those are invasive. Now you actually have a blood test.

A neuron, in blue, is surrounded by a plaque of amyloid-beta protein, in yellow, which causes the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease. Tests can be used to detect biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease.

But that degree of precision, for lack of a better term, is not available in the other branches of psychiatry. Nonetheless, there are clues that other pathways and mechanisms are involved.

I mentioned immunology as one. Another big elephant in the room is genetics.

Most people think of genetics as an abnormal gene or a mutation — meaning a gene switches or changes and confers increased risk — as one mutation causing one disease. That's how most people in the general public think about mutations: They cause disease.

But when you get into complex diseases like heart disease and diabetes, there are multiple genes involved. And diseases may or may not be caused by a gene. Abnormal genes may or may not cause the disease, but they increase risk.

With mental disorders, the situation becomes immensely more complicated. It's not just a few genes here and there. There are hundreds of genes, each increasing the risk for depression, schizophrenia and anxiety disorders by a small amount.

So while there is no single genetic test that can now be used, large numbers of genes have consistently been shown — and many of the recent studies are strong — to be associated with certain disorders. But because there's no single gene or small group of genes, we cannot walk away from the science. Complexity doesn't mean we throw our hands up and say, "Well, it's all too much."

It may seem overwhelming, but genetic profiles are better understood today than they were 20 years ago. So that's something else this committee is thinking about and I think should take into account going forward: to somehow incorporate that into the diagnostic categories.

KHC: Do you think there's any sort of risk with adding those biological factors into the DSM?

AK: I don't think so, because if you think about genetics, it's not going to be introduced as a biological test.

Most folks know that mental disorders, like other medical disorders, run in families. And genetics is the most plausible explanation for that. What this does, I hope, is introduce a degree of more comprehensive description of these disorders. So when a busy clinician looks at it, it confirms what they already suspected: There's a family history here, and family history means genetics.

It's complex, many genes are involved, and it produces a better characterization of this. The diagnosis is still going to remain clinical, but this provides a biological context, very much like, say, diabetes or heart disease.

Genes and environment cause a variety of medical disorders. With heart disease, there's no one gene. When cardiologists develop a risk profile for heart disease, it includes genes, other physiological factors such as BMI, which is the weight-height ratio, diet and a variety of environmental factors.

That degree of classification is missing today in mental health and psychiatry. We hope this is a first step in correcting, if you will, those conceptions about what causes these disorders.

KHC: How would you end up using this in a psychiatrist's office to guide treatment?

AK: I can give you one possible example. I'm reaching a bit.

There's a term commonly used in clinical psychiatry and psychology called comorbidity. What it means is that people who are diagnosed with depression also have anxiety, or people who are diagnosed with an anxiety disorder also have substance abuse or alcoholism in general.

That is not coincidental. It's not something that we just somehow find. A lot of these disorders share genes.

For example, about 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with a major mood disorder also have an anxiety disorder. And you flip that around: About 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with an anxiety disorder — it could be generalized anxiety disorder, what we call PTSD, or a phobia — also have a mood disorder.

Patients with anxiety may also be diagnosed with a mood disorder.

I think when clinicians classify them together, not as the same disorder but as sharing a lot of psychological as well as genetic risk, clinicians should be on the lookout for both. A patient with a mood disorder, for example, could either now or at some later point develop an anxiety disorder. Or someone with an anxiety disorder is at risk for substance abuse.

So treatments need to be tailored a little more broadly. I'm hoping that'll be something clinicians think about when they talk to patients and their families.

KHC: What do you think is the most unique aspect, from your perspective, of this upcoming DSM-6?

AK: My bias is the biology. I say this because a lot of the other things, the cultural factors, etc., are largely appreciated, and they'll be better characterized. Some things like cognitive changes, such as working memory and attention [tests], are not unique to any given disorder.

Biology will be qualitatively new when introduced into the DSM, and I hope it's done well. I hope that they do it appropriately, and I think they will [do it] correctly.

It's not going to be perfect, but it's going to be a first step. I think introducing the idea that genetics, immunology and other factors are very important in the causation of mental disorders, and explain some of the phenomena that we previously could not find an explanation for, is — I hate to use the word "leapfrog" — but that's kind of what it is.

It moves the field conceptually forward, and not as a slow, steady, gradual increase. For the DSM, it would be an important step forward.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.
