#6325. NASA captures two powerful Pacific storms with a surprising connection

NASA satellites captured a rare super typhoon with an enormous eye as another powerful Pacific storm transformed and moved toward Alaska.

In late October 2026, two powerful storms dominated opposite ends of the North Pacific Ocean.

One developed an enormous, nearly circular eye, while the other transformed into a sprawling weather system that swept toward Alaska.

Yet both began as tropical cyclones in the western Pacific, and both appeared in a remarkable satellite view captured by NASA on October 29, 2026.

Super Typhoon In-fa was still an intense tropical system near the Mariana Islands.

Far to the north, the remnants of Typhoon Champi had transformed into an entirely different kind of storm.

Together, they offered a striking demonstration of how dramatically storms can change as they travel across the planet.

Super Typhoon In-fa stood out for its unusual structure.

NASA’s Terra satellite captured a closer view on October 30, revealing a remarkably symmetrical storm just west of the Mariana Islands.

In-fa displayed characteristics of an annular typhoon, a rare type of tropical cyclone with a distinctive ring-shaped structure.

Most typhoons develop long, spiraling bands of thunderstorms that extend outward from their centers.

Annular storms typically have fewer prominent outer rainbands, giving them a smoother, more circular appearance.

Their unusual structure has earned them comparisons to doughnuts and truck tires.

Only about four percent of tropical cyclones in the western North Pacific develop annular characteristics.

These storms also tend to have larger eyes. While the eye of a typical tropical cyclone averages around 15 miles across, annular storms average nearly 30 miles.

Their structure can also help them maintain their strength longer when environmental conditions become less favorable.

While In-fa maintained its tropical identity, Champi was undergoing a dramatic transformation thousands of miles away.

Earlier in its journey, Champi had become one of the most powerful typhoons of 2026, with sustained winds approaching 185 miles per hour.

The storm brought damaging winds and heavy rainfall to several western Pacific locations, including Taiwan, Guam, China, and Japan.

But tropical cyclones depend on warm ocean water for energy. As Champi traveled northward, it encountered conditions that fundamentally changed how the storm operated.

Through a process known as extratropical transition, Champi’s remnants became incorporated into a larger weather system over the Bering Sea.

Instead of drawing energy primarily from warm ocean waters, the developing system was driven by temperature differences between air masses.

The change also transformed its appearance.

Tropical cyclones are generally organized around a central core, with powerful thunderstorms circling the eye.

Extratropical storms often look quite different from space. Their clouds can spread across enormous areas, forming sweeping bands that resemble giant commas.

These storms can also develop weather fronts, where contrasting air masses meet.

One particularly important change involves the area covered by strong winds.

NASA meteorologist Gary Partyka explained that a transitioning storm does not necessarily develop faster winds. Instead, its wind field can expand dramatically.

This means a storm can affect a much larger region even as its original tropical structure disappears.

Champi’s remnants became intertwined with an existing midlatitude storm over the Bering Sea, likely helping intensify the larger weather system.

The resulting weather brought strong winds, heavy rainfall, and snow to parts of Alaska.

Alaska might seem an unlikely destination for a storm that began in the tropical Pacific, but the connection is well established.

Former typhoons sometimes travel northward and become part of the large weather systems that move across the North Pacific.

Champi was already the fourth former typhoon to reach Alaskan waters in 2026.

The others were Bang-Lang in August, Dujuan in September, and Choi-wan in early October.

University of Alaska Fairbanks climatologist Rick Thoman noted that even the exceptionally strong El Niño years of 1997 and 2015 each brought only three former typhoons into the region during autumn.

Approximately 60 former typhoons have affected Alaska since 1970.

The unusually busy 2026 season raised questions about the broader atmospheric conditions helping steer these storms northward.

One possible contributor was the strong El Niño underway in the Pacific.

El Niño develops when surface waters across parts of the equatorial Pacific become warmer than usual, altering weather patterns across distant regions.

In the Northwest Pacific, these changes can influence where tropical cyclones form and how they travel.

Rather than moving steadily westward toward Asia, some storms are more likely to curve northward.

That shift can bring tropical cyclones closer to Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Japan, and the Korean Peninsula.

It can also increase the opportunities for former typhoons to reach higher latitudes and interact with powerful northern storm systems.

El Niño is not responsible for every individual storm, but its influence on atmospheric circulation may help explain why the Pacific experienced such an active period.

The 2026 Northwest Pacific season had already produced more than two dozen named storms by late October.

In-fa was the fifth typhoon to affect the Mariana Islands that year, while Champi added to an unusually long list of former tropical cyclones reaching Alaska.

NASA’s satellite imagery captured an extraordinary contrast between two powerful storms, revealing how tropical cyclones can evolve as they move across different parts of the Pacific.

While In-fa retained its remarkable circular structure, Champi had become part of a much larger weather system.

Together, the storms offered a striking glimpse into the powerful atmospheric forces shaping weather across the Pacific.

#6323. Cutting more trees could actually help forests store more carbon

A new study suggests that carefully managed tree harvesting could increase long-term carbon storage by reducing tree deaths and preserving carbon in wood products.

The surest way to keep carbon in a forest seems obvious: stop cutting it.

Trees left standing continue growing and storing carbon. But as forests age, growth can slow and more trees die, gradually releasing their stored carbon.

Researchers who modeled every forest in China project that cutting more trees, earlier and in the right places, would store more carbon by 2100 than today’s restrictions do.

But the calculation only works when carbon stored in harvested wood products is included.

The gain is a calculation, not a measurement. It depends on the harvested wood being turned into products that last, and it comes from a model run under a single climate model.

Zhen Yu of Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology and Shirong Liu of the Chinese Academy of Forestry led the work, with co-authors at the U.S. Forest Service, the University of Exeter and CREAF in Spain.

The authors wrote that their findings challenge a widely held assumption: cutting the least always stores the most.

China swung from heavy logging to strict protection in the late 1980s, and its forest area has grown ever since.

Over the same years, its wood consumption rose more than tenfold, to 0.534 billion cubic meters in 2020, and more than 40% of that wood is imported.

The country now buys more wood from abroad than any other.

The authors drew on 15.5 million tree measurements from 415,000 inventory plots surveyed between 1999 and 2018.

Harvests got lighter over that period: more plots were cut, but the volume taken per cut fell by nearly half. Meanwhile the number of plots with dying trees kept rising.

Between the sixth and ninth national inventories, harvested volume dropped 46% while the volume lost to tree death rose 24%.

The pattern was strongest in old stands, which lost roughly four to five times as much wood to death as younger forests did.

China sorts its forests into timber forests, protection forests kept for soil, water and wildlife, and multifunctional reserves where commercial logging is excluded.

The reserves held 23% more standing wood per hectare than the timber forests, and their tree deaths rose 53% between 1999 and 2018.

The team ran two futures through an ecosystem model it first checked against the inventory record from 1980 to 2018. One continued current practice.

The other adjusted how much timber to harvest, when to harvest it, and where to cut based on forest age and type.

It opened suitable reserves to regulated harvesting and left protected areas and fragile ground alone.

Under current practice, the model projects that wood lost to tree death would climb to 0.43 billion cubic meters a year by 2100.

Dead trees amounted to about 71% of the timber harvest in 2020, and the authors estimate that by 2100 they would exceed it. More wood would rot than would be cut.

The adjusted plan harvests some stands before their trees die.

The model estimates it would cut mortality losses by 1.82 billion cubic meters (64 billion cubic feet) between 2020 and 2100, a 6.7% reduction.

Timber output would rise from 0.32 billion to 0.44 billion cubic meters a year, a 38% increase.

The extra timber would cut China’s reliance on imports, the authors wrote.

They calculated that the country’s wood self-sufficiency would rise from 59% to 81% under the plan. Domestic production met 46% of demand in 2023.

More cutting leaves less carbon in living trees, and the model shows that. By 2100 the standing stock under the adjusted plan is 2.41 billion cubic meters lower than under current practice.

Counting the carbon held in harvested wood products changes the sum.

Assuming wood use remains at 2020 levels, the model projects 4.2% more total carbon storage under the adjusted plan, equivalent to an additional 520 million metric tons of carbon.

The team’s supplementary accounting puts the climate benefit at roughly 550 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent annually.

None of this is a case for indiscriminate logging. The modeled benefit depends on forest age, ecological limits, and what happens to the wood after it leaves the forest.

The researchers didn’t track soil carbon, which can rise or fall after harvesting.

Their model moves a dead tree’s carbon straight into the soil pool, skipping the years or decades a standing dead trunk can hold carbon.

And every future ran under one climate model across four emissions pathways. The authors wrote that the difference between the two plans is therefore more trustworthy than either plan’s absolute numbers.

The 4.2% figure also rests on wood products being used the way they were in 2020.

How much of a harvested log becomes a beam that lasts 50 years, rather than paper or fuel, is a market question the forest model can’t answer.

The aging-forest problem is not China’s alone, the authors wrote. Europe and North America face the same mix of older stands, rising disturbance and growing demand for wood.

Whether carefully managed harvesting could deliver similar carbon benefits elsewhere remains an open question.

The full study was published in the journal National Science Review.

#6322. NASA’s Swift telescope faced a fiery demise after a failed rescue

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

During more than 22 years, the Swift Observatory made itself indispensable

This artist’s rendition shows NASA’s Swift Observatory in orbit around Earth.

NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab

For two decades, when the high-energy universe called, NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has answered. But now, the spacecraft’s tenure has ended, just when its skills might be more valuable than ever. On November 4, Swift reentered Earth’s atmosphere, where it was expected to burn up. This fiery end capped an uncontrollable fall from space.

The telescope launched in 2004, tailored to reveal the secrets of gamma-ray bursts. These outbursts are the most powerful kind scientists have ever seen, but they often faded before earlier telescopes could respond. Swift took its name from its ability to jump to work when a flash went off. That talent both illuminated these elusive bursts and made the observatory a cornerstone of modern astronomy for far longer than scientists ever dreamed.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“This was designed to be a two-year mission,” says astrophysicist Brad Cenko of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md. “We’re coming up on year 22. We are so fortunate to have had the opportunity to do all the things that we have.”

Over the decades, the spacecraft has lost about half its original altitude as it constantly slammed into molecules in the atmosphere. Those minuscule impacts infinitesimally slowed the observatory, pushing it closer to Earth. The sun’s relatively high activity in recent years has accelerated the process, leaving the spacecraft unable to continue into the 2030s as engineers hoped. A spacecraft commissioned by NASA to loft Swift out of danger launched in early July, but by late August, technical issues made a boost attempt impossible.

Swift was doomed — with nothing lined up to replace its unique capabilities.

When scientists dreamed up the Swift mission, the massive energy and elusive nature of gamma-ray bursts made them one of the most tantalizing phenomena out there. Astronomers desperately wanted to understand how they worked.

Swift was equipped with three instruments. Its Burst Alert Telescope gave scientists eyes on gamma-ray emissions from up to half the visible sky, with the resolution to pinpoint where light is coming from. The agile spacecraft could then swing itself and its other instruments — one tuned to X-rays and the other to visible and ultraviolet light — to quickly give scientists a view of a patch of sky across a swath of types of light. It was a combination unlike any observatory before or since.

“It’s such a unique telescope,” says astrophysicist Wen-fai Fong of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill., who is not part of the mission team. “It has all these views of the universe, all in one observatory, which by itself is rare, but it can also rapidly point any of these instruments.”

Swift’s roster of accomplishments speaks to the power of that recipe. “Almost immediately after launch, Swift started discovering things,” says astrophysicist Lynn Cominsky of Sonoma State University in Rohnert Park, Calif. That’s not an exaggeration: One record-breaking observation, taken just the month after launch, revealed that stellar corpses with powerful magnetic fields undergo outbursts that create a distinct kind of gamma-ray signature.

Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab/NASA

That observation pushed back against scientists’ existing categorization of gamma-ray bursts. Before Swift, the bursts fell into two buckets. Long gamma-ray bursts lasted as long as minutes, and scientists believed they stemmed from exploding stars triggering supernovae. Short gamma-ray bursts, in contrast, lasted less than two seconds and were believed to originate in merging neutron stars, the superdense remains of a star large enough to explode but too small to create a black hole.

Swift confirmed this basic sketch, but also complicated it by finding bursts that didn’t cleanly fit into this binary. “The more data you get, the more confused you get,” Cominsky says. Other notable bursts the telescope observed included the brightest (gamma-ray burst) of all time, nicknamed BOAT, the highest-energy photons from such a burst, and multiple claimants to the title of most distant burst.

Notably, all of Swift’s data was public right away, even as team scientists were still working to understand what the telescope had seen. “That was very new,” Fong says, crediting the mission with inspiring other observatory teams to follow suit.

As other astronomers heard about Swift’s work, they realized how powerful the observatory might be for their own interests as well. As Swift’s tenure unfolded, astronomers started asking to borrow the nimble observatory to study a whole range of objects changing on the sky.

“With scientists, if you give them a tool to do something, they will other find other things that you can do with that tool,” says astrophysicist Phil Evans of the University of Leicester in England. In its later years, Swift observed between five and 10 “targets of opportunity” most days, tallying hundreds or even thousands in a year.

Perhaps its most ground-breaking collaborations were partnerships with observatories hunting for ghostly neutrinos that travel nearly as quickly as light but don’t interact often, and for gravitational waves, the ripples in spacetime triggered by massive objects. In 2017, Swift participated in back-to-back discoveries: the unique explosion caused by two neutron stars merging, then the first neutrino traced back to its origin.

Since then, all efforts to observe light affiliated with a neutrino or gravitational-wave signal have come up empty. “We had these two really close together and then nothing since,” Evans says. “Which is frustrating, but also kind of fun.”

A range of current and future observatories will be able to take over some of Swift’s work, but not all of it. Even during the six months this year when Swift paused operations to prepare for the boost attempt, scientists felt its loss, says astrophysicist Judith Racusin of NASA Goddard. Racusin worked with Swift during its early years before turning her focus to NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which launched in 2008 but boasts different strengths than its colleague. “We’re going to miss out,” she says of Swift’s loss. “Not just on the common events we have thousands of, but the really rare, unusual ones, which are often the ones we learn the most from.”

Mission personnel had Swift cram in as much science as possible as its demise approached. After the boost attempt was called off, the team turned Swift’s instruments back on for a scientific swan song. That included technical observations to ensure the utility of all its recent data, as well as indirect observations of Earth’s atmosphere at lower altitudes than many spacecraft are able to withstand. Swift even caught glimpses of a comet in its final weeks.

And, of course, there were gamma-ray bursts. One particularly intriguing burst came in late September and was rather far away but remarkably energetic.

“It feels a little bit like a last hurrah of Swift,” Racusin says of the event. “It’s a burst that we’ll be studying for some time, so I’m really glad we got Swift data on it while we could.”

#6321. The happiness curve has changed, and young adults are struggling most

A global study of nearly 54,000 adults reveals a troubling shift in happiness, with young people reporting the lowest levels of well-being.

For decades, research suggested that happiness reaches its lowest point in middle age, with people feeling better in their younger and later years.

Researchers surveying adults around the world have now found little sign of that midlife dip.

Young adults reported the lowest well-being of any age group, and scores rose fairly steadily from there with age. The researchers call the pattern alarming, and wealthy countries were not spared.

Kai Ruggeri, a professor of health policy and management at the Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, led the work.

His team of 261 researchers, all of whom took part as volunteers, surveyed nearly 54,000 adults in 92 countries.

Most people answered online and chose to take part, so the results describe the people who responded rather than whole nations. The authors make that point again and again.

“These findings are more than just a sign to policymakers that solutions are necessary to improve mental health among young people or those struggling to make ends meet,” Ruggeri said.

“In fact, they are a flashing red light that entire populations are already struggling and feel their resilience is diminished here and now, not only a concern for an uncertain future.”

Each participant rated ten statements about their own life. The scale ran from 1, meaning absolutely disagree, to 7, meaning absolutely agree.

The statements included “I feel full of energy,” “I feel calm and peaceful,” and “I recover quickly from things that go wrong in my life.”

Together, the statements measure different aspects of well-being, including optimism, resilience, and a sense of purpose.

The ten-part framework came from the well-being researcher Felicia Huppert and a colleague. Huppert died shortly before the work began, and the team dedicated the study to her.

She was told the day before her death that it would be carried out in her name.

Popular rankings such as the World Happiness Report rely on a few broad questions.

The authors wrote that two countries with the same life satisfaction score, say 7 out of 10, offer no clue about how either one could improve.

Samples from Denmark and Norway made the point. Both had an average life satisfaction of 6.2 out of 10, yet across the ten statements Denmark’s scores were spread more widely than Norway’s.

Participants also answered four standard screening questions about depression and anxiety over the previous two weeks.

People took the survey between June and August 2025, in 50 languages, and a typical participant finished in about six minutes.

People rated their relationships and their sense of meaning highest. On the 7-point scale, having support from people they’re close to averaged 5.05, and a sense of meaning averaged 4.93. Feeling full of energy came last, at 4.20.

Calm and the ability to recover from setbacks scored near the bottom too. The authors suggest those low scores fit with high rates of stress and burnout.

The difference was also clear among participants who gave the highest ratings of 6 or 7.

Just over 38% gave that answer about having support when they need it, but only 19.3% said the same about feeling full of energy.

The authors offer one possible reading of that gap. People may judge their own lives fairly kindly while feeling harmed by things they can’t control, such as unstable politics and economies.

Polls have described something similar, an optimism gap in which people feel better about their own lives than about society.

Only 6.5% of participants met a rough bar for flourishing. That meant scoring at least 60 out of a possible 70 on the ten statements while showing few signs of depression or anxiety.

The 38,133 participants who completed the screening questions showed the same age pattern.

Among people aged 18 to 25, only 14.7% showed no signs of depression or anxiety, compared with 23.6% of all participants.

At the other end, 28.6% of the young adults scored in the moderate to severe range, compared with 22.6% overall. Older groups did better, almost without exception.

Young adults in some wealthy countries fared worse still. In the UK sample, for example, only 6.1% showed no signs of depression or anxiety, while 42.8% scored moderate to severe.

The researchers’ first instinct was that their sample had produced the result. But a young and highly educated sample would typically skew results the other way, they wrote.

Other recent research has also found that younger adults now report the most distress.

Being free of depression and anxiety wasn’t the same as doing well, since many participants with no signs of either still scored low on the ten statements.

Well-being scores were higher at nearly every step up in household income, and the team found no clear point where the gains stopped.

That cuts against the common claim that money stops adding happiness past a certain income.

People who grew up in wealthier families scored higher as well.

Education followed a similar pattern. Each additional level of schooling was associated with higher average well-being.

The authors wrote that the education pattern contradicts claims that a university degree has lost its value.

People without paid work, whatever the reason, scored lower than workers, students, and retirees.

“Leaders can no longer use vague platitudes that hand-wave toward investing in non-specific mental health initiatives,” Ruggeri said.

Instead, he said, leaders need to make specific commitments.

Those include protecting livelihoods against job losses driven by AI, tackling burnout in young and working-age people, and improving access to care for mental illness.

People who lived with more family members or housemates generally reported higher levels of well-being than those living alone. Living alone was particularly common among older adults.

Among participants aged 75 and older, 44.9% lived by themselves, compared with 27.1% of all participants.

Among workers, people who split their time about evenly between home and the workplace scored highest, at 48.2 on a scale running from 10 to 70.

Those who worked entirely from home or entirely on site scored lowest, at 46.3 and 46.6.

The gaps between work arrangements were small. The researchers also couldn’t tell whether hybrid work helps or whether jobs that offer it are simply better jobs to begin with.

People in military service, a small part of the sample, scored highest of any work group.

The authors wrote that this likely reflects the relationships, energy, and sense of purpose common in a military unit.

Men scored slightly higher than women, though the difference was extremely small.

Everyone answered once, so the survey shows links rather than causes. The samples were uneven too, and in Chad almost everyone who took part was an academic.

Ruggeri’s team warned against ranking countries, because the statements may not mean exactly the same thing in every language.

A low average for Sweden, they wrote, doesn’t mean an employed, well-educated Swede is worse off than an unemployed person with little schooling in Uzbekistan.

Young people with unaddressed worries may have been eager to take part, and the oldest participants may have been unusually connected and energetic.

The authors wrote that those effects alone can’t explain a pattern this large.

Why young adults scored so low remains open. The authors raised two possibilities they didn’t test, starting with a steady stream of messages about stress, conflict, and lack of opportunity.

The other is loneliness, since young adults meet people in person less often than in the past, according to an OECD report.

Ruggeri’s team plans deeper analyses of wealth and well-being and calls for local studies within countries. In the authors’ view, those studies can best show governments which changes would help.

The full study was published in the journal Social Indicators Research.

Researchers identified a 5,300-year-old kidney stone in the burial of a Bronze Age cattle herder in Russia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Bronze Age man buried in a monumental tomb near the Black Sea may have died from complications of a urinary tract infection (UTI) more than five millennia ago, according to a new study. Archaeologists identified a grape-size object consistent with a kidney or bladder stone in the man's burial.

"He lived with a chronic urogenital infection," study lead author Natalia Berezina, an anthropologist at Lomonosov Moscow State University in Russia, told Live Science in an email.

"It was not a brief episode," she said. "His last years were probably marked by considerable and more or less constant pain."

Berezina and colleagues investigated a small, stone-like object found in an Early Bronze Age burial in the Stavropol Upland region of southwestern Russia. They published their findings Sept. 30 in the journal Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences.

The burial was part of a kurgan cemetery, an ancient steppe funeral tradition that involved constructing a large mound of dirt over a grave. Archaeologists discovered a catacomb when they excavated the mound, and inside was the skeleton of a man who was in his 40s when he died around 5,300 years ago. The researchers found a flint arrowhead near the man's pelvis.

But during a laboratory analysis after the skeleton was excavated, researchers noticed an odd stone-like object in the collection of hand bones. The brownish object was round with several protrusions and measured about 0.8 inches (2.1 centimeters) in diameter, or roughly the size of a grape. A small crack in the object showed a crystal-like structure inside.

To learn more, the researchers used several analytical methods to determine what the tiny object was made of. First, X-ray fluorescence analysis revealed that the main components of the object were calcium and phosphorus. Then, they used X-ray powder diffraction analysis to identify the crystal structures.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In addition to common minerals, the researchers discovered the presence of whitlockite, a rare calcium salt that is known to occur in kidney, bladder and prostate stones. These "stones," collectively called calculi, are hard masses of minerals, such as calcium-containing salts. They differ in terms of the organ they form within, the exact mechanism of how they form, and their chemical makeup, although kidney and bladder stones tend to contain very similar compounds.

Whitlockite is strongly associated with bacterial infections in the human body, which suggests that the Bronze Age man had a chronic infection that resulted in the stone, the scientists concluded.

"On the balance of the available evidence, we regard a renal [kidney] stone secondary to chronic upper urinary tract infection as the most probable origin," the researchers wrote. That is, the man dealt with chronic or recurrent UTIs, which led to the formation of the stone and likely caused him considerable discomfort. UTIs can contribute to the formation of kidney stones by altering the acidity of urine and making minerals more likely to accumulate.

The researchers aren't sure why the man had urinary tract issues or whether it contributed to his death.

Notably, kidney stones can sometimes travel to the bladder, so it's unclear exactly where the stone was in the man's body when he died. If the stone had obstructed the man's ureter ‪—‬ one of the two long tubes that connect the kidneys to the bladder ‪—‬ it may have caused kidney swelling, a secondary infection or sepsis. These conditions were frequently fatal prior to the invention of antibiotics.

Other possibilities for what caused the stone include a bacterial infection of the man's prostate gland or even a sexually transmitted infection.

The man was likely on the move frequently within this Early Bronze Age steppe society, and other injuries to his skeleton suggested he had a physically demanding life, the researchers wrote. His bones showed that he was well muscled but was also dealing with degenerative joint disease in his spine, shoulders, hips, hands and feet. He had a series of healed fractures in his right shoulder, ribs and forearm.

"These were people who worked with cattle and heavy wagons on the open steppe," Berezina said, "and the injuries that follow from that are the injuries we find." In a previous study at a nearby cemetery, Berezina and colleagues found the skeleton of a man who was injured when a wagon ran over him, several years before his death. "Against that background, four healed fractures in our man look unremarkable," she said.

But the urinary tract stone would have made the man's life difficult, the researchers noted. "This individual suffered from a painful and debilitating chronic urogenital infection, a condition that would have significantly impacted his quality of life," they wrote.

Berezina, N. Ya., Statkus, M. A., Kalmykov, A. A., Abdrashitova, I. V., Kolesnik, I. V., Platonov, V. B., Shashurin, D. A., Garmay, A. V., Korobkova, V. V., Ryleeva, V. S., & Gresky, J. (2026). Urolithiasis in the Early Bronze Age of the North Caucasus: A paleopathological case study and insights into ancient lifeways. Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences, 18(10), 209. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12520-026-02574-7

#6318. Astronomers discover a ghostly green star that shouldn’t exist

Astronomers have identified a ghostly green white dwarf, along with dead stars that appear pink, purple, yellow, and cyan, challenging expectations about stellar colors.

Stars typically glow in shades of red, orange, white, or blue, with their colors revealing their temperatures. Even burned-out stars, known as white dwarfs, were thought to follow this rule.

But astronomers have discovered something extraordinary: a dead star that would appear green to the human eye.

The unusual color comes from sodium in the star’s atmosphere, which absorbs orange light and leaves behind a ghostly green glow.

Astronomers say no green star of any kind has ever been credibly reported.

The team’s research also revealed white dwarfs that would appear pink, purple, yellow, and cyan, with each unusual color linked to the chemical makeup of the star’s atmosphere.

Mark Hollands, a Warwick Prize Fellow in the Astronomy and Astrophysics Group at the University of Warwick, led the work.

Boris Gänsicke and Pier-Emmanuel Tremblay at Warwick, along with Detlev Koester at Kiel University in Germany, were his co-authors.

No white dwarf is close enough for its color to be seen directly. Instead, astronomers calculate the color from the star’s light, and the green star’s measurement is a noisy one.

A white dwarf is what’s left when a star like the Sun runs out of fuel and its core is all that remains. The coolest ones have atmospheres about as dense as water, and that density is the key.

Like a piece of iron heated to increasingly high temperatures, ordinary stars glow red, orange, or white depending on how hot they are.

Bright stars like Betelgeuse look redder than their neighbors, but they stay inside that range.

“Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like ‘perfect radiators,’ so their color is set almost entirely by temperature. But nobody had really looked into what else might be possible for white dwarfs,” Hollands said.

In an atmosphere that dense, a trace of carbon, calcium, or sodium absorbs light across a wider band of colors than it would in a thin gas.

That absorption can give a star colors that its temperature alone cannot explain.

A star’s spectrum is its light split by wavelength, the way a prism splits sunlight into a rainbow. Astronomers record spectra routinely.

The team ran spectra from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and from their own atmosphere models through a mathematical description of human color vision that dates from 1931.

Each spectrum came out as the color a computer screen would need to show it.

The one thing a screen can’t show is brightness, because a real star’s surface is millions of times brighter than any monitor.

In an interview with Earth.com, Hollands said the calculation is more direct than a photograph would be.

Research telescopes record light through filters chosen for science rather than to match the eye, so their color images are false color.

A consumer camera on a research telescope could in principle show the same colors the team calculated, he said, but the spectrum already holds all of the star’s visible light.

“So this is the most accurate way to determine these colors short of actually going to visit these stars, which sadly won’t be happening at any time soon!” Hollands said.

The green star is WD J1330+6435, with a surface at about 7,200°F (4,000°C). Its helium atmosphere carries calcium, lithium, and sodium.

Those are the leftovers of asteroids or comets from its own planetary system, the same kind of debris seen falling onto other dead stars.

“The traces of sodium in the atmosphere of this white dwarf absorb the orange part of the spectrum, leaving behind a ghostly green glow,” Hollands said.

Calcium removes the violet as well, so the light that remains peaks near 500 nanometers. In the team’s model the star comes out chartreuse, which is a yellowish green.

Of all the unusual colors revealed by the research, one stood out to Hollands more than any other: the chartreuse green of WD J1330+6435.

“Green is generally considered an implausible colour for a star to have,” Hollands told Earth.com.

What would the sky look like from a planet around the star?

On an Earth-like world it would probably still be pale blue, in a slightly different shade, Hollands said. The star’s green would show up on you instead.

“If you were wearing a white shirt (or space-suit), then you would see your outfit illuminated the pale green color that we determined from its spectrum,” he said.

Two other white dwarfs in the sample came out a much paler green.

A cousin of the green star, WD J2356-2054, carries so much sodium that almost no light escapes from the middle of the spectrum.

At the same temperature, it comes out a vivid blue.

At the other extreme is WD J1011+2845, just 48 light-years away, with a surface near 7,300°F (4,000°C).

Movement within the star has carried carbon from its interior to the surface. There, the carbon forms molecules that absorb most of the blue, green, and yellow light.

Almost all of its visible light comes out beyond 600 nanometers, at the red end, and the result is a deep, salmon pink.

The team called it likely the reddest star known in terms of perceived color.

Among 36 carbon-rich white dwarfs the team examined, the cooler ones mostly came out in shades of pink.

Stars like it are hard to model, and a strong magnetic field may be distorting this one’s light in ways that the models don’t fully capture.

Hydrogen can tint a cool white dwarf as well, Hollands said. A trace of it forms H2 molecules, and their collisions with the dense helium can leave the star looking cyan or turquoise.

To find out how common the oddities are, the team took every white dwarf within 65 light-years (20 parsecs) of the Sun, 152 stars in all.

Five had colors too far from a heated-iron glow to be assigned a temperature: two yellow and three pink.

Five of 152 is about 3.4 percent, or roughly one in 30. For the rest, the team measured the color temperature, the scale printed on light bulb boxes, where 3,000 kelvin is warm white and 6,000 is cool white.

The median came out just under 6,800 kelvin, which the eye sees as white.

Gänsicke said the result corrects a habit.

“One in thirty might not sound like a huge fraction, but across the entire population of white dwarfs in the Universe, that is still a lot of oddly colored stars out there,” he said.

White dwarfs are usually drawn blue because the hot, blue ones are the brightest and show up most often in surveys. The nearby sample has no such bias. Within it, 95 percent of the stars fall between 3,800 and 18,700 kelvin.

The green star and the blue one are the same kind of object with different amounts of sodium.

The team therefore expects to find other white dwarfs with colors ranging from green to cyan and blue.

No other star quite like the green one is known yet, Hollands emphasized.

“Right now there are multiple spectroscopic surveys coming online which will be taking spectra of hundreds of thousands of white dwarfs, so hopefully we’ll find a few more, perhaps even more vivid green examples,” Hollands told Earth.com.

No white dwarf is bright enough to see without a telescope, but the team has developed a way to create color-accurate images of these stars.

As new surveys examine hundreds of thousands of white dwarfs, astronomers may soon discover even more unexpected colors hiding among the stars.

The full study was published in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments.

#6316. Tiny ocean buoys could transform how we predict powerful storms

Scientists found that drifting weather buoys in the Mediterranean Sea helped improve forecasts during a powerful storm that battered Sicily.

Modern weather forecasting relies heavily on satellites watching the planet around the clock.

Yet, when storm Harry drowned parts of Sicily in rain this January, a handful of barometers bobbing in the Ionian Sea helped the forecast.

Until the previous fall, that patch of sea had almost no weather instruments at the surface. Scientists dropped the barometer buoys there on purpose.

A project called the Mediterranean Extreme Events Experiment, or M3E, began releasing them in September 2025 to fill a long-standing observation gap. Storm Harry was its first big test.

A team led by David Lavers of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts found that the buoys’ pressure readings reduced forecast error during the storm.

“The Mediterranean is a relatively small sea, but it can generate very powerful storms, and the countries around it pay a high price,” said Emanuela Clementi, a senior scientist at the CMCC Foundation in Bologna and a co-author of the study.

“With M3E we are filling a gap in the observations precisely where these storms form. Storm Harry gave us the first evidence that these data help forecasts,” she added.

Every forecast starts from a snapshot of the atmosphere. That snapshot comes from millions of measurements a day, from satellites, aircraft, balloons and ground stations.

But thick clouds and heavy rain blur what a satellite sees in the lower atmosphere. So a barometer at the surface in the right place still carries unusual weight.

Yet surface weather instruments have long been scarce across the Ionian Sea and central Mediterranean.

The region has seen extreme storms since biblical times, the authors wrote, and persistent cyclones tend to form there.

Three recent ones, storm Apollo in 2021, storm Daniel in 2023 and now Harry, did heavy damage around the basin.

The barometer buoys that filled the gap drift with the current. An underwater drogue hanging 49 feet (15 meters) below each one keeps it from washing ashore too quickly.

Fifteen came from the Global Drifter Program at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, and five more were paid for by Italy’s OGS oceanography institute.

Each buoy measures air pressure and sea surface temperature, relays the numbers by satellite every hour, and feeds them into the global weather data stream within minutes.

The first seven went into the Ionian Sea in early September 2025, five from the research vessel Laura Bassi and two from a passing container ship.

More followed through February 2026. By late March, 10 of the 20 were still working; the rest had run aground in southern Italy or Greece, or been picked up by sailors.

One buoy drifted out of the Ionian Sea into the Adriatic and ended up along its eastern shore, tracing the regional current as it went.

Storm Harry formed as a small low over Morocco and deepened over Algeria a day later. Then it stalled over Tunisia and the central Mediterranean for days.

A steady southeasterly wind built waves of about 26 feet (8 meters) and drove moist air into the mountains of Sardinia, Sicily and Calabria.

Between January 19 and 21, 23 weather stations recorded more than 11.8 inches (300 millimeters) of rain. Eight of them passed 15.7 inches (400 millimeters), and eastern Sicily recorded the highest total, 19 inches (482.5 millimeters).

The toll was heavy. Losses in Sicily alone were estimated at more than €1 billion, a landslide hit the town of Niscemi, and people died in North Africa.

The European forecast model saw the Sicilian deluge coming about seven days ahead, helped by mountains like Mount Etna, which force moist air upward in the same place every time.

Northern Tunisia fared worse. One station there recorded 8.1 inches (207 millimeters), while the forecast issued at the start of January 19 had a median of just 1.6 inches (41.4 millimeters).

The authors suspect four small low-pressure systems between the Balearic Islands and North Africa contributed to the forecasting difficulties. Such systems are difficult to predict far in advance.

The team used two tests. The first scores every observation on whether it made the next day’s forecast better or worse.

Throughout the winter, the buoys’ scores were small but mostly positive, as expected when forecasts are already accurate.

On January 19, as Harry crossed the Ionian Sea, pressure at one buoy dropped sharply. Its readings proved particularly helpful in improving the forecast.

In the second test, the team reran the forecast for the storm’s two peak days with every drifting barometer buoy in the Mediterranean removed.

Near the Balearic Islands, where those four small lows sat, the two versions differed by about 2 hectopascals of pressure.

That pressure difference may seem small, but it can matter when forecasting compact weather systems.

The small lows were sensitive to pressure readings taken hundreds of miles to the east.

“These systems highlight the importance of collecting observations directly at sea,” Clementi said.

“The Ionian Sea and central Mediterranean have historically had limited coverage of in-situ atmospheric measurements, despite being areas where intense storms and persistent cyclones can develop.”

The authors call this a preliminary assessment. It rests on a single storm and a two-day rerun.

Four buoys received slightly negative scores after being deployed during relatively calm weather in late February, when their readings offered little opportunity to improve the forecasts.

The buoys are also a tiny fraction of everything the model takes in.

The team expects each one to count for more than a reading from a well-covered area, because it fills a gap.

Whether more buoys could help prevent forecasting errors like those seen in Tunisia remains uncertain.

The researchers now plan to focus on the small low-pressure systems that contributed to those errors.

Another 20 to 30 buoys are due to go into the Ionian and Tyrrhenian Seas starting this fall. The next Mediterranean storm will meet far more eyes at the surface.

The full study was published in the journal Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society.

#6315. ‘Exhumed’ recounts the true story of America’s first vampire

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A historian digs deep to show how fear shapes culture

Science, history and fear intersect in a new book from award-winning podcast creator Aaron Mahnke.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

October is my favorite month. I love when the leaves change colors and the air gets brisk. My hunger for media that sends a shiver down my spine is at an all-time high. This spooky season, I found satiation in Exhumed, a new book by historian Aaron Mahnke.

Mahnke draws on rich science-based history and folklore to show how fear of the unknown has shaped culture throughout history, even into the present day. He cites Taylor Swift, Twilight and other pop culture phenomena in his analysis — a choice that injects fresh air into the otherwise miasmic atmosphere. And thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Exhumed kicks off with the true story of America’s first “vampire.”

Walk with me for a moment back in time to Exeter, Rhode Island in 1892. Rampant tuberculosis is killing scores of people, including three members of the Brown family: matriarch Mary and her daughters, Mary O. and Mercy L. Then a son, Edwin, falls ill with the same symptoms — sparking concern that one of the women is an undead vampire who is sucking his life away. The town exhumes the bodies.

Mercy is surprisingly well-preserved. Her hair and nails appear longer and blood dribbles from her skin when it is pierced, “evidence” that confirms everyone’s worst fear: Mercy is indeed a vampire. (Nevermind that she perished in the dead of winter, when temperatures were probably cold enough to substantially slow decomposition.) The town burns Mercy’s heart, though it doesn’t save poor Edwin. These events helped inspire Bram Stoker’s Dracula, which was published five years later.

Interestingly, the cause of tuberculosis — a bacterium — was discovered a full decade before Mercy’s story unfolded. But news doesn’t always travel fast and entrenched beliefs can be difficult to change, even in the face of hard evidence. Exhumed explores this idea far beyond Mercy’s tragic tale.

Fear has led people to do some extremely odd things by today’s standards: burning hearts to kill “vampires,” setting boobie-traps in graves to prevent the dead from rising or drinking the blood of freshly hanged men to “cure” epilepsy.​ Without modern science to explain the unexplained, people often filled in the blanks with stories, Mahnke explains.

He implores readers to withhold judgement. After all, storytelling is one of the main ways that humans make sense of the world. “All of us, both then and now, are simply making the best of what we have, trying to find a way to improve our lives,” Mahnke writes.

Perhaps this practice continues today in different shades.

At one point, eating mummies, or “mumia,” was considered cure-all for most ailments —headaches, stomach troubles and general sickness. Is it too far from the expectations some people have of buying a “health shot” from Whole Foods? Not really!

More than a century after Mercy Brown’s heart was incinerated, we’re still clinging to stories and rituals that offer us a sense of control over the thing we fear most: death. Exhumed makes it clear that we haven’t outrun this instinct, we’ve just given it different packaging.

#6314. Telling wild frogs apart often means clipping toes, but one treefrog can be recognized by its eyes

An Amazonian treefrog’s golden eyes carry a distinct pattern of black lines, letting scientists recognize frogs without clipping their toes.

Field biologists who need to follow individual frogs often mark each one by clipping off a toe. In one Amazonian treefrog, the eyes carry a mark of their own.

The egg-eating spiny-backed frog, Osteocephalus oophagus, has golden irises crossed by thin black lines that spread out from the pupil, and the pattern differs from frog to frog, a bit like a fingerprint.

So a frog that has been photographed once can be picked out later from a picture of its eye, without cutting it and, most of the time, without touching it.

Mélissa Peignier, a researcher in the University of Bern’s Division of Behavioural Ecology in Switzerland, ran the project with eight colleagues, including first author Lauriane Bégué.

Over three rainy seasons in French Guiana, the team photographed the eyes of 103 frogs and recognized most of them again later in the same season.

Peignier first noticed the treefrogs while working on a different animal, a poison frog common in South American rainforests.

“At the time, I was doing my Ph.D., studying Allobates femoralis in the field in French Guiana,” Peignier said.

“My first reaction was simply something along the lines of, ‘Wow, what beautiful eyes!’ That initial curiosity gradually turned into a genuine interest in the species, and I realized how little we actually know about them.”

Wildlife researchers have long marked animals with tags, brands or clipped toes so they can tell them apart later.

For amphibians, toe-clipping has often been the standard method, even though it can affect a frog’s survival, body functions and behavior.

Osteocephalus oophagus spends its days in the forest canopy and comes down at night to about 6.5 feet (2 meters) above the ground.

“Other studies have used toe-clipping, which involves removing some of the digits. Personally, I was uncomfortable with this approach, especially given that these are arboreal frogs that rely on their limbs to climb trees,” Peignier said.

Many frogs can be identified by their skin markings, the way zebras can by their stripes, but this species’ back markings are faint, patchy and missing on some frogs.

Iris recognition was first built for people and has since been tested on geckos, cattle, goats and tigers. Frog irises had been used to tell species apart, but never to recognize individual frogs.

The fieldwork ran from March to May in 2021, 2022 and 2023. The team worked on a river island of about 12 acres (5 hectares) in French Guiana’s Nouragues Nature Reserve, near the Nouragues Ecological Research Station.

Male treefrogs come down from the canopy every night to call for mates. Females come down every four to seven days.

The team searched from 6:40 p.m. to 2 a.m. They checked 39 sets of small flowerpot pools set about 4 feet (130 centimeters) off the ground, along with tree hollows and other natural pools.

The first time a treefrog turned up, a researcher caught it by hand, photographed it and let it go where it was found. Close-ups of its eyes went into a photo library on a rugged tablet.

At every later meeting, the researchers photographed both eyes without touching the frog. If they found a match in the library, they left the frog alone. One eye was usually enough, and the second served as a check.

“Honestly, the frogs themselves are incredibly beautiful and surprisingly chill, which makes working with them a real pleasure,” Peignier said.

Across the three seasons, the team logged 392 captures of 103 different frogs. In 2021, 16 of 24 frogs were found and recognized again, later that season. This amounts to 66.7 percent of initial captures.

In 2022 the share was 47 of 59 (79.7 percent), and in 2023 it was 13 of 23 (56.5 percent) initial captures.

Every season, more than half of the frogs turned up again and were matched by their eyes alone. So the iris patterns stayed stable long enough for the team to follow frogs through a breeding season.

The researchers checked their identifications with Wild-ID, free software developed at Dartmouth College to match animals’ coat and skin patterns. They ran it once on left-eye photos and once on right-eye photos, so each eye was checked on its own.

Mating pairs of treefrogs posed no problem. The team could photograph a male clinging to a female’s back and didn’t have to pull the two apart.

When a pair did have to be handled at a first meeting, the frogs usually resumed their mating embrace within an hour.

Three frogs first caught in 2021 were found again in 2022. None of the 23 frogs seen in 2023 had been recorded before.

The three returning frogs showed little to no visible change in their irises. The team’s best explanation is that frogs moved away or were replaced by new ones, not that their eyes changed.

But the researchers used no second marking method, so they couldn’t tell whether missing frogs were still on the island and simply went unrecognized.

Results from other animals are mixed. Human iris patterns stay the same for life.

In Atlantic salmon, iris patterns held steady for only several months, while in one gecko species they stayed stable over the long term.

Several other frogs have complex irises, including Osteocephalus taurinus, Hyloscirtus tigrinus and Sachatamia ilex. But a pattern can be too complex to match quickly in the field, as may be the case for Trachycephalus hadroceps.

In contrast, the plain irises of the red-eyed treefrog, Agalychnis callidryas, may not differ enough from frog to frog.

The authors recommend testing the method species by species before it’s used more widely. Peignier hopes other researchers will adopt it.

“In a world where biodiversity is declining at an alarming rate, it is essential that we minimize our impact on the animals we study,” she said.

“If we can reliably identify individuals using naturally occurring features, we may be able to reduce the need for more invasive marking techniques while still collecting the data needed to answer important scientific questions.”

For O. oophagus, the open question is whether one photo can identify a frog for life. Answering it will take frogs studied in captivity, or eye photos paired with a second identification method, such as genetic testing or a permanent mark.

The full study was published in the journal Herpetozoa.

Rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what Mars-bound astronauts might face showed higher levels of scar tissue in their hearts, indicating they were more vulnerable to heart failure.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Exposure to space radiation may increase astronauts' risk of a dangerous heart condition, a new study in rats hints.

The research, published Sept. 30 in the journal PLOS One, found that rats exposed to levels of radiation similar to what an astronaut might experience on a long-term trip to Mars developed more scar tissue around the small blood vessels of their hearts than rats that were not exposed to this radiation. This scar tissue is indicative of a condition known as cardiac fibrosis, which is known to increase the risk of heart failure.

This scar tissue was observed nearly a year after the rats were first exposed to the radiation.

But since this study was in rats, it cannot definitively say whether this effect will play out in humans. For example, given that humans have a longer life expectancy than rats (80 years versus 2 to 4 years), the effects seen in rats may take around 30 years to show up in humans. However, the study authors say the research highlights the importance of following astronauts' health long after they return to Earth.

"The message that we try to convey … is that the follow-up time is really important," study co-author John Baker, a professor of surgery in the Radiation Bioscience Laboratory at the Medical College of Wisconsin, told Live Science. "When astronauts come back to the Earth, they expect ‪—‬ and we expect ‪—‬ that they're going to live for a long time. I think we have to be wary that they could well develop at least some type of cardiac disease."

The link between exposure to radiation and cardiac issues has been well documented. However, "no astronaut has ever been exposed to galactic cosmic radiation for long periods of time," Baker said, which makes it difficult to determine exactly how space radiation affects the heart.

Although Baker and his team previously pinpointed cardiac issues among rats exposed to radiation, this new study utilized NASA's Simulated Galactic Cosmic Ray Simulation (SimGCRSim). This new simulator provides a more precise comparison of the levels of space radiation an astronaut might experience while exploring deep space for more than a year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

During the study, the researchers exposed rats to several minutes of radiation proportionate to their size, similar to what they might experience on a trip to Mars and back (a roughly 18-month round trip, with current technology). Some of the rats' hind legs were suspended, to "simulate conditions of weightlessness," Baker said.

After 360 days, the rats that were exposed to cosmic radiation developed twice as much scar tissue around the heart's small blood vessels than unexposed rats. This buildup of scar tissue means "the heart can't relax to the point when it needs to," thereby increasing the risk of heart failure, Baker said.

This effect was not seen in the rats who were exposed only to simulated weightlessness, confirming "it was only the radiation that produced the damaging effect on the heart," Baker said. However, long-term testing revealed that this group of rats had lower levels of key immune cells, suggesting that microgravity also may affect aspects of long-term health. (Numerous studies have shown various short-term health impacts related to microgravity.)

This study "is a very valuable contribution to space biology," Rupak Pathak, an associate professor of pharmaceutical science at the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences who was not involved in the study but holds a doctorate in radiation biology, told Live Science. While rats and humans have clear differences, "they share more than 90% of genetic information," he said, as well as very similar cardiac systems.

Given that the study authors were able to expose the rats to radiation only once, Pathak would like to see further experiments exploring whether chronic radiation exposure affects the function of the heart and other vital organs.

Baker and his colleagues hope that future experiments can be used to help NASA implement safeguards for astronauts on long-term missions, such as providing astronauts heart medications or improving shielding for the spacecraft.

"The more we know before we start, then the better NASA is going to be at working out what types of countermeasures can be developed," said Baker.

#6311. NASA’s Psyche spacecraft is heading to a metal-rich asteroid using gentle engines that push with the weight of an AA battery

NASA’s Psyche spacecraft now runs on nearly nonstop thrust, powered by sunlight and xenon, on its way to a metal-rich asteroid by 2029.

Standard spacecraft thrusters burn a lot of fuel in short, powerful bursts. NASA’s Psyche spacecraft does the opposite. From now until it arrives, its engines will run almost nonstop, with a push no stronger than the weight of a single AA battery in a person’s hand.

The tiny push adds up. It will carry Psyche to the metal-rich asteroid it’s named after, in the main asteroid belt, by the summer of 2029.

Psyche switched to nearly constant thrust on Sept. 28, according to a NASA mission update. Once a week, the spacecraft pauses to check in with mission controllers on Earth.

Don Han is the Psyche mission’s navigation lead at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, which Caltech runs for the agency.

“It’s now ‘pedal to the metal’ to the asteroid Psyche,” Han said. “We will be running our propulsion system at every available opportunity, pausing only for necessary engineering activities. The thrusters will be operating nearly 90 percent of the time from now until we reach the asteroid.”

After the October 2023 launch, the lab’s team used the thrusters on and off to steer NASA’s Psyche toward the right spot near Mars.

This past May, the spacecraft passed within 2,864 miles (4,609 kilometers) of the Martian surface. Mars’ gravity sped it up and changed its path slightly, without costing any propellant.

Each thruster uses electromagnetic fields to push out atoms of xenon, a gas that doesn’t react easily with other substances.

The atoms carry an electric charge, which makes them ions. Pushing them out creates thrust and a bright blue glow. Engineers call this kind of engine a Hall-effect thruster.

NASA’s Psyche carries four of them and fires one at a time. Each one’s push tops out at 250 millinewtons, the force of that AA battery’s weight in one’s hand.

Because the thrusters provide a gentle but continuous acceleration over years, and there is little resistance in space, the spacecraft’s speed keeps climbing.

At its fastest during the cruise, Psyche will be moving more than 100,000 mph (160,900 kph) compared with someone watching from Earth.

That’s fast enough to circle Earth’s equator about four times in an hour.

The power comes from two cross-shaped solar arrays of five panels each. Together they collect sunlight across 800 square feet (75 square meters), roughly the floor size of a one-bedroom apartment.

The electricity charges the batteries and runs the thrusters.

Sunlight fades with distance. Steve Snyder, the mission’s lead engineer for propulsion operations at JPL, said the thrusters will run at full power for about three more months.

After that, they’ll slowly throttle down to about half power as Psyche gets farther from the Sun and its arrays make less electricity.

Psyche left Earth with nearly 2,400 pounds (1,090 kilograms) of xenon in seven tanks. In three years, it has used about a third of that supply. The rest is enough to finish the trip and to support two years of science at the asteroid.

As the xenon ions leave, the thruster’s magnetic field makes them swirl, and the swirl creates a slight twisting force called torque. Left alone, that twist would throw off the direction the spacecraft is pointing.

Psyche handles it with reaction wheels, spinning wheels inside the spacecraft. By speeding up or slowing down, they absorb the extra twist.

After several hours, too much of that motion has built up. So engineers have the spacecraft shut off its thruster and rotate.

It then runs a different thruster at low power, aimed another way, for several minutes. That clears the built-up motion out of the reaction wheels.

“For a propulsion engineer, it’s a fun thing that you can only measure this torque in space and not on Earth, as it’s so small,” Snyder said.

“In fact, this is the first time anyone has been able to measure this effect on a Hall thruster as a function of power level and of operating time, and for such a long duration in space.”

Early in the solar system’s history, planets grew from smaller bodies called planetesimals. Scientists think the asteroid Psyche, about 173 miles (280 kilometers) across at its widest, is part of the core of one of them.

Earth has a metal core too, but it can’t be seen or measured directly. If Psyche proves to be the metal core of an ancient planetesimal, it could give scientists a one-of-a-kind look inside rocky planets like ours. Understanding iron cores is one of the mission’s goals.

Lindy Elkins-Tanton of the University of California, Berkeley is the mission’s principal investigator, the scientist in charge.

“The Mars flyby was an incredible opportunity for the team to calibrate instruments and practice procedures for a planetary encounter ahead of arriving at the asteroid Psyche,” Elkins-Tanton said.

“Now we are cruising with confidence deeper into the solar system, powered by sunlight, ready to explore a mysterious new world in the asteroid belt.”

Whether the asteroid really is a leftover core is still an open question.

Answering it will have to wait for 2029. Once Psyche arrives, it will put itself into orbit and map the asteroid from a series of orbits, first dropping lower and later climbing higher.

Information from an online NASA mission update.

#6309. Evolution may work very differently than scientists thought

Scientists propose a surprising new way species may evolve, revealing how changes in body size could drive evolutionary divergence without competition.

Many stories about how one species branches into several eventually land on the same driving force: competition. Two populations start fighting over the same food, the same space, the same mates.

The losers adapt or disappear. It’s a tidy narrative – but Bryan Jennings, an evolutionary biologist at the University of California, Riverside, thinks it skips a chapter.

Jennings has spent years puzzling over a gap in adaptive radiation theory – the framework that explains how one ancestor species can fan out into many.

Darwin’s finches are the textbook example: different beak shapes for different seeds, sculpted by competition.

But what happens before two species even share the same turf? What sets the divergence in motion?

In a new study, Jennings proposes that the answer is deceptively simple: a change in body size. And the consequences of that change, he argues, are far wilder than anyone predicted.

Here’s the thing about growing bigger or smaller: your parts don’t all follow the same script. A human baby’s head is enormous relative to its body; by adulthood, the proportions have shifted dramatically.

The same logic applies across species. As organisms evolve different body sizes, their traits – tail length, limb proportions, beak shape – scale at different rates. Biologists call this allometry.

Jennings initially hypothesized that when one population evolves a different body size, its traits would change proportionally.

This process is called geometric scaling. Think of it like enlarging a photograph. Everything gets bigger, but the ratios stay the same.

His data, however, told a very different story.

To test his hypothesis, Jennings turned to pygopodid lizards. These are bizarre, snake-like creatures found across Australia and New Guinea that have lost nearly all their limbs over evolutionary time.

In some species of the genus Delma, tails can reach 4.5 times the length of the body. That extreme variation made them perfect subjects.

The work had roots in Jennings’s PhD research at the University of Texas at Austin, but the theory crystallized during COVID-19 lockdowns in 2020, when he revisited the data alongside classic work by Stephen Jay Gould on geometric similarity.

To push the analysis further, he secured funding for a 40-day museum blitz across Australia in 2023, measuring more than 1,000 preserved specimens at six institutions.

A follow-up visit to Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology brought the total to 1,755 specimens spanning 31 species.

He tracked three traits tied to locomotion and predator escape: snout-to-vent length, tail length, and body girth. Across 126 pairwise species comparisons, the results were unambiguous.

The geometric-scaling-first model predicted that recently diverged species would show proportional trait changes. Instead, Jennings found the opposite.

Among the six most recently diverged species pairs – those that split less than two million years ago – none consistently followed the geometric scaling pattern across all three traits.

When Jennings estimated interspecific scaling slopes for these pairs, only 3 of 18 measurements (17%) even roughly approximated geometric scaling.

A full 72% showed what he calls “reverse evolutionary allometry.” The trait changes were far more extreme than proportional scaling would predict.

“Rather than simple geometric scaling, the data showed evidence of a more extreme decoupling between trait development and body-size evolution,” Jennings said.

“I call this broader process disassociational scaling.”

Jennings’s revised model proposes two stages.

First comes disassociational scaling: a population evolves a different body size, and the relationships between its traits begin to shift dramatically.

Tails that should scale proportionally don’t and body girth changes at rates nobody predicted. The initial divergence is messy and extreme.

Then comes re-adaptation. Natural selection steps in over longer evolutionary timescales to fine-tune those scrambled proportions, restoring or improving trait function.

The data were consistent with this proposed sequence.

Among species pairs that diverged over two million years ago, 63% to 90% of trait relationships had shifted toward the more stable evolutionary patterns the model predicted for later stages.

“In other words, competition between species is not necessary for the initial divergence,” Jennings said.

The implications stretch well beyond Australian lizards.

If a simple change in body size can dramatically reshuffle an organism’s proportions, some of those new trait combinations might accidentally unlock access to entirely different ecological resources.

“If changes in body size produce substantial changes in the proportions of traits, those changes could sometimes result in trait combinations that allow a population to exploit a different ecological resource,” he said.

“I call this proposed process ‘niche scaling’ when it occurs in the context of adaptive radiation.”

“Competition could subsequently refine those differences through natural selection. Instead, I’m proposing that an important part of the story occurs earlier – when one population first begins diverging from another.”

Jennings is careful to position his theory as a complement to existing ideas, not a replacement.

Competition and natural selection still matter, but competition may not be necessary to initiate the divergence.

“My theory more fully accounts for beak evolution in the iconic Darwin’s finches and antler evolution in the enigmatic, extinct Irish elk,” he said.

“We still need to determine how widespread disassociational scaling and niche scaling are across different groups of organisms.”

The study is published in the Evolutionary Journal of the Linnean Society.

#6308. Forests planted to fight climate change may be fueling wildfires

A global study reveals that planting forests can increase wildfire risk, threatening carbon storage and challenging climate strategies.

There’s something darkly ironic about planting a forest to store carbon and watching it go up in flames.

But new research suggests that planting trees can sometimes increase wildfire risk, threatening the very carbon those forests were meant to store.

A new global study reveals just how much that risk varies across different landscapes.

An international team of researchers from Spain, Chile, and Finland analyzed satellite records spanning more than two decades to track what happens when non-forested land gets converted into planted forests.

Their dataset was enormous: 67,248 patches across the world’s temperate regions, monitored from 2001 to 2023 using MODIS land-cover and fire records.

After accounting for climate, accessibility, and patch size, afforestation was associated with a 26% increase in fire occurrence per hectare per year and a 23% increase in expected burned area when fires did ignite.

“Forest plantations change the fuel conditions in which fires start and spread,” said lead author Irene Repeto-Deudero from the University of Cádiz and the University of Eastern Finland.

“We wanted to understand how these changes differ across landscapes, rather than assuming that tree planting has the same consequences everywhere.”

Those global averages, though, hide enormous variation. The researchers compared fire patterns across four major types of temperate landscapes.

Temperate conifer forests took the worst hit. Fire occurrence there surged 2.7-fold, and the expected burned area roughly doubled.

These landscapes already contain large amounts of vegetation and face increasingly extreme fire weather.

Adding dense plantations can create more continuous fuel, allowing fires to spread more easily.

Mediterranean forests, woodlands, and scrub saw a 38% jump in fire occurrence and a 9% rise in burned area. In absolute terms, the probability of fire per 100 hectares over a decade climbed from 7.8% to 11.0%.

These regions already contend with seasonal drought, flammable vegetation, and frequent human-caused ignitions.

Piling more biomass onto that tinderbox gives extreme fire weather more fuel to work with.

Temperate broadleaf and mixed forests told a stranger story. Fire occurrence actually dropped by 23% after afforestation – but expected burned area grew by 20%.

Fewer fires, in other words, but the ones that did ignite burned larger. That trade-off matters more than it might seem.

Nearly half of the world’s planted forests sit in this biome. Even modest shifts in fire behavior could carry substantial consequences.

Temperate grasslands, savannas, and shrublands were the one bright spot. There, fire occurrence fell 18% with no significant increase in burned area.

“These contrasting responses show why local ecological conditions must guide afforestation decisions,” explained study co-author Alejandro Miranda from the University of La Frontera.

“The same intervention can have very different consequences depending on the vegetation, climate, and existing fire regime.”

Geographically, the increases in wildfire activity clustered in regions that are already under fire stress.

These include western North America, central Chile, southern Europe, southwestern Australia, and parts of South Africa.

In these regions, expanding plantations and increasingly dangerous fire weather could combine to intensify wildfire risks.

The study also highlights a data point that deserves more attention. Plantations are roughly twice as likely to burn as native temperate forests.

And monoculture plantations – single-species stands planted in uniform rows – have been linked to particularly extreme fire behavior.

All of this creates a serious accounting problem for climate policy.

Afforestation has become a flagship mitigation strategy, with temperate regions identified as high-priority planting zones.

But wildfires don’t just destroy trees. They also release stored carbon back into the atmosphere, potentially reducing or even reversing the climate benefits of tree planting.

“These results therefore require that tree planting initiatives consider their exposure to fire,” said Susana Gómez-González from the University of Cádiz.

“As the climate warms, increased wildfire risk may impact the capacity of forest plantations to store carbon in the long term.”

Planted forests provide wood, protect soil, and deliver a range of ecosystem services. The point isn’t to stop – it’s to think harder about where to plant them.

“Plantations are necessary in many cases to produce wood and other ecosystem services, including soil protection,” said Blas Mola-Yudego from the University of Eastern Finland.

“However, their location must be carefully planned to avoid unintended consequences on local fire regimes.”

“Fire risk needs to be considered from the outset, alongside production goals and environmental benefits.”

The findings challenge the assumption that planting more trees automatically delivers greater climate benefits.

In some landscapes, the additional wildfire risk could undermine the carbon gains that plantations are meant to provide.

For policymakers counting on planted forests to help combat climate change, the message is clear: where trees are planted may matter just as much as how many are planted.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
