#6307. This Halloween, amateur astronomers may be in for a dwarf planet treat

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Astronomers also have their eyes on objects near Neptune that may be solar system building blocks

This 3-D view of the solar system shows the orbit of the dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138 in the location it held on May 8, 2026. It is among the largest and brightest objects discovered beyond Pluto, but had gone unnoticed until now.

NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R. Proctor

The outer solar system is yielding its secrets to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

Less than five months into the observatory’s decade-long survey of the sky, a potential new dwarf planet has already popped up in its data, astronomers reported this week at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division of Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Another team reported a handful of new Neptune Trojans, icy objects that share an orbit with Neptune, at the meeting and in the Astrophysical Journal Letters. The findings are filling in astronomers’ picture of the Kuiper Belt at the solar system’s frigid fringes.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“It feels a little bit like we’re replicating the 1800s and early 1900s, discovering what the solar system even looks like in general,” says Sam Deen, an amateur astronomer based in Simi Valley, Calif. “We’re finding out what there even is in the first place that makes up most of the Kuiper Belt.”

Perched on a mountaintop in Chile, the Vera Rubin Observatory is on a mission to map the entire southern sky every couple of nights, searching for faint and fast-moving cosmic objects. The observatory took its first images in June 2025 and officially began a decade-long survey in June 2026.

Even before the official survey started, Rubin had detected the motion of an object orbiting billions of kilometers beyond Pluto. Rubin observed the object 30 times on 20 nights from March 4 to July 11. But no one knew it was there until October 13, when astrophysicist Matt Holman of the Smithsonian Astronomical Observatory in Cambridge, Mass., ran a search for moving dots of light in the data.

The object, called 2026 ED138, appeared to be about 47 times as far from Earth as Earth is from the sun. Its brightness suggests it’s between 600 and 1,500 kilometers wide, potentially as large as other dwarf planets like Ceres and Makemake. That’s probably big enough to be spherical, making it a dwarf planet.

“It’s really big. It’s damn huge,” Deen says. “No matter what you call it, it’s still the biggest thing we’ve found in the entire solar system in 19 years.”

When Holman realized what he had found, he was thrilled but doubtful. “It’s quite an exciting thing,” Holman said in a news briefing at the meeting on October 27. “But one of the things that you need to do when you discover something potentially of this size is to try to verify that it’s true.”

Holman and colleagues were able to find observations of the same object in archived data from the Dark Energy Camera, located on an adjacent mountaintop in Chile, taken in 2016.

Deen was able to trace it back even farther, to photographic plates taken as part of a sky survey at Palomar Observatory in California in 1954. Other amateur astronomers independently found the same sightings.

“They took an image from Palomar in 1954, and another about half an hour after the first one, that both by pure chance happen to point at where ED138 is,” Deen says. “And it’s really obvious. If you know it’s supposed to be there, it’s not particularly faint.”

So why didn’t anybody notice it until now? It’s partly because ED138 practically crawls across the sky, orbiting the sun once every 280 years. It was also moving against a dense background of Milky Way stars, where it blended in.

By combining observations spanning decades, astronomers can calculate the object’s orbit with more precision.

Deen is hoping to observe the potential new dwarf planet pass in front of a distant star on Halloween. That sort of observation, called an occultation, can help reveal more details of the putative dwarf planet’s size and shape, and even whether it has moons or rings. Usually, it takes years to understand an object’s orbit well enough to predict an occultation, Deen says. “Getting to do it immediately is like being a kid in a candy shop, really.”

Caltech, Space Telescope Science Institute

Caltech, Space Telescope Science Institute

A crop of newly spotted Neptune Trojans were masked by the Milky Way, too. These asteroids gather in the same orbit as Neptune, but offset from the planet at 60 degrees. Astronomers think they were some of the original building blocks of the solar system and contain an ancient record of planetary formation and evolution.

Other planets have Trojans, too. Jupiter has thousands. Astronomers think Neptune has many more, but so far they have seen only 30 in the cluster of space objects that orbit ahead of Neptune, and just two in the cluster behind it.

“We would expect these [groups of Trojans] to be symmetric in numbers, so you have to get more than two,” planetary scientist Meg Schwamb said in a news conference at the meeting on October 28.

The trailing cloud happened to have been moving in front of the Milky Way from the perspective of Earth for the last 15 years. Spotting individual Trojans against that crowded background was “like finding a needle in a sequined dress,” said Schwamb, of Queens University Belfast in Northern Ireland.

Schwamb and colleagues examined Vera Rubin data taken from the commissioning phase — the period when engineers were testing the telescope. In this early data haul, the team found two more trailing Trojans, plus one candidate. They seem to be similar in composition to the leading ones, which matches theories of how the solar system formed.

“It just kind of got lucky,” Schwamb said. “These objects photobombed the commissioning survey.”

“This is really the appetizer for what Rubin Observatory is going to do in its mission for the next ten years,” she added. “There’s hundreds more of these objects likely to be found.”

Some of the excitement about these discoveries is dampened by fears of losing observations to bright satellites crisscrossing the telescope’s field of view, says astronomer Sam Lawler of the University of Regina in Canada.

“I have to put in the constant downer of how the increasing numbers of satellites will make these discoveries harder,” Lawler says. “There are one hundred new satellites launching every week, and they keep getting bigger and brighter. These discoveries will be hindered by that.”

But even with the satellites, Lawler anticipates many more cool discoveries from Rubin.

“Just finding a dwarf planet so quickly, maybe we’ll find something even bigger,” she says. “There could be something the size of Mars out there. And then we’d have the whole planet debate all over again. It would be fun.”

An American astronaut on board the ISS recently snapped a spectacular "fireball" streaking across the nighttime sky over West Africa. The striking "light show" shows a Russian rocket being vaporized as it reenters the upper atmosphere.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What's in the photos? Space debris from a Russian rocket burning up upon reentry

Who took the photos? NASA astronaut Chris Williams

Earlier this year, an astronaut on board the International Space Station (ISS) snapped some striking photos, and an eerily beautiful video, of a "fireball" streaking over Earth as chunks of space debris burned up in the nighttime sky.

NASA's Chris Williams, who lived and worked on the ISS between November 2025 and July 2026, captured the eye-catching images from the station's cupola — a large, roughly dome-shaped series of windows that constantly points down at our planet — and later shared them on the social media platform X.

"Just as we were passing over West Africa, I saw a bright object directly below us, streaking through the upper atmosphere," Williams wrote in the post. "I saw its tail grow and then split apart into a shower of smaller pieces," he added. "It was quite a light show!"

Williams initially peered down at Earth to catch a glimpse of the Russian cargo spacecraft Progress 95, which successfully delivered essential supplies and additional equipment to the ISS later the same day. Instead, he saw what he believed was "some piece of orbital debris or a satellite breaking up as it entered the atmosphere."

Live Science's sister site Space.com later revealed that Williams had actually witnessed the burning remains of the Russian Soyuz rocket that had carried Progress 95 into space, after it lifted off from a recently repaired launchpad at the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.

The Soyuz rocket launched the cargo spacecraft Progress 95, which later docked with the ISS. (This photo shows the Progress 46 mission docking with the station in 2011.)

Shortly after deploying the resupply shuttle into low Earth orbit, the rocket's fairings and booster fell back toward our planet as expected, breaking apart into smaller pieces that were superheated and later vaporized by intense friction as they hit the upper atmosphere, according to Space.com. A very similar fireball was seen above Australia in August 2023, when another Soyuz rocket reentered the atmosphere.

Russia's prior resupply mission, Progress 94, also made headlines earlier this year when one of its antennae failed to deploy after separation from its Soyuz rocket, forcing cosmonauts (Russian astronauts) to use a remote control "backup system" to dock the spacecraft to the ISS.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Historically, the only fireballs visible in Earth's skies have been those caused by meteors, which can similarly break apart in flames. We were recently reminded of this when fireballs were spotted above the U.S. this spring, including one space rock that exploded with a massive sonic boom over Ohio and another that crashed through the roof of a house in Houston. (A NASA statement said the fireball Williams witnessed also may have been caused by meteor activity but was more likely to be the Soyuz rocket.)

However, fireballs from human-made objects are becoming more common. The number of spacecraft orbiting Earth has skyrocketed (pun intended) in recent decades, and "what goes up must come down."

Williams' photographs show how the remains of the Soyuz rocket exploded in a bright flash before stretching out into a train of flaming debris.

Most spacecraft and large pieces of space junk burn up around 50 miles (80 kilometers) above Earth's surface — just below the imaginary boundary with space, known as the Kármán line. While this may lead to visually stunning spectacles like the one Williams captured, scientists are starting to realize that these fireballs may be having a bigger impact on the upper atmosphere than they previously expected.

In recent years, researchers have detected a sharp increase in atmospheric metal pollution from vaporized spacecraft. And while they are still trying to figure out what effect this may have, some scientists have proposed that it could affect the ozone layer or potentially alter Earth's magnetic field.

Additionally, as the number of falling spacecraft rises, the chances that debris may fall to Earth's surface — after failing to properly burn up upon reentry — also increase. This came to the fore in March 2024, when the remains of a 3-ton battery pack that was discarded from the ISS crashed into a family home in Florida.

This 2011 astronaut photo captured one of NASA's iconic space shuttles passing between Earth and the International Space Station for the very last time.

During the Sept. 11 attacks, NASA astronaut Frank Culbertson — the only American not on Earth at the time — snapped a "sobering" shot of smoke pouring across New York City as the second tower fell.

A 2016 satellite photo shows Hurricane Madeline and Hurricane Lester heading straight toward Hawaii. When viewed from above, the twin cyclones and the surrounding clouds look eerily like a giant smiley face.

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. #6304. Eliminating invasive rats could help islands survive rising seas

Removing invasive rats could help protect low-lying islands from rising seas by restoring seabirds, boosting coral reef growth, and increasing sand production.

Low-lying atoll islands are usually written off as the first places a rising sea will cover. Around some of them, though, the coral reef is growing fast enough to keep pace with the sea through the end of this century.

One important factor is whether invasive rats have driven away the island’s seabirds.

Where seabirds nest, their droppings feed the reef.

Lagoon reefs there build upward almost twice as fast as reefs beside rat-overrun islands and produce more than twice as much sand.

Native forests produce more than four times as much fine root growth as areas dominated by coconut palms. This can hold the island’s soil in place.

Nick Graham, a marine ecologist at Lancaster University‘s Lancaster Environment Centre, led a team that measured all three factors on 28 islands in the Indian and Pacific Oceans.

The team compared islands as they are today, with and without rats.

“Atoll islands are not static, they are naturally active systems that can change and adapt to their environmental conditions if they are allowed to do so,” Graham said.

Boobies, frigatebirds, terns and noddies feed at sea, up to 620 miles (1,000 kilometers) from the island where they nest. They come home to roost, and the guano they deposit on the island contains nitrogen.

On islands with the largest seabird colonies, their droppings deposited more than 320 pounds of nitrogen per acre (366 kilograms per hectare) each year.

Rats that arrived on ships eat seabird eggs and chicks, and on most atolls the bird colonies are gone. Many islands have also lost their native forest to coconut plantations.

These palms now make up about 60 percent of the forest on Pacific atolls.

The team counted nests on islands in the Seychelles, the Chagos Archipelago and Tetiaroa Atoll in French Polynesia.

Islands with no rats and mostly native forest got the heaviest rain of bird nitrogen. The rest got very little.

Corals near seabird islands photosynthesized more and laid down more limestone skeleton. From that, the team estimated how fast each reef could build upward.

Lagoon reefs beside rat-free islands rose by an estimated 0.23 inches (5.9 millimeters) a year.

This is 1.8 times the rate of reef rise beside rat-infested islands. Ocean-facing reefs showed a smaller and less certain edge.

For the central Indian Ocean, the sea is projected to rise about 0.24 inches (6 millimeters) a year by 2100 if the world warms by 2°C (3.6°F).

The bird-fed lagoon reefs could nearly match that. The reefs beside rat islands, however, are predicted to fall short of even today’s rise of about 0.16 inches (4 millimeters) a year.

A reef that keeps pace with rising seas helps weaken waves before they reach the shore.

“The study shows beautifully how atolls are an intimately interconnected island-reef system, a geo-ecological system,” said Yadvinder Malhi, an ecologist at the University of Oxford and a co-author.

Parrotfish scrape coral and excrete it as sand. On some Indian Ocean reefs they produce up to 85 percent of the new sand.

Around islands with seabirds, parrotfish had more energy available, and the surrounding reefs produced 2.3 to 2.8 times as much sand.

In an interview with Earth.com, Graham was asked what surprised him most.

“The increase in sediment production by seabirds was something that had not been investigated before, and the increase is quite dramatic,” he said.

He put a figure on it for a hypothetical island of about 35 acres (14 hectares), roughly three quarters of a mile long.

With seabirds present, the surrounding reefs would produce about 220 cubic yards (170 cubic meters) more sediment each year than reefs around an island without seabirds. That’s roughly 20 dump truck loads.

“That is a really meaningful quantity,” Graham said.

Not all of that sand reaches the beach. The grains on the reef and the grains on the shore match closely, though, which points to a steady supply.

On Tetiaroa, the team measured fine roots in forest plots for two years.

Where native trees such as Pisonia grandis covered more than 75 percent of the ground, each square yard of soil held an estimated 8.2 miles (13.2 kilometers) of fine root.

Where native cover was below 75 percent, the figure was 1.8 miles (2.9 kilometers).

Coconut palms have short, rounded root systems. Native broadleaf trees grow long, dense roots that hold sand in place when storm waves wash over an island.

Seabirds strengthened that effect. With plenty of bird nitrogen in the soil, root growth rose by about 9 percent for every extra 1% of native forest cover. With few birds, more native forest didn’t change root growth at all.

The reef growth and sand figures come from six islands in the Chagos Archipelago, and the root figures from 19 forest plots on five islands of Tetiaroa.

The team inferred the gains from islands that already differ, rather than following one atoll from rat eradication through to a faster-growing reef.

How much reef sand actually reaches an island, and how reef growth changes the scouring of a shoreline, still have to be measured. Island size and local currents also shape what happens to any one atoll.

Jennifer Appoo, a co-author at the University of Seychelles, said the results matter most where seawalls and other engineering are unaffordable or out of place.

Many of the Seychelles’ atolls are uninhabited or sparsely inhabited, she said.

Graham told Earth.com that eradicating invasive predators such as rats should be the top priority for island managers.

It helps the island’s wildlife and the reef around it, he said, and this study shows it can boost the islands’ climate resilience too.

“I think what is key here from a policy perspective is that restoring atoll islands can have major gains in two core areas: biodiversity conservation, and climate adaptation,” he said.

Rats have already been removed from about 1,000 islands worldwide.

Asked by Earth.com which islands he is watching next, Graham said he has just started an Island-Ocean Research Hub at Lancaster.

It will study islands from the tropics to the Arctic, in the Seychelles, the Red Sea, the Mediterranean, the U.K. and Arctic Norway.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6303. The 9 Best Binoculars, According to Our Tests and Research

See the world in greater detail with one of these recommended models.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Despite ubiquitous satellite imagery, incredible smartphone cameras, and a video doorbell on almost every house, there’s still incredible power in witnessing something with your own eyes. Unfortunately, despite eyesight being our dominant sense, our optics have some real limitations. Binoculars are considered relatively old technology, but they’re still recognized as the best tool to reach for when identifying a far-off animal or examining details on a backyard bird.

Hunters use binoculars to spot and pick out details on their quarry thousands of yards away, birders confirm species they’re identifying, and stargazers zoom in on constellations. They’re also just handy to keep in your house or even your vehicle for those moments when you just want to “see for yourself.”

You can extend your vision with telescopes, spotting scopes, and even zoom camera lenses, but the comfort and ease of use are why binoculars have such enduring appeal. Monocular devices—spotting scopes, for instance—can put strain on your eyes after only a few minutes, while binoculars offer a much more natural extension of normal vision, making them more comfortable for long sessions and easier for beginners to use. Binoculars are also lighter than those similar devices, which makes them packable and portable for trips into nature where they offer a more intimate look at shy creatures.

The challenge in shopping for a pair of binoculars is the sheer number and diversity of options from big, high-powered zooms that require a tripod to pocket-sized budget versions and everything in between. To help you narrow your search, we dive into how to select a pair that fits within your price range and how you intend to use them. We also share our favorites from years of testing in the field.

I’m a lifelong hunter and wildlife enthusiast who uses binoculars year-round for hunting as well as volunteer wildlife surveys for bighorn sheep and goats. Long hours behind glass, as well as more than a decade of testing dozens of pairs of binoculars in the field for editorial reviews, have informed my picks, along with conversations with brand representatives and optics dealers. For this update of my long-running guide, I tested six new pairs of binoculars that are new releases from established optics brands. Not all of them made the cut here, but several did, including the Nikon Trailblazer II 10x25, the first time I enjoyed a microcompact binocular enough to include it.

The new Leupold BX-3 Alpine HD binoculars deliver premium-enough outdoor optics while maintaining a price point almost everyone can stomach. The BX-2 Alpine HD, which occupied that exact niche for years, did it well enough that it became my favorite binocular in the midrange category and my everyday hunting optic.

This is a compact, lightweight binocular with good clarity and low-light performance, which makes it a solid choice for basically everyone from birders to stargazers, even though Leupold tends to market mostly to hunters and target shooters. While not the cheapest bino on the market, it’s worth the upgrade over the lowest-tier optics and, like any Leupold optic, comes with a lifetime warranty, meaning it could conceivably be the last pair you’ll ever buy.

The BX-3 doesn’t reinvent anything, but Leupold subtly refined the binos, updating coatings, tweaking ergonomics, and adding a few quality-of-life improvements while keeping the same general form factor, magnification options, and modest price point that made the BX-2 so successful in the first place.

The price jumped up slightly with the release of the BX-3, so while I’d buy the BX-3 for the improvements if you’re paying full price, retailers appear to be deeply discounting the existing stock of BX-2s, so it’s worth considering the older model if there’s a great price on it, at least until retailers run out of the now-discontinued model.

Read the Full Review of the Leupold BX-3 Here

Zeiss is synonymous with good glass in consumer camera lenses and sport optics, so the mid-tier-priced Terra ED 10x42 binoculars are somewhat of a surprise in the manufacturer’s lineup. I’ve tested several higher-end Zeiss binoculars, which were unsurprisingly great given their price tags, but finding nearly as good clarity and color in this $500 pair was unexpected.

While $500 isn’t cheap for most casual binocular buyers, I’d argue getting Zeiss quality at this price presents a serious value if you’re looking for good glass but aren’t ready to put down a mortgage payment to get it.

The 10x42 Terra ED uses ED glass and Zeiss's hydrophobic multicoating to produce a bright, high-contrast image that will feel like a serious upgrade to budget options. It's not going to match the edge-to-edge perfection or low-light performance of Zeiss's flagship binoculars, but it delivers enough optical quality to be an obvious jump in clarity for the investment.

The 10x42 configuration is a versatile middle ground for hunting, hiking, birding, and general wildlife observation. The Terra ED has a 330-foot field of view at 1,000 yards and a 5.3-foot close focus, so it is adequate for birding, casual stargazing, and wildlife watching. At 25.6 ounces, it's also light enough to carry comfortably in a chest harness (not included) for long stretches without pulling on your neck.

The fiberglass-reinforced housing is waterproof and nitrogen-filled to minimize fog and condensation outdoors. The hydrophobic coating helps keep moisture from becoming a major distraction when you're using the binoculars in wet weather or going between temperature extremes. The large focus wheel is also easy to find and operate quickly.

The Terra ED isn't the cheapest 10x42 on the market, but that's not really the point. It's a relatively affordable way into a serious optics brand, and the difference is visible when you use them side by side with cheaper binos.

Most hunters don't need the biggest or most expensive binoculars they can buy, but many with the budget and obsession with the sport will spend thousands hoping expensive optics can buy success. While $3,000 binoculars are overkill for most, hunters do ask a lot of their optics. Early morning and late evening light and long distances expose the weaknesses of lower-quality glass, so many hunters get the advice to buy the best glass they can afford.

While the top-tier binoculars are undoubtedly better, there’s a mid-tier sweet spot that gives you most of the performance of those four-figure binos at a fraction of the price. The Vortex Viper HD 10x42 binoculars are squarely there. Vortex’s Triumph binoculars are our Best Budget pick above for the value they provide at $100, but dedicated hunters who get up early and stay out late will eventually want to upgrade.

The Viper HD 10x42s have a list price around $729, but can be found at most retailers for closer to $500, a good value for the upgrade. Still, that’s $400 more than the Triumph, so you’ll want to be sure you value the improvements. The benefits over cheaper options are better light transmission and reduced distortions such as chromatic aberrations. If you’ve used cheaper binos, you’ve seen off colors such as purple fringes on trees. In broad daylight, this isn’t a problem you can’t adjust your eyes to, but in low light and longer distances it can result in straining and struggling to tell a stump from a bear or deer.

A relatively low 24.9-ounce weight and compact form factor enabled by the roof prism design make these comfortable to carry in a chest harness over long days in the field or a tree stand. The rubber housing offers satisfactory grip and I notably appreciated the underside thumb grooves, though they don’t look as high-end as magnesium housings. The included chest harness is capable enough, but will be a throwaway for hunters who already own a specialized hunting chest rig.

Turned off by cheap compact binoculars in the past? These are worth it. They offer quality optics with powerful-enough magnification for bird-watching, hunting, and a range of everyday uses. In addition, they’re sealed, so they're waterproof and fogproof, and there is a lifetime warranty on the optical parts so you won’t need to replace them if you drop these binos even once.

Nikon’s Trailblazer II 10x25 compact binoculars make some compromises on field of view and low-light performance, but on the plus side, they’re small enough to fit in your pocket. These are binoculars you can toss in a daypack for when you want them, rather than committing to positioning them on you, front and center, and dealing with the weight.

The trade-off, however, is the 25mm objective lens. There's simply less glass available to gather light than you'll get with a 42mm binocular, and the field of view isn’t bad but feels cramped if you’re used to bigger binos. The 10mm eye relief also isn't particularly generous for eyeglass wearers. But for quick looks during daylight, the compact size makes these much easier to have on you when you need them.

Bigger is typically better when it comes to optical performance in binoculars, but there is always a give-and-take. With standard 10x42 or larger binoculars, you get better performance, but usually at least a pound of weight and a bulky item. Bird-watchers and hunters use chest harnesses to distribute the weight and keep them accessible, but that’s a commitment you don’t always want for a casual hike.

The Trailblazer II has a more palatable price at $130 than you’ll find with larger binos with similar optical quality, making these a no-brainer if you’re shopping for casual use.

Like Leupold, Vortex has a great reputation, in large part due to its accommodating lifetime warranty program—a comfort to those of us who are hard on our gear. One challenge with Vortex is the sheer number of lines and models, but the newer Triumph line is easy to understand: it’s the brand’s cheapest pair of binoculars in the 10x42 build and arguably its best value at $100. While the optical clarity and quality aren’t on par with that of the more expensive lines, the Triumph does surprisingly well, especially in daylight.

Like most cheaper binos, the clarity falls off the closer you get to the edges of the field of view, but is sharp and color-true in the center. Yes, you can spend less, but I wouldn’t recommend it, having tried a lot of $25 to $50 binoculars over the years. Despite the attractive price, the Triumph ships with a case, harness, and neck strap as well.

Full Vortex Triumph 10x42 Binoculars Review

Nikon is best known for its cameras and lenses, but this Japanese optics brand makes a wide range of excellent binoculars as well. I’ve tested several models over the years, but the Monarch M7 stands out for the optical clarity it delivers at a mid-tier price point.

Nearly any pair of binoculars will work for birding, but for most species, you’ll be in trees and fairly close quarters where higher magnifications can make it harder to spot and track birds with the more zoomed-in view. Even when you spot a bird, even the slightly tighter 10x magnification can make it harder to follow flight.

The 8x42 version of the Monarch M7 binos gives you enough magnification to confirm details without spooking wildlife, but the wide field makes it easier to track them. The M5 series is also good and about $200 cheaper, but it has a narrow field of view even in the 8x42 configuration.

Like most binoculars, they’re nitrogen-purged and O-ring sealed, which just means they’re waterproof and fogproof. (Note: Fogproof only means there won’t be interior fog. You can still steam up the glass if, for example, your face is warm and the air or binos are cold.)

More money can, of course, get you even better glass from Nikon and other companies, but this is one of the best mid-tier options that delivers a clear and comfortable birding experience. Less money will downgrade your clarity, but cheaper and smaller options that weigh and cost much less abound if those are your priorities. (The entry-level Nocs Provisions Standard Issue 8x25 binos, for example, weigh about half as much.)

There are times when 10x binoculars simply aren't enough—and that’s especially true in Western hunting country where the animal you're looking for might be thousands of yards across a canyon. A 15x binocular like Maven's C.4 gives you considerably more reach while retaining the depth perception and comfort of looking through both eyes.

Extra reach is the reason to buy these. At 15x, details that can be frustratingly ambiguous through a conventional 10x42 become much easier to pick apart. I've found high-power binoculars particularly useful for searching large expanses of terrain where the ability to use both eyes makes extended glassing considerably more comfortable than squinting through a spotting scope. At distances of a mile or more, you’ll still want a spotter that’s 20x and up, but the 15x is a meaningful middle ground that’s wide enough to use in a forest, but reaches far enough for big mountain hunting.

The C.4 combines 15x magnification with large 56mm objective lenses, giving it a 215-foot field of view at 1,000 yards. This is noticeably tighter than, for example, the 342-foot field of view of the Leupold BX-3 10x42s, but that’s by design and the trade-off for 50 percent more zoom.

The other big trade-off is the weight and size. At 45 ounces, they’re still lighter than a spotting scope, but you’ll likely also be carrying a tripod, which adds several pounds to your pack. Compare this to 10x42s, which are usually 1 to 2 pounds total, and it’s a big difference. Still, if you’re using binoculars to cover big mountain distances and need the clarity and zoom to identify animals precisely, it’s likely a weight penalty you’ll be willing to pay.

The ED glass and phase-corrected, dielectric-coated prisms produce a surprisingly sharp image, and the 92 percent light transmission is key around dawn and dusk—impressive for the price. Most high-quality, high-power binoculars are at least four figures, but Maven delivers the C.4 for $550. Unlike the rest of its line that uses Japanese and Chinese components that are assembled in Wyoming, the C.4 is produced entirely in China. Despite this difference, I didn’t notice a sharp drop-off in build or optical quality from other Maven binos I’ve tested.

There's a catch: These aren't really handheld binoculars. At 45.1 ounces, the C.4 is almost twice the weight of many conventional 10x42s, and 15x magnification makes even small hand movements obvious. I used the C.4 handheld fine for short periods, but the size and weight wear on your stability much faster than lightweight hunting binos. Once mounted, however, the extra weight only affects your pack and the C.4 becomes a remarkably capable long-distance optic.

Any decent pair of binoculars can enhance casual stargazing, but if you’re closer to “astrophile” than “occasional noticer of the night sky,” you’ll want a somewhat specialized pair and the best low-light performance you can afford. As binoculars go up in price, into the thousands, the returns are diminishing, giving you small increments of improved clarity and edge-case benefits, but they are better.

Celestron is a budget binocular brand, but its SkyMaster series is astro-focused and worth a look if you’re focused on stars. The massive objective lenses, high magnification, and Porro prism combine for a heavy build, but one that’s designed for night use at the distance of light-years.

The 25x magnification won’t be much good for backyard bird-watching or any handheld use, but they’re designed for tripod mounting, and for use as a stationary sky-watching setup that’s more comfortable for longer sessions than telescopes.

Going with binoculars for sky watching, especially ones as zoomed-in as these, adds a layer of dimensionality that’s lost looking with the naked eye (or with one eye as with telescopes). Unlike cheap Amazon optics brands, Celestron has friendly price points but still gives you a lifetime warranty. If your stargazing habit sticks, you may eventually want to upgrade to a higher-end model, but this pair will show you what you’ve been missing for a few hundred bucks.

Any decent pair of binoculars can enhance casual stargazing, but if you’re closer to “astrophile” than “occasional noticer of the night sky,” you’ll want a somewhat specialized pair and the best low-light performance you can afford. As binoculars go up in price, into the thousands, the returns are diminishing, giving you small increments of improved clarity and edge-case benefits, but they are better.

Unlike cheap Amazon optics brands, Celestron has friendly price points but still gives you a lifetime warranty. If your stargazing habit sticks, you may eventually want to upgrade to a higher-end model, but this pair will show you what you’ve been missing for a few hundred bucks.

Yes, this is an article about binoculars, but I humbly present the little-known monocular as a better tool for certain jobs. Like spotting scopes, monoculars aren’t as natural to use since you have to close one eye and miss out on the depth of a stereo picture. However, there are times when the weight and bulk of binos mean you leave them at home even though you might want them in the field.

I personally carry this Nocs Field Tube monocular every time I go backcountry skiing and find it quite literally worth its weight for scouting potential approach and descent lines, using it to pick out details about snow quality, avalanches, and terrain that my naked eye regularly misses. It’s also easy to throw in a pack or pocket for casual hikes or pre-hunting season scouting walks where I never know when I might want a closer look at something but am not motivated enough to harness up with my binoculars.

There aren’t a lot of companies making monoculars, but Nocs has several options. I love the 8x32 size of the Field Tube, but you can get a 10x32 version that offers a bit more zoom but a slightly narrower field of view in the same size package. There’s also the newer 8x32 Zoom Tube that’s significantly cheaper and slightly lighter and smaller but isn’t fully waterproof.

Not everything we test or like ends up in our buying guide, but some are products that still warrant a mention. Here are a few.

Vortex Crossfire HD 10x42: These budget binos fall between the Triumph and Viper models we recommend above. They’re solid optics for the cost, but in a no-man’s-land for the price. If you’re on a tight budget, the Triumph 10x42s are less than half the price and nearly as good. And if you’re looking to upgrade to the mid-tier, it’s worth saving up for the Vipers or the Zeiss Terra ED 10x42s for a more noticeable jump in quality in a compact all-arounder.Nocs Field Issue 10x42: Give us some fun colors and a grippy, overmolded texture like on these 10x42s. But similar to the Vortex Crossfire, they’re not enough of an improvement on our best budget pick to justify double the cost. If you like the design that stands out from a crowd of bland black options, you won’t be disappointed, but we prefer to pay for performance.Zeiss SFL 12x50: These are awesome high-end binoculars that pack a little extra zoom as well as a large, 50mm objective lens that pulls in extra light for early and late. They also are incredibly compact and light despite their specs. The problem is the $2,000 price tag that puts them out of reach of most casual users. They’re really good, just not 10 times as good as a solid $200 pair from our list above.

The magnifications of most consumer binoculars are fixed (i.e., not zoomable), making it one of the most important decisions for buyers. More isn't always better and can feel claustrophobic in tight quarters such as trying to track a small bird in dense forest, while wider-angle, lower-power lenses can feel underpowered if you're trying to see across longer distances.

Most binos range between 7x and 18x. Much less than 7x isn’t enough of an effect to bother with for most applications, while 15x and up becomes difficult to use without a tripod. In general, lower-power binoculars are a better fit if you’re mostly glassing shorter distances, such as in forests, and don’t need precise detail. Higher-power binoculars make sense if you’re looking to avoid also carrying a spotting scope and glassing longer distances up to a mile or need precise detail for identifying wildlife.

Objective lens diameter is the size of the lens farthest from your eyes and impacts the field of vision you get, as well as how bright the image is since, generally, bigger lenses capture more light. Jeremy Bentham, senior manager of SRO Sales & Operations for Nikon, explains the trade-offs associated with objective lens size.

“One of the key things that needs to be decided is brightness versus weight,” he says. “Larger objective lenses allow more light into the optic but are also heavier to pack and carry with you.”

Objective lens sizes in binoculars range anywhere from 20 mm to 100 mm, but the common sizes are mostly in the 30 mm to 60 mm range. I find ultracompact binoculars of less than about 30 mm annoying to use for more than a quick look at something nearby since the field of view is small and it can be harder to keep in position on your eyes. On the other end of the spectrum, most binoculars larger than about 55 mm become heavy and unwieldy if used without a tripod.

Binoculars are listed by size spec, where the first number is magnification and the second is objective lens diameter. Probably the most common size is 10x42, which permits a big enough field of view and magnification for viewing things as near as 15 feet but still allows you to spot larger objects such as wildlife as far as a mile away.

For backcountry hunters and hikers, weight is one of the most important considerations in a binocular. You need to balance the desire for a larger, brighter optic with your ability and interest to carry it around your neck over long distances. For me, anything heavier than about 35 ounces is too much to carry in a chest harness when actively hunting and covering several miles a day. If you’re a hunter or hiker who doesn’t need ready access to your binoculars and can keep them in a pack until you need them at specific spots, you may be able to tolerate heavier options.

Even folks who mostly use binoculars at home or from a vehicle need to consider weight. Heavier binoculars are harder to use for longer periods of time since your arms and shoulders do eventually fatigue and become shaky. If you’re mostly using binoculars on a tripod (a must for higher-magnification binos), you may want to prize optical quality over weight savings.

Aside from range-finding binoculars, most have surprisingly little tech as we usually think of it in terms of electronics and connectivity. What makes great binoculars hasn’t changed much over the years and still boils down to quality glass and craftsmanship.

Where tech does show up is in the glass quality and the coatings used. High-tech coatings are used to make colors true, enhance brightness, and protect your expensive lenses. Coatings and glass often use nonstandardized terms such as ED, HD, and UHD glass, or proprietary branding such as LotuTec or Swarobright, making it hard to compare apples to apples when talking about something as subjective as optical quality. What you can look for is whether lenses are “fully multi-coated,” meaning that all glass surfaces have multiple coatings for durability and performance, whatever the branding.

#6302. Melting permafrost has birthed a new type of large landslide

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Wildfires and water underneath the ground could dislodge large chunks of frozen earth

In 2018, an immense landslide in Canada’s Mackenzie Valley dammed the Redstone River (shown) and created a 3.5-kilometer-long lake. Researchers say the event was a new type of large landslide called a permafrost detachment slide.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In 2018, a strange and enormous landslide occurred in Canada’s Northwest Territories. A slab of earth roughly equivalent in volume to seven Great Pyramids of Giza suddenly began sliding downhill, leaving behind a barren scar in the forested landscape. But what puzzled scientists was that the slide had initiated in frozen ground that had been glued in place for years.

An analysis of the event reveals that it represents a new class of catastrophic landslides called permafrost detachment slides, researchers report in the Sept. 28 Geophysical Research Letters. The slides may be set in motion by wildfires that occurred decades earlier, destabilizing the ground and opening cracks through which water infiltrated deep underground. Over time, that water may have thawed the frozen layer from below, eventually unleashing the entire frozen layer in a catastrophic slide.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Large landslides don’t normally mobilize so much still-frozen material, and when they do begin in thawing layers they usually move slowly, says Dmitry Nicolsky, a geophysicist studying permafrost at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who was not involved in the study. But he says this new research suggests scientists need to better study what’s occurring beneath the surface in permafrost regions, because “we don’t know how [the ground] will move — it might go slowly or it might go catastrophically.”

The inspiration for the research manifested in 2019, when permafrost geologist Joseph Young, based at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, at the time, was helicoptering to a field site in the Northwest Territories to assist a colleague’s research. In some of the valleys out there, the slopes were “just collapsing with landslides everywhere,” says Young, who is now at an engineering firm in Edmonton. That was surprising because they were in an area where the permafrost — ground that has been frozen for at least two consecutive years — shouldn’t have been thawing much.

Once on the ground, more puzzling details emerged. “Traditionally with permafrost, it melts from the top down, and that releases this slurry of muddy material,” Young says. But at some of the landslide sites, large blocks of still-frozen ground seemed to have been moved hundreds of meters, he says.

Young and his colleagues studied two of the largest slides in the region that had moved big chunks of permafrost. These were the 2018 slide, which mobilized 18 million cubic meters of earth and dammed the Redstone River, and another event in 2017 that moved 4.5 million cubic meters of material.

Field observations revealed that both events had initiated along flat sliding surfaces roughly 20 meters underground, where the permafrost layer’s base was identified. Meanwhile, satellite observations showed that the ground at both sites had been gradually moving meters each year for decades.

Young and his colleagues hypothesized that climate warming and wildfire had somehow played a role in causing the slides. They set up instruments nearby that tracked ground temperature from 2020 to 2022, focusing on spots either with undisturbed forest or where wildfire had burned about 25 years earlier.

They then plugged that data into computer simulations to estimate how the ground would have evolved in the decades after a fire. Based on the results, the researchers concluded that wildfire and extreme summer temperatures can warm and weaken the frozen ground surface, causing it to start creeping and form tension cracks. As these cracks grow, water can penetrate deeper into the frozen ground and eventually reach beneath the permafrost layer, causing it to thaw from below and eventually detach.

More than 150 other slides in the region, identified via satellite observations, may also have been permafrost detachment slides, Young says. This could occur wherever there’s a relatively thin and warm permafrost layer and a rapid warming event to set things in motion, he says.

Permafrost is thawing in cold regions around the world, and these huge slides are very visual manifestations of that, Young says. “This is a direct reality of a changing climate.”

J.M. Young et al. Recent intensification (2004 – 2020) of permafrost mass‐wasting in the central Mackenzie Valley foothills is a legacy of past forest fire disturbances. Geophysical Research Letters. 2022. doi: 10.1029/2022GL100559

NASA's Swift Observatory is about to make a fiery reentry through Earth's atmosphere after a private mission to save it failed. Most of the spacecraft will burn up in orbit.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note: As of 11:15 a.m. EST on Wednesday (Nov. 4), NASA and the Aerospace Corporation both predict that the Swift observatory could have reentered Earth's atmosphere by now. However, no new details on reentry have been provided. Stay tuned for more updates about where and when the telescope will fall.NASA's decades-old Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is rapidly falling out of orbit and could tumble back to Earth any moment now, the space agency says.

According to NASA's latest estimates, shared Monday (Nov. 2), the roughly 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) spacecraft was likely to reenter Earth's atmosphere around 3:30 a.m. EST Wednesday (Nov. 4), with an uncertainty of plus or minus 11 hours — meaning the defunct observatory could have plunged down as early as Tuesday evening, and as late as Wednesday afternoon.

An independent analysis from the private nonprofit Aerospace Corporation, which tracks thousands of objects in orbit, similarly estimates that the telescope should have reentered the atmosphere at 6:56 a.m. EST Wednesday, give or take three hours. Both estimates suggest the Swift spacecraft could have already met its demise as of Wednesday morning, though no official confirmation has been shared.

As with all spacecraft reentries, the risk to humans is minimal. Most of the Swift telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere, according to NASA. Any surviving fragments will likely fall somewhere between 20.6 degrees south latitude and 20.6 degrees north latitude — a range that includes parts of Mexico, the Caribbean, Central and South America, the Arabian Peninsula, India, Africa and Oceania, but also a lot of ocean.

NASA predicts that the chances of Swift debris falling over a populated area are approximately 1 in 2,100. For comparison, the odds of a person being struck by lightning in their lifetime are 1 in 15,300, according to the National Weather Service.

NASA will continue to update their predictions as the reentry window draws closer.

Swift has detected thousands of deep-space explosions, including sudden flares from neutron stars (illustrated here).

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is a multiwavelength optical, ultraviolet and X-ray telescope that launched in November 2004 on a mission to study the most powerful explosions in space. Initially designed for a two-year primary mission, the telescope ultimately spent more than 10 times that duration hunting for supernovas, gamma-ray bursts and black-hole-induced eruptions around the universe.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Swift has been rapidly losing altitude for more than a year, after rampant solar activity increased the drag on the aging spacecraft. This past August, a costly mission to boost Swift's orbit with a private spacecraft failed shortly after launch, hammering the final nail in Swift's coffin.

Engineers on the Swift team officially shut down the observatory's science operations on Oct. 20, after the spacecraft fell too low in orbit to continue taking steady observations of the sky.

As Swift goes out with a fiery bang, it leaves behind a trove of scientific data, including contributions to more than 7,000 scientific papers so far, according to NASA. This number will only increase as Swift's final observations are processed.

#6299. What is the physical size of a 1-billion-solar-mass black hole compared to the Sun?

When a supermassive black hole is measured as 1 billion solar masses, what would be its actual physical size relative to the size of our Sun?

The size of a black hole is generally taken to be the size of its event horizon. The event horizon is a mathematical boundary around the black hole that marks the “point of no return” — anything that crosses this boundary is trapped inside and becomes part of the black hole forever.

The size of the event horizon can be calculated from Einstein’s field equations, and it depends on (1) the mass of the black hole, and (2) how fast the black hole is spinning. For a nonspinning black hole that has the same mass as our Sun, the radius of the event horizon (also called the Schwarzschild radius) would be about 1.8 miles (3 kilometers). A nonspinning supermassive black hole that is a billion times more massive than our Sun would have an event horizon radius that is a billion times larger, or 1.8 billion miles (3 billion km). This is 4,300 times larger than the radius of the Sun, or about the typical distance between the Sun and Uranus. However, if a billion-solar-mass black hole is spinning very rapidly, then the radius of the event horizon would shrink by about 30% (to around 1.3 billion miles or 2 billion km) because of the way the black hole distorts and drags space around it.

It is important to note, however, that while the event horizon is considered the outer boundary of the black hole, the mass inside the black hole has likely collapsed into a much smaller size under its own self-gravity, often referred to as a singularity. But we don’t actually know if the mass has collapsed into an infinitely small point in space, and, unfortunately, we can’t really say more than that because our understanding of physics breaks down under the extreme conditions that are present inside a black hole. So we use the event horizon as a convenient reference for the black hole’s size, because everything inside the event horizon is part of the black hole.

Misty BentzProfessor of Physics and Astronomy, Georgia State University, Atlanta

#6298. How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

The gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.)

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.)

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

#6297. Sun Joe Electric Wood Chipper Review: Turn That Storm Cleanup Into Usable Mulch

This light-duty wood chipper is ideally suited and priced for the average yard.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

My backyard runs up to a wooded area. Although there are few trees on my actual property, any storm that comes through pushes twigs and branches from the wooded area onto my lawn. And with several large rose bushes to tend to, I have a fair amount of clippings to break down. Gathering this debris up in a large waste container has been my approach for cleaning up my yard. But leaving this debris on the curb to be hauled off to the local landfill or burning it in my fire pit seemed like a waste, especially since I have landscaping beds and a garden that could benefit from this yard waste.

Purchasing a gas-powered wood chipper to break this waste down into usable mulch felt like overkill. Plus, I didn’t have space to store a gas chipper, nor did I want to fork over $600 or $700 for one of these machines. Enter the Sun Joe CJ603E electric wood chipper.

It doesn’t have the wood-chipping power of a gas wood chipper like the Champion portable gas wood chipper or the Earthquake K32 wood chipper, but it does what I need it to do. It can chip small branches and twigs, and costs a fraction of a gas-powered wood chipper. Plus, it’s a manageable weight and size, so it’s easy to move around and store. I spent several months testing the Sun Joe for our Best Wood Chippers buying guide earlier this year and have been using it to assist with yard cleanup ever since. It’s proven to be up to the task.

What better way to test the Sun Joe CJ603E’s wood-chipping abilities than to feed it as many twigs and branches as possible? And since my property backs up to a densely wooded area, I had plenty of fodder for it to chew on. Keeping to its listed max branch diameter of 1.73 inches, I crammed dead, dry branches into the Sun Joe.

Along with its ability to chew up dead wood, I also wanted to see how it handled green material, so I used the CJ603E to break down clippings trimmed from several large rose bushes on my property. Lastly, I also considered how well the Sun Joe was able to chip material into bits that were small enough to serve as mulch.

The Sun Joe CJ603E is one of the easiest wood chippers I’ve tested. For starters, assembly took just a few minutes. It only weighs 38 pounds and sits on two wheels, so moving it from my garage to my backyard felt effortless compared to moving gas wood chippers that weigh well over 100 pounds. The Sun Joe CJ603E uses a standard wall outlet for power, so it requires an extension cord, which limits its range compared to a gas-powered model. That said, the CJ603E also starts at the push of a button, so there’s no wrestling with a pull starter. At about 3 feet tall assembled on its stand, the Sun Joe is roughly the size of a counter-height bar stool with a backrest. That’s much smaller than a full-size gas wood chipper, which is important for garages like mine that are strapped for space.

We at Popular Mechanics are already familiar with Sun Joe’s line of wood chippers, having tested an earlier model a few years ago. Sun Joe’s CJ603E is a clear upgrade. The addition of a pressure plate that forces branches and twigs up against the blades gives this updated model more cutting power than its predecessor. The results were noticeable during testing.

I began my testing with dried-out dead wood, beginning with smaller twigs before working up to larger branches. The Sun Joe handled it all well, even consuming branches that were pushing beyond its listed 1.73-inch-diameter capacity.

The CJ603E is a prolific eater. I was able to feed sticks into it continuously without having to wait for the blades to chew through already-loaded material. And since the machine pulls sticks into it, there’s no need to use a separate stick to push material down its throat (though the CJ603E does include one).

The CJ603E does have an Achilles’ heel, and that’s with thicker, greener branches that exceed 1.5 inches in diameter. This “wet” wood had a tendency to clog the output chute, creating torn pieces rather than cleanly cut chips. While this wasn’t a huge issue for me, it could be for someone who uses a wood chipper to clean up live branches brought down during a storm.

Another benefit of the CJ603E is that it operates more quietly than the loud gas-powered models I’ve tested and does not produce exhaust, though you should still wear hearing protection when operating it. The CJ603E also requires far less maintenance since it doesn’t use a gas engine.

The Sun Joe CJ603E produces wood chips suitable for mulching, but don’t expect them to have a uniform look. Depending on what I was chipping, the CJ603E produced anywhere from 1/2-inch- to 1-inch-long wood chips, which was coarser than I expected given its listed 21:1 reduction ratio. I also noticed that the CJ603E would allow some longer twigs to pass through without being completely chopped. Since these irregularities make the wood chips less ideal for use in decorative landscaping, I use them as a base layer with a top layer of commercial mulch in my landscaping.

Sun Joe’s CJ603E wood chipper does what it’s designed for well. It can chip branches and twigs up to 1.73 inches in diameter into wood chips for easy disposal or use as mulch. Its compact size and comparatively light weight make it easy to move from garage or shed to yard and back again, and it doesn’t take up a huge amount of space in a shed or garage.

Homeowners will also appreciate the ease of use an electric wood chipper offers compared to gas models, since there’s no gas-powered engine to start or maintain. These factors, along with its low purchase cost, make it a smart option for homeowners looking for something that can handle modest yard cleanup.

That said, it’s important to understand that the Sun Joe CJ603E does not match the power of gas-powered wood chippers designed for residential use. Gas-powered wood chippers are more capable, with most able to chew through branches up to 3 inches in diameter. Their powerful engines also make them capable of moving through branches at a higher rate. There’s also a difference in durability. While the Sun Joe has numerous plastic parts, gas wood chippers have mainly metal construction, so they can better endure bigger jobs and more frequent use.

The Sun Joe is also a dedicated wood chipper. Unlike chipper/shredders, the CJ603E doesn’t have a shredder function that will reduce leaves into mulch. If you're looking for a wood chipper that can handle bigger branches and shred leaves, we suggest one of our other recommended models below.

This gas wood chipper chewed through 3-inch branches with ease when we tested it, and it also doubles as a very effective leaf shredder. Couple that performance with a reasonable price tag, and it’s an ideal gas wood chipper for homeowners with wooded lots to manage.

This is the most affordable gas wood chipper we could find that still has the chops to get the job done. It’s capable of grinding through branches up to 3 inches in diameter and has a chute that makes it easy to deposit those wood chips directly into your landscaping. It only chips wood, though. If you’re looking for something that can also shred leaves, you’ll need to look elsewhere.

Earthquake’s K32 wood chipper boasted some of the most impressive wood-chipping power we experienced of any of the models we tested. What’s more, it produces some of the smallest wood chips. If you’re looking for a machine to create high-quality mulch for your landscaping, then spring for this one.

#6296. South Korea eyes rocket debut and China lines up four launches

On Monday, Nov. 2, Rocket Lab launched The Sea God Surveys on an Electron rocket from its Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula at 11:41 a.m. EST. Aboard was a QPS-SAR satellite for private Japanese company iQPS It marked Electron’s 10th flight for iQPS. The company is building out a fleet of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites with the goal of handing customers worldwide radar views in close to real time.

On Monday, Nov. 2, CAS Space — the commercial launch company founded by the Chinese Academy of Sciences — is targeting 7:10 p.m. EST for a Kinetica 2 launch from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been disclosed, but the only prior Kinetica 2 launch carried a batch of SpaceSail satellites. SpaceSail, also known as Qianfan or “Thousand Sails,” is a Chinese broadband megaconstellation designed to beam internet service from low Earth orbit (LEO).

On Wednesday, Nov. 4, SpaceX will launch the classified USSF-432 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California at 8:28 p.m. EST. After stage separation, the Falcon 9 first stage will aim for a landing on the droneship Of Course I Still Love You, stationed in the Pacific Ocean.

On Wednesday, Nov. 4, South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development (ADD) may attempt a demonstration flight of its Mir rocket from Jeju Island, off the country’s southern coast. That date comes from Next Spaceflight’s tracking; South Korean officials have said only that the launch will happen before the end of the year. ADD, the military research arm of South Korea’s defense ministry, has been developing the solid-fueled rocket since 2021. The military plans to use it to launch small military reconnaissance satellites into orbit. The demo was originally set for June 30 but slipped over safety concerns.

On Thursday, Nov. 5, China’s state-owned launch provider, the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), has two launches scheduled, according to Next Spaceflight. First, a Long March 2C is slated to lift off from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center in southwestern China at 11:00 a.m. EST with an undisclosed payload. Then at 4:15 p.m. EST, a Long March 12 will launch from the Wenchang Space Launch Site on Hainan Island, also with an undisclosed payload.

On Friday, Nov. 6, Chinese commercial company Galactic Energy will launch a Ceres 2 rocket from Jiuquan at 6:35 p.m. EST, according to tracking from Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been disclosed. This will be the second test flight for the Ceres 2 after the rocket suffered a first-stage failure and fell short of orbit on its first flight in January.

On Tuesday, Oct. 27, SpaceX launched Starlink Group 15-16 from Vandenberg at 3:25 a.m. EDT, with the booster landing on Of Course I Still Love You.

On Friday, Oct. 30, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) launched the NVS-03 navigation satellite, also known as IRNSS-1L, aboard a GSLV Mk II rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota. The satellite joins NavIC, India’s regional satellite navigation system — the country’s homegrown counterpart to GPS.

SpaceX followed early Saturday, Oct. 31, with Starlink Group 15-18, lifting off from Vandenberg at 12:04 a.m. EDT. Its booster also touched down on Of Course I Still Love You.

No earlier than Friday, Nov. 13, United Launch Alliance (ULA) is targeting the launch of Amazon Leo (LV-01) on a Vulcan rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The flight will loft a batch of satellites for Amazon Leo, Amazon’s broadband constellation formerly known as Project Kuiper.

No earlier than Saturday, Nov. 14, Rocket Lab plans to fly The Mountain God Rises from Māhia — Electron’s 100th launch. The milestone flight goes to a familiar customer: another QPS-SAR radar satellite for iQPS, bound for a low Earth orbit.

#6295. Newborn survival improves when families receive financial support

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Rx Kids, a cash transfer program, boosted infants’ health in Flint, Michigan

Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield announces Rx Kids' Detroit debut in 2025. The program began in Flint, Mich., in 2024. “We know how to deliver this support efficiently and with dignity," pediatrician and Rx Kids director Mona Hanna told Science News.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.

The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”

Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.

“Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.

The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.

Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.

#6293. The Sky Today on Tuesday, November 3: The Moon passes Regulus

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 2: The Moon passes Jupiter and Mars

The Moon now passes 0.8° south of the bright star Regulus in Leo at 4 A.M. EST. Some regions of the world will see our satellite pass in front of Regulus in an occultation, but again, the event is not visible from North America.

The pair rises together shortly after midnight on the 2nd, following Jupiter and Mars by roughly an hour. By 5 A.M. local time on the 3rd, the Moon-star pair is nearly 50° high in the southeast. Despite its brightness (it is ranked as the 21st brightest star in the sky), magnitude 1.4 Regulus will be the faintest object in this region, as magnitude 0.8 Mars and magnitude –2.0 Jupiter to its west (upper right) far outshine it.

The waning Moon has shrunk from roughly 43% lit yesterday morning to 33% lit today. It is just under a week from New phase, which occurs on the 9th. Between now and then, the phase will continue to diminish and the Moon will rise later in the morning each day, until it travels across the sky in tandem with the Sun when it is New.

Venus passes 2° south of Spica at 8 A.M. EST this morning — they’ll be in the same configuration tomorrow morning, so keep reading below for details on how to observe them.

Sunrise: 6:31 A.M.Sunset: 4:55 P.M.Moonrise: 12:34 A.M.Moonset: 2:07 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (26%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Venus sits 2° south of Virgo’s brightest star, Spica, in the early-morning sky. The pair is joined by a lovely crescent Moon high above them in Leo, creating a gorgeous sight that early risers won’t want to miss.

By 6 A.M. local time (roughly half an hour before sunrise), the sky is growing bright and Venus and Spica are about 8° high in the east. Venus, at magnitude –4.4, far outshines the magnitude 1.0 star, which sits just to the planet’s upper left. A waning crescent Moon, just over 20% lit, hangs high above the pair, to their upper right. Through a telescope, Venus’ large, 58”-wide disk is also a crescent, now 5% lit. In the coming days, Venus’ phase will start to grow as its diameter slowly shrinks.

Also glance to Venus and Spica’s upper left, where you’ll spot magnitude –0.1 Arcturus, the brightest star in Boötes the Herdsman, which borders Virgo to the north.
