#6292. Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

After 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

There was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.

It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

If you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

Over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.

Tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.

And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.

But as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

And, since I was looking for a lively place for New Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.

And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

The island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.

So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.

And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”

But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”

And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.

A visit there will only make things worse.

It pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.

And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.

Go somewhere else that is better managed.

Riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got big because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.

Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.

But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

A crewed mission to Mars could be one of humanity's greatest achievements, but getting there may come with serious health risks. Beyond the challenges of surviving in space for months at a time, astronauts would face prolonged exposure to cosmic radiation ‪—‬ high-energy particles in space that can penetrate the human body and potentially damage vital organs.

A new study suggested that cosmic radiation could pose a particular threat to heart health. Researchers found evidence that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what human astronauts might encounter during a mission to Mars and back developed more scar tissue around the small vessels in their hearts compared with rats that weren't exposed to space radiation.

Although the findings haven't been confirmed in humans yet, they add to the growing concerns about the long-term health effects of sending astronauts on long-duration space missions.

NASA and other space agencies are working on ways to eventually send humans to Mars and beyond. Given these latest findings, would you travel to Mars? Vote in the poll below, and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

#6290. Your Brain Keeps a Hidden Stash of Everything You Don’t Consciously See. Scientists Just Found It.

Scientists gave monkeys 3D glasses to find that ‘invisible’ images are stored almost as sharply as the ones we see.

What we think we perceive in the present moment is far from everything we actually perceive. We’re guided by more than just the things we’re aware of. Even someone in deep concentration who believes they’re focusing on nothing else may not realize that their brain is constantly shifting back and forth between the conscious information they’re focusing on and unconscious information that never reaches awareness.

The human brain is thought to switch between processing conscious and unconscious information extremely fast, about 15 times per second, and only a fraction of the information it processes ever reaches conscious perception. Neuroscientists Janis Hesse and Doris Tsao of the University of California, Berkeley, wanted to learn why some neural activity becomes consciously available and some does not, so they studied what happens when the brain is faced with conflicting images. To do this, they needed a situation in which the physical stimulus stayed the same throughout the experiment while perception changed. With this setup, any differences in neural activity could be attributed to perception rather than to the stimulus itself.

One way to create such a situation is to show a different image to each eye. In binocular rivalry, each eye is shown a conflicting image, and the observer can consciously perceive only one image at a time. In a related phenomenon known as binocular flash suppression, the image first shown to one eye is suddenly suppressed, and becomes invisible, when a second image flashes before the opposite eye and is perceived instead. Neurons that respond more strongly to one type of image fire more when that image is perceived, even though both images are physically present. What especially puzzled the researchers was why these same neurons, while responding to the perceived image, still hold onto information about the suppressed one.

“Previous studies have not revealed a pure neural representation of conscious perception, i.e., one uncontaminated by suppressed representation and closely resembling the representation of a perceptually-equivalent unambiguous stimulus, in any recorded region of the brain during rivalry,” Hesse and Tsao wrote in a study recently posted to the preprint server bioRxiv, which is still awaiting peer review. In other words, scientists had never before found a part of the brain that holds a “clean” version of what we consciously see, free from the image we’re suppressing.

To investigate, the researchers implanted electrodes in the brains of macaques, fitted the animals with 3D glasses (the kind with red and blue lenses that let each eye see a different image), and showed them a series of images. Because each eye saw a different image, binocular flash suppression separated the physical stimulus, including the suppressed image, from conscious perception. The macaques’ brains prioritized the newly flashed image and pushed the other one aside. Human subjects who were tested with the same technique confirmed that the second image took over their perception.

The images were faces, so the researchers could track how face-selective neurons responded. In the inferotemporal cortex, which is critical for visual recognition, Tsao and Hesse found that the macaques’ brains kept alternating between states of perception and suppression, even though the stimulus stayed the same and only perception changed. Each state could be read out from the activity of these neurons, although the consciously perceived face was easier to detect than the suppressed one. The researchers were especially surprised that the second image, after briefly dominating the first, did not stay at the forefront of perception. After the initial flash, neural activity kept rapidly alternating between the perceived and suppressed images. This effect turned out to come from the same neurons switching which stimulus they represented. The same alternating pattern appeared in the prefrontal cortex, which is involved in higher-order cognition. So rather than being discarded, suppressed stimuli are temporally interleaved with everything else the brain processes.

“Neural activity not only allows discriminating between two different suppressed stimuli but allows reconstruction of the suppressed stimulus with high fidelity,” the researchers said. “Thus, the suppressed stimulus is not represented as a weak residual trace but occupies the same high-dimensional face space as the conscious stimulus during complementary [times].”

It turns out that what we consciously see really is only part of what the brain perceives.

#6289. Nov. 3, 1957: The flight of Laika

Less than a month after the launch of Sputnik 1, the Soviets launched Sputnik 2. The mission was readied quickly in order to keep the propaganda momentum from Sputnik 1 and to coincide with the 40th anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution.

Carrying mixed-breed dog Laika, Sputnik 2 was the first flight to carry a living animal to Earth orbit. A small stray from the Moscow streets, Laika had undergone training to help her become accustomed her to the close quarters and gravity changes. Electrodes attached to the dog sent data back to Earth, for future research into the biological effects of space travel. Unfortunately, Laika died a few hours after takeoff – always the expected outcome of the mission, as the life-support systems on Sputnik 2 were imperfect and there was no plan for recovering the satellite or its passenger after launch. Sputnik 2 burned up on reentry in 1958, after its batteries died the previous year. In 2008, a statue commemorating Laika was erected in Moscow.

#6288. A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

#6286. Why This Company is One of the Best for Finding Work

Most travel is extractive and passive. You show up somewhere, take photos of the same landmarks everyone else takes photos of, eat at a restaurant the guidebook recommended, and hit up some bars. You take some tours to learn about the place and, if you’re lucky, get to meet some locals on your trip. You don’t really go deep.

Even long-term travelers who talk about how they “aren’t tourists” do the same – just at a slower pace and while trying to spend less money.

And there’s nothing wrong with that. That’s just the nature of travel. While we all imagine dropping into a place, befriending locals, and having this crazy time like we’re in some movies. But that doesn’t happen. Because we’re just passing through and, for the most part, locals don’t want to become friends with tourists. In fact, most locals don’t interact with tourists. (I mean it does happen but it’s not the norm.)

If you really want a deep travel experience, you need to stay. If you want to understand a place, you need to stay. The most transformative travel experiences I’ve ever had involved contributing something and staying somewhere long enough to build real relationships. It was being embedded in a place rather than just passing through.

I think that more travelers should give back when they travel. In the old days, it was hard to find out what organizations and opportunities were legit, vetted, and actually made the lives of locals better.

Now, there’s a ton of companies that can help you not only find meaningful volunteer jobs when you travel but also paid jobs when you travel and one of the best ones is Global Work & Travel. Use code NOMADICMATT to unlock a discount on your next trip.

Global Work & Travel is the world’s largest gap year company and has been placing people on working holidays, volunteer programs, teaching positions, internships, and more for nearly 2 decades. They’ve helped over 116,000 people and they cover destinations across, the UK and Europe, the Americas, Asia, Africa, and the Pacific.

Even for experienced travelers, moving abroad can be difficult. Finding employment as a traveler, securing permanent accommodation or getting stuck in shared rooms for months on end, transport costs in a new city, interview after interview competing against locals… This is just the beginning of what long term travelers need to consider.

Fortunately, companies like Global Work & Travel provide the scaffolding or safety net that makes working abroad possible for people who don’t want to figure everything out themselves. They handle job matching, pre-departure support, visa guidance, placement, and ongoing assistance through their gWorld portal, a personal trip management app that keeps everything organized in one place. For first-timers especially, having that support structure can be the difference between actually going and endlessly deliberating. The programs they offer span a wide range:

For the past decade, “digital nomad” has been the aspirational version of long term travel. Work remotely, earn in a strong currency, live somewhere cheaper, repeat.

But that model only really works for a small subset of people. You need a remote job, a certain income level, and often a level of career stability that most younger travelers simply don’t have yet.

Instead of bringing a job with you, you get one when you arrive. You integrate into the local economy instead of floating above it. You meet people through work, not just coworking spaces or short-term hostels. And you build a life somewhere, not just a temporary routine.

In a lot of ways, working holiday makers are having a more grounded and accessible version of what people think digital nomad life is. You’re not just passing through, you’re actually living there. You have coworkers, a schedule, a reason to stay longer than a week, and a chance to build real lifetime connections.

It’s also far more realistic for most people. You don’t need a remote business or years of experience. You just need the willingness to go and the right setup to make it happen.

That’s why I think we’re seeing a shift. Less “how do I work remotely?” and more “how do I actually live and work abroad for a year?”

And that’s exactly where structured programs like Global Work & Travel come in. They remove the biggest barriers, finding a job, navigating visas, getting set up, so people can actually make that shift from idea to reality.

For a lot of travelers, this isn’t just an alternative to digital nomad life. It’s a more sustainable, accessible, and realistic way to actually live and work abroad.

Volunteering abroad has a complicated reputation, and it’s worth being honest about that. There are lots of bad volunteer programs out there in the world. Programs that don’t really give back and are designed to make travelers “feel” like they did something but really are just profit driven campaigns. Global Work & Travel’s vets programs in the areas such as wildlife conservation, community development, education, and healthcare in the locations and countries it operates so you know the program you sign up for is legit.

The case for ethical, well-structured volunteering is genuinely strong. When you work alongside local Zanzibar communities on problems they’ve defined as priorities, or with wildlife and conservation in South Africa or Elephant rehabilitation in Thailand — something shifts in how you understand the world. Not only are you helping to give back to a place but you also understand the true needs of a the people and ecosystems living there, but also helping overcome the struggles they go through. It opens your mind and shifts your perspective.

Their Global Animal Welfare Fund also channels resources directly into conservation projects at their partner sites, so the impact extends beyond individual placements.

Working holidays let you truly experience a country instead of just visiting it. You immerse yourself in the culture by living like a local every day. You meet more people both locals and fellow travellers while building real friendships. Best of all, you get paid to travel, so you can stay much longer instead of rushing through in a few weeks. This lets you experience local life deeply, discover hidden spots, and understand how people really live in different places. You also build valuable skills, boost your resume with international experience, and make long-term travel more affordable since your income covers the costs. Plus, you gain a real cultural understanding that no short holiday can match. All that while stil getting paid? Not bad right?!

Working holidays turn travel into a true lifestyle, not just another 2 week vacation.

Global Work & Travel are the world leaders in long term travel and offer a ton of options for travelers looking to volunteer, work, or spend extended time in a destination. Some things I like about them.

Do I need prior experience to work abroad with Global Work & Travel? For most trips, generally nothing more than basic work experience is required. Teaching programs include TEFL training, and volunteering can be started from no experience.

What’s the minimum age? Most programs are open from age 18. Working holiday visas typically cap at 35 depending on the destination country but volunteer and teach programs are open to ages 18–80.

How long does the whole process take? It varies by programs and destination. Most people book their trips 6-12 months in advance for proper planning, job matching and visa quotas. You can get started for as little as $1 here.

Is my money safe if things change? Global Work & Travel and their lifetime deposit policy means your initial payment doesn’t expire. They are also members of many consumer protection services to further support travelers.

Can I go as a solo traveler? Yes, and this is actually one of the most common scenarios. The gWorld Community and programs group connections mean you’ll be meeting others in the same position quickly.

Travel has always been best when it’s been more than tourism. The moments that stay with you — that you actually tell people about five years later — are never the ones where you queued to see a famous landmark. They’re the ones where you connect with people. #6285. The Quantum World Is Bursting With Chaos—Scientists Just Found What's Holding It Together

By mixing classical nudges with quantum circuits, scientists found rhythms hiding in many-body chaos that could help build better quantum computers.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

In new research, scientists in China and England have sketched out and tested a setup that allows them to pick out and boost the longest strands of quantum potential within a chaotic area of particles. The secret, they explain, is to combine quantum and classical ideas into one assembly in which behaviors are easier to see. By doing this, they’re able to jump from few-body quantum mechanics to the more complicated many-body quantum mechanics, with an updated understanding of what causes the quantum phases in their experiment to either change or stay the same.

“The coexistence of regular and chaotic motion is a universal feature of dynamical systems, ranging from planetary orbits and ocean waves to turbulence and transport in complex materials,” the team writes. In this context, chaos is a measure of predictability, or the lack thereof. Remember when Jeff Goldblum’s Dr. Ian Malcolm suggestively dripped water onto the waiting hand of Laura Dern’s Dr. Ellie Sattler in Jurassic Park? It was as unpredictable as their romantic tension.

Sometimes, the appearance of chaos is misleading: ancient people would have guessed that many phenomena, like weather or the germination of a seed, were chaotic, but with today’s knowledge we know that those things can be accurately modeled and predicted. Today, physicists are even more incentivized to understand chaotic systems, because these include the cutting-edge fields of quantum computing and quantum networks.

There’s a huge jump in the complexity of physics between a few-body quantum system and a many-body one. The goal of the new research is to pin down the dynamics of chaos and order in a many-body system. To do that, the team used a superconducting circuit, meaning an arrangement of logical gates cooled to near-absolute zero in order to reach zero resistance.

A circuit runs your light switches, where different positions connect or disconnect the wire that carries current to your lightbulb. In a quantum setup, the logic is controlled by entangled particles, for as long as that entanglement can be maintained. In the experiment, the quantum circuitry was chosen and designed because it’s relatively easy to observe (by quantum mechanics standards) and the researchers could continue measuring it after repeated short periods of activity in the circuit.

By noting how the different entangled “gates” changed between those short windows of time, the scientists could also tune the gates using classical physics. This, they write, represents a hybrid approach that shows how a many-body quantum system shifts between pockets of order and chaos. The classical interventions moved the circuit toward a more ordered state. The researchers’ conclusions differ from the simpler way that a few-body quantum system shifts from order to chaos—and offers a definitive theory that other teams can continue to test and explore.

Their research appears now in the peer reviewed journal Nature Physics. “Our approach gives us a practical way to explore this landscape experimentally,” senior author Zlatko Papić told Phys.org. “Over successive rounds, this process can home in on motion that repeats regularly, without our having to specify that motion in advance.”

A new mom experienced intense feelings of sadness whenever she breastfed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: About two weeks after her baby's birth, the woman began experiencing intensely negative emotions at every breastfeeding session. These feelings of "extreme unhappiness" would start just before her milk ejection reflex (during which milk moves from the breast ducts to the nipples) and last up to two minutes.

The feelings would end abruptly when she finished breastfeeding and then appear again the next time she was about to release milk, according to a report of the case, which the patient co-authored. The patient was a breastfeeding counselor for the United States Department of Agriculture Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) Program.

Until the baby was about 18 months old, this phenomenon would happen every time the woman breastfed — about five times per day, on average. Unlike postpartum depression,‬ which can cause persistent feelings of despondency, anxiety and mood swings in new parents,‬ the woman felt "helpless, hopeless, [and] worthless" only during her milk release. She reported that she otherwise felt happy and bonded with her new baby.

What happened next: When her baby was 7 months old, the woman began meeting with a lactation consultant, who later co-authored the case report. They worked together to track the mother's symptoms over time, noting when negative feelings began and if any intervention made them subside or worsen.

The diagnosis: Because the woman's condition did not have a formal name at the time, she began calling it "dysphoric milk ejection reflex," or D-MER.

The case report authors initially suspected that fluctuations in the woman's oxytocin levels might be causing D-MER, since the hormone is released into the bloodstream prior to the milk ejection reflex during breastfeeding. However, external factors that are known to affect oxytocin levels, such as tobacco use, did not always trigger the woman's symptoms.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Next, they looked at dopamine. The chemical messenger's fluctuations during breastfeeding are less studied than those of oxytocin and prolactin, another hormone linked to lactation. However, dopamine levels have otherwise been connected to strong emotional responses. Activities that seemed to ease the patient's D-MER symptoms — such as taking the cold medication pseudoephedrine, smoking cigarettes or binging on chocolate ice cream — are also known to increase dopamine levels. Meanwhile, acute stress, which reduces dopamine, worsened her symptoms.

The authors hypothesized that an abrupt drop in dopamine prior to milk release might be a trigger for D-MER.

D-MER differs from postpartum depression in that the feelings of sadness are very specific to lactation.

The treatment: The woman began taking bupropion (better known by the brand name Wellbutrin), an antidepressant that increases the amount of dopamine in the brain. She saw a dramatic reduction in her D-MER symptoms within a day, and five days later, her symptoms were almost entirely gone.

However, she stopped taking the drug after a few weeks due to unwanted side effects (which aren't described in the report), and the symptoms came back. She then tried an herbal remedy containing roseroot (Rhodiola rosea), a plant historically used in some places to manage depression. Some recent studies suggest that compounds in R. rosea interact with receptors for chemical messengers in the brain; however, there is little reliable evidence demonstrating its purported therapeutic benefits, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health.

She took R. rosea three to four times per day, reporting that her symptoms became "much milder" but returned if she skipped a day. As her daughter grew older and the woman breastfed less often, the woman stopped taking the supplement. When the child was 3 years old and no longer breastfeeding, the woman's D-MER symptoms went away entirely.

What makes the case unique: Prior to this report, published in 2011, D-MER was not widely recognized or documented in the scientific literature, and there was no research into its causes or treatment.

The patient and co-author of the report created the website D-MER.org in 2007 to share information about the condition more widely. She hoped to raise awareness among medical professionals and to help breastfeeding people who experience this condition by providing resources and support and encouraging them to understand that what they were feeling was a physiological side effect of nursing. Since the site's launch, hundreds of visitors have described having negative feelings while breastfeeding, according to the report.

Over the past two decades, more case reports describing the condition have been published. In a 2025 paper in the European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, researchers estimated that roughly 14.2% of lactating parents experience D-MER and that 1 in 6 stop breastfeeding as a result. Dopamine is thought to play a part, but the exact cause of D-MER has not been definitively established in peer-reviewed research yet.

There is no definitive treatment for D-MER, although some have anecdotally found relief through techniques for stress reduction, such as meditation and breathing exercises, and by seeking support from partners, friends and breastfeeding groups online.

Short-lived negative feelings resembling D-MER have also been reported in people who are not lactating. These anecdotal accounts describe intense, negative feelings brought on by nipple stimulation. One online discussion group referred to this phenomenon as "sad nipple syndrome," according to the authors of the case report. As with D-MER, dopamine may play a part, but the overall neurochemistry underlying that emotional response is unknown.

Breastfeeding and parenthood can be an emotional roller coaster even under the best circumstances, the authors noted. In that sense, they explained, people with D-MER have "the same emotional peaks and valleys" as all new parents do. Yet the negative feelings that accompany D-MER are nonetheless different from the normal range of emotions in the parents of newborns, and they can cause extreme distress if they are not correctly identified and addressed as being specific to breastfeeding.

People with D-MER, the authors concluded, "serve as a reminder to us all that we do not yet have a complete understanding of human lactation."

#6283. The Sky Today on Wednesday, November 4: Venus and Spica stand close

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Venus sits 2° south of Virgo’s brightest star, Spica, in the early-morning sky. The pair is joined by a lovely crescent Moon high above them in Leo, creating a gorgeous sight that early risers won’t want to miss.

By 6 A.M. local time (roughly half an hour before sunrise), the sky is growing bright and Venus and Spica are about 8° high in the east. Venus, at magnitude –4.4, far outshines the magnitude 1.0 star, which sits just to the planet’s upper left. A waning crescent Moon, just over 20% lit, hangs high above the pair, to their upper right. Through a telescope, Venus’ large, 58”-wide disk is also a crescent, now 5% lit. In the coming days, Venus’ phase will start to grow as its diameter slowly shrinks.

Also glance to Venus and Spica’s upper left, where you’ll spot magnitude –0.1 Arcturus, the brightest star in Boötes the Herdsman, which borders Virgo to the north.

#6282. How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

Drones are huge. And, while there’s lots of restrictions around them, a lot of travelers take them on road because they produce some amazing sweeping aerial shots.

There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1. Released in late 2025, attempts to render the traditional gimbal obsolete for a vast segment of creators. By leveraging a dual-lens 360-degree capture system, the A1 records everything in every direction simultaneously. The result is a “fly now, frame later” experience that feels less like piloting a drone and more like directing a virtual camera in a pre-recorded digital environment.

I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.

What make’s Antigravity 360’s so special is the two lenses. Most drones feature a single lens that points forward. However, the A1 features two ultra-wide-angle lenses positioned on the top and bottom of the central fuselage that each captures a 200-degree field of view. When those images are combines, they overlap to create a seamless 360-degree sphere.

And, in the final exported footage, the drone itself is digitally removed, creating the illusion of a camera floating in mid-air with no visible means of support.

The sensors themselves are 1/1.28-inch CMOS units. While smaller than the 1-inch sensors found on some “Pro” level photography drones, they are massive compared to typical 360 action cameras. This allows for significantly better low-light performance and a higher dynamic range, capturing details in the highlights and shadows that would typically be lost in the harsh contrast of a midday sun.

Most countries require drones weighing 250 grams or more to be registered and subject to stricter flight rules. Antigravity clearly understood the importance of this threshold because they made the A1 to weigh exactly 249 grams with its standard battery meaning it’s not considered a commercial drone so you don’t have to register it.

And the drone feels remarkably sturdy. It utilizes a high-grade carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer that offers a better strength-to-weight ratio than the standard ABS plastic found in cheaper models. The folding mechanism is satisfyingly tactile, clicking into place with a precision that suggests long-term durability. When folded, the drone is roughly the size of a large smartphone, though about three times as thick.

The Vision Goggles: These are sleek, lightweight, and feature dual 4K micro-OLED displays with a 120Hz refresh rate. The latency is nearly non-existent and they have integrated head tracking. Because the drone is recording in 360 degrees, you aren’t limited to seeing what is in front of the drone. When you turn your head to the left, the goggle feed pans to the left. If you look down, you see the ground passing beneath you. This provides a sense of presence and spatial awareness that is simply impossible with a traditional fixed-camera drone.

The drone uses a single-handed motion controller. You point the controller where you want to go and pull the trigger to accelerate. Tilt your wrist left to bank, or raise the nose of the controller to climb. It is an incredibly intuitive system that allows even a novice to fly through complex environments within minutes. For professional FPV pilots who prefer the precision of manual acrobatic flight, the A1 does support a traditional “Mode 2” stick controller, but the motion controls are so fluid that most users will likely never switch back.

The marketing for the Antigravity 360 proudly displays “8K Resolution.” In a traditional camera, 8K means every pixel is packed into a 16:9 rectangle. In 360 video, those pixels are spread across a full sphere. When you “reframe” that 8K sphere into a standard flat video, you are looking at a “crop” of the total image.

The color science is noticeably improved over previous 360 cameras. The A1 features a “Vivid” profile for those who want punchy, social-media-ready colors, and a 10-bit “Log” profile for professional editors who need to match the footage to other cameras in a color-grading suite. The stabilization, powered by Antigravity’s “FlowState” algorithms, is nothing short of miraculous. You can fly in 20mph winds, and the footage remains as steady as if the camera were on a tripod.

The “Antigravity Studio” app allows you to download footage wirelessly (at speeds up to 80MB/s) and reframe your video using your phone’s gyroscope. You simply watch the video and move your phone around to “film” the scene in real-time. The app also features “Auto-Frame,” an AI tool that identifies subjects and automatically generates a cut that keeps them in focus. For a solo creator, this effectively provides a virtual camera crew that never misses a shot.

Battery technology remains the bottleneck for all small drones. The A1’s standard Intelligent Flight Battery provides a theoretical 24 minutes of flight. In real-world conditions with moderate wind and constant recording, expect closer to 19 or 20 minutes.

While 20 minutes sounds short, the “work per minute” is much higher than a traditional drone. Because you don’t need to re-fly a path to get different angles, a single 20-minute flight can yield the same amount of usable footage as three flights with a Mavic. For those who need more time, the “Pro Battery” (which pushes the weight over 250g) offers a staggering 39 minutes of flight time, though it does compromise the drone’s agility slightly.

In terms of flight dynamics, the A1 is a “cinewhoop” style flyer. It is stable and predictable rather than aggressive and twitchy. It has a top speed of roughly 36 mph, which is plenty for following bikes or cars, but it won’t keep up with a professional racing drone. The “Turtle Mode” is a life-saver; if you crash and end up upside down, the drone can flip itself over using its propellers, allowing you to take off again without a “walk of shame” to recover the aircraft.

The Antigravity 360 is a niche product that is rapidly becoming mainstream.

The Antigravity 360 (A1) is the most exciting drone I have tested. By removing the need for a gimbal and the stress of manual framing, it allows the pilot to focus on the one thing that truly matters: the story they are trying to tell.

While the image quality isn’t quite at the level of a high-end cinema drone, and the lenses are admittedly delicate, these are small prices to pay for the creative liberation the A1 provides. It bridges the gap between traditional cinematography and the immersive world of VR.

If you are a creator who is tired of the same old “drone shots” and want to push the boundaries of what is possible in the air, the Antigravity 360 is an essential addition to your toolkit.

#6281. Your voice can now say things you never said

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI can replicate a person’s voice. That raises questions about who has the right to use it and what happens when its owner can no longer give consent.

AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.

Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. And some uses fall into murky gray zones, such as voice clones that “speak” after a person has passed away. What happens to a person’s digital voice after they’re gone?

In this episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, hear more from Farid, as well as from a former hospital chaplain and AI researcher, and from Jules Rodriguez, a man who communicates with a voice clone. You’ll also hear about a choice Jules made about what will happen to his voice once he’s gone.

Laura Sanders: What’s a voice you like to listen to?

Kate Nilson: That is a great question. I hope my students don’t listen to this. I was having Snoop Dogg read their assignments to me the other day, just because I thought it was funny. But I don’t know if I would say that’s my favorite.

Sanders: That’s speech language pathologist and professor Kate Nilson. And if you’re wondering, this is a real, legitimate thing that anyone can do.

Snoop Dogg audio: Vector mathematics. Think about a car trip. Your displacement from your starting point is a vector.

Snoop Dogg: I’m glad to be the voice of reason so you can focus better, understand more, and enjoy listening to the internet in the voice of Snoop Dogg.

Sanders: Welcome to The Deep End, Talk To Me. In this episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into the new digital world we all live in. We’re going to get into some of the good, bad and strange scenarios that come up when voices can be cloned and let loose in the world. Let’s talk about it.

[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.

Sanders: As we’ve heard in earlier episodes, ultra-realistic voice clones can be extremely meaningful to people who can no longer speak.

Jules Rodriguez: So when I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice. I knew of the potential of this technology at that moment.

Sanders: These digital copies of voices have restored connections to their loved ones.

MA Fernandez: You know, the first thing he played for me, I was like chills all over.

Patrick Darling: The first time I performed with the AI voice, I was surprised how physically connected I felt with it.

Sanders: These voice clones have been transformative for people who have lost the ability to talk. But the existence of realistic digital copies of voices has effects that ripple farther out into society.

Hany Farid: So here’s where sort of state of the art is. Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.

Sanders: That’s Hany Farid. He’s a computer scientist at Dartmouth College and cofounder of Get Real Security, a firm that sorts real from fake. I called him to ask how these voice clones have changed our world.

Farid: If you had asked me, I don’t know, five years ago, is this possible? I would say, yeah, maybe, but not anytime soon. And then all of a sudden, boom, it just came out of nowhere.

Sanders: This shift happened in a very, very short amount of time, and it has big implications, both good and bad.

Farid: And so we are living in, I think, in equal parts an exciting time and a terrifying time, and somehow those are coexisting.

Sanders: Farid tells me about some of his research, which asks people to decide whether something, like a voice or a video, is real.

Farid: My bread and butter is developing technologies to distinguish real from fake. And we work with media outlets and law enforcement and courts, et cetera. But one of the questions you always want to ask when you’re in my business is, well, do you need the mathematics and the computation? Just let somebody listen to it or look at it. And can they tell the difference?

Sanders: It turns out they cannot. In laboratory tests, people can’t reliably say whether a voice they hear was created by a machine or by a real living, breathing person.

Farid: It’s essentially like they’re flipping a coin.

Sanders: But there’s another, even higher bar for voice clones to pass. That’s whether they can mimic a specific person well enough to slip by undetected.

Farid: The other question too is what if I, for example, play a real voice sample of your voice, Laura, and then I clone your voice using my favorite AI cloning technology, and then I type something and I get you to say something, and I play those two samples to somebody, and I don’t ask them if it’s real/fake. I say, is this the same person? Is the AI not only able to make something that is natural, but is it identity preserving?

Sanders: Okay, give it a try yourself. Is this the same person?

[Sanders voice clone] And how about now? Is this the same person?

Farid: And when you ask them, is it the same person? They say yes, which means the AI has figured out with roughly 20 seconds or so of your voice how to make their AI sound like you, which is mind-blowing.

Sanders: In the earlier episodes of this season, you’ve heard examples of the good that’s been created by these technological leaps. In many cases, that good comes because these voices are both extremely realistic and extremely good at sounding like a specific person. People want their voice to sound like theirs.

Farid: People with ALS can speak with what sounds like their voice. We’ve seen beautiful examples of that. Translation, right? We can now translate things in real time from any language and it’ll sound like you. I’ve made videos of myself speaking any language I want and it sounds like me, and it’s amazing. It’s really cool.

Sanders: These new ways to connect are very impressive, but as with any technology, these powerful realistic auditory dupes can be repurposed to cause harm.

Farid: Some pretty bad stuff’s happening, right? So let’s just go through a few of these. So first, you’re seeing massive types of fraud. Everything from romance scams to people calling parents and saying your kids have been taken, pay a ransom, to geopolitics. People are getting on calls with who they think are leaders of other countries, and it’s not. It’s a deepfake. It’s an AI-generated voice or face.

Sanders:  What Farid is saying feels especially relevant right now. I’m recording this episode in the fall of 2026, and midterm elections in the U.S. are upon us. Political ads are everywhere. Some of these ads use deepfake audio and video to make opponents say or do things they never did. Here are a few recent examples of deepfakes compiled by the New York Times.

[Audio] Hi, I’m Zohran Mamdani and I’m Kathy Hochul and together, we’re making New York, don’t say affordable. I’m voting for Hochul because she basically gave me an early retirement. They stopped prosecuting people for crime, so now I get to sit back and play Candy Crush all day. Is New York getting a little expensive? I’m Kathy Hochul, and I’ve got just the thing. Clinton lover, Trump hater.

Farid: When you can steal somebody’s likeness, their voice, and their face, you can do some damage. We’re seeing people doing content credential resets at companies. They call up and say, oh, I’m employee X. Will you reset my credential? That’s how they’re now attacking companies. We’re seeing North Korean IT workers penetrating Fortune 500 companies by disguising their voices and their accents and their identities. So lots of bad things, and not unpredictably bad.

Sanders: There are romance scams, political scams, employment scams, money scams of all sorts. Farid was even involved in one himself.

Farid: My voice was cloned by an attacker. I was working a very sensitive case with an attorney. Not many people knew about it. And he got a call from my phone number in my voice talking about the case. And after about three minutes, got suspicious, hung up, called me back. Wasn’t me.

Sanders: Bigger picture, we’ve reached a point where it’s safe to say we can no longer automatically trust digital versions of other people. That applies to the images and sounds on my computer screen as I talked with Farid. Maybe this 2-D picture and sound coming from my laptop is a fake.

Farid: So this two-dimensional version that you and I are sharing now, all right, I can’t control that. That can be stolen. The three-dimensional is right now still me, right? We don’t have the robots that can mimic us. Yet is the end of that sentence.

Sanders: So my interview with Farid was alarming. There are parallels here to any new technology, though. Today, people talk about brain rot from junk online. But remember that television was also going to rot our brains.

[Audio] Its content affects us. So does the sheer weight of the hours we watch.

Sanders: Phones today are the downfall of society, but actual wired telephones encountered really similar resistance when they first started appearing in homes.

[Audio] In Chicago, Sharon Krall’s 15-year-old daughter Angie got so addicted to one teen talk line, she ran up an $850 bill in one month.

Sanders: No big technological advance has escaped this fear.

[Audio] We need teachers who are deeply concerned about how the modern media of communication are changing education.

Sanders: Electricity, bicycles, railways, novels, even the printing press all had their skeptics. So this fear of the new thing has been around a long time. Are synthetic voices created by AI any different? Here’s Karina Nagin from Bridging Voice.

Nagin: Taking off my Bridging Voice hat and just as like a human being in the world, I think there’s a lot of things about AI that I’m very concerned. Deepfakes, the ability to make videos and audio that sound and look just like someone saying something that they’re not saying, I think is a huge, huge concern to our news and public information.

Sanders: Nagin then pivots back to the good, the possibilities here.

Nagin: And then I put on my little hat in my space that I am like, this is how we can harness this to impact people’s lives in our space right now. And I think both conversations need to happen.

Sanders: It occurs to me that I’m seeing the ends of the spectrum here. The stories Farid told me were awful. And the stories that Jules and Casey and others have told me were really, really life-changingly good. Yet these ends of the spectrum are the easy ones. The ones you can look at and say, that’s a horrible way to use this technology. Or that is a powerful and good way to use a voice clone. Between those two poles is the middle ground. That’s the place where Snoop explains cell biology.

[Audio] The membrane separates the material outside the cell.

Sanders: Good, because it’s helping people learn more about mitochondria and who couldn’t use more of that in their lives. Bad, because Snoop never actually said those words, and it’s weird to pretend otherwise.

[Audio] The artists of the Renaissance said that man’s main concern should be for man.

Sanders: There are deepfakes of the late great physicist Richard Feynman delivering famous lectures.

[Audio] The problem is the laws of physics themselves. Let me start with something basic. The next star over from us is called Proxima Centauri.

Sanders: Good because it introduces some amazing physics to people who would otherwise scroll past? Bad because it’s somewhat disrespectful and possibly inaccurate? There aren’t easy answers here. This murky middle gets even murkier with the invention of griefbots. Those are digital versions of people who have passed away. And that means that special voices can keep talking to us long after the body that created them is gone.

I read a poignant post online written by a guy who had lost his dad after years of dementia. He missed his dad’s voice, he wrote, so he cloned it. He paid for the starter pack, submitted three minutes of his dad’s audio, and he wrote, quote, a few minutes later, I had a scarily accurate clone of my dead father’s voice. He goes on to write, quote, my family and I had a good cathartic cry upon hearing the results. I had his cloned voice read the Lord’s Prayer as well as ‘Twas the Night before Christmas. Just hearing his simulated voice again is such a blessing and is helping me in the grief process. End quote.

There are lots of companies now offering this exact thing. A casual search online gets me to a company that sells chats with dead loved ones. There’s a big orange button to click that says bring them back to life. A 2024 documentary called “Eternal You” follows the stories of people as they grapple with this idea. Here’s a little bit of the trailer.

[Audio] We are on the verge of a new era. Hi. It’s like, it’s the funniest thing. It’s like, what’s the first thing you say to someone that’s dead? Like, welcome back.

Sanders: Griefbots or digital avatars of loved ones offer a bridge from the past to the present, a way to remember vividly. But they are also a denial, of sorts, that all life must come to an end.

[Audio] And what I can tell you is that AI really is changing the way that we interact with death.

Sanders: That’s from a 2025 TEDx talk from Dylan Thomas Doyle. He’s a former hospital chaplain, current academic researcher at Northwestern University and self-described philosophy bro. His work explores death and AI.

[Audio] Imagine that you are at a funeral, and you’re sitting there in silent reflection, and all of a sudden, on the back screen in the auditorium, a woman’s face appears. And it’s the face of a woman named Marina. And her hologram, she starts talking to you, and she starts asking you how you’re doing today. And you answer her, and then you ask her a question back. And she responds as if she is still there.

Sanders: I called Doyle to ask about the implications of using technology this way.

Doyle: It was on my radar as a chaplain and a technology researcher, I started thinking through, well, what is the actual impact of this technology on people? So what is it like to hear the voice, in the context of this podcast, the voice of, say, your father who’s passed away while you’re actively grieving their death? And they’re not just repeating what they said or a journal entry in their voice, but like, creating new stories and new relationships through their voice. It gives a lot of people existential ick, is what I’ve heard. And that’s something that I really, I’m curious about.

Sanders: There’s tension here, Doyle tells me.

Doyle: So there’s this push force where you’re like, this is not right. We don’t have the narrative or cultural script to understand what’s going on there. But then as people are beginning to use it, there’s a comfort that comes out of it. So we’re working in that tension space between this comfort that comes, then you’re still dealing with this push away from this technology of it just being weird in a way that people are still grappling with language, I think, to describe.

Sanders: It’s not clear how these types of interactions might affect grieving. They could help or they could hurt.

Doyle: There is this tension between more healthy continuing bonds. So continuing that relationship by, say, writing letters to your dead loved one or, you know, talking out loud to them and continuing that relationship in a positive way that moves us through a healthy grief process and a grief journey. Or hanging on to our relationship with that person to a degree where we can’t actually do any sort of moving on.

Sanders: Doyle points out that we don’t have good data on how many people might be using griefbots.

Doyle: I just don’t want us to get ahead of ourselves when it comes to people like using these. So the capability to do everything we’ve talked about with griefbots is there. But the actual use cases of individuals in their homes using this, it’s still pretty unclear about the adoption of those technologies.

Sanders: But even if griefbots aren’t widespread, the questions they raise aren’t going away. These voices are blurring the lines between a memory and a present-day experience, between alive and dead. Here’s Karina Nagin again.

Nagin: It’s an interesting conversation that we’re having right now of what happens to your voice once you pass away. Some people are starting to integrate this into their wills or their sort of final wishes of, do you want your voice to be able to speak at your own memorial service?

Do you want to have messages saved in your voice that are for your child at graduation that they listen to? Who and when can use that? I think that these are things that people are starting to think about. Who owns your voice? Can your children use your voice to write a speech for their children’s graduation? Or do you want that voice to be deleted once you pass away? Very tricky questions.

Sanders: Rules about who can use voice clones are all over the place. Regulations vary by state and by country, and even companies have their own individual policies in place. There are no clear guidelines, and that makes sense given how young this technology is. Conversations about digital voices and how to use them are inherently very personal. There are as many different takes as there are people. I asked MA if she and Jules had talked about this.

MA: I love that question. Both of us love this question because it’s so important. And we talked about it before he got the trache. Like when he was already using the voice, we were talking about different things in bed at night. And he said, you know, I have a very clear request that my voice like dies with me, basically, that, you know, I ask that you don’t use the voice to keep me alive in any way,  that there’s no… And I was like, 100 percent clear. I hadn’t even thought about that. But yeah, it would make sense to be like, I miss him so much. I want to, whatever or. But no, as far as we’re concerned, his voice dies when he does. And his voice will live on in whatever videos or things we captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally. And that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: So when Jules is gone, his voice will be gone too. But right now is a different story.

MA:  Well back in 2021, I was writing an Instagram post about something. It was him playing with Skylar in the backyard while he was already like, you know, had trouble with everything, but he was doing what he could. And I asked him like, you know, what, what do you want to caption it? And he just said that, right here, right now phrase, something else, and like right here, right now. And it became our family mantra. It became something that we wanted to just to share and in both a sense of like do the things that you want to do.

And also something that’s always been big for Jules that I’ve admired him articulate is that it’s not just about, oh, just go forward and do all the things and like suck the marrow out of life. It’s like just also, like, settle. Like it doesn’t have to be that extreme, you know. There’s a beautiful thing about that presence and that settling in. And again, with ALS being something where you’re given the diagnosis, which is terminal, it’s basically a death sentence. Most people are given, you know, two to five years. You don’t know where you’re going to fall in that. We’ve known people that have passed away in a year and a half. We’ve known people that are six years in like Jules, but can still kind of walk around, speak a little bit. ALS touches everybody really differently. So you really don’t know what’s coming. And there’s a lot of like forward thinking that you can do that detaches you from being in your life. So how are you here? And then there’s a lot of backwards, you know, reminiscing and grieving about all the things we’ve lost and how we wish things were different. But then that also takes you out of like this moment right now and this part of your story.

Sanders: This part of the story is the important part. Right here, right now.

On the next and final episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me. We’re going to look at what’s next for Jules and Casey and what’s next for the science racing to give voices back to people.

Vikash Gilja: We can see all the pieces coming together. All of the emphasis, capital, quite frankly, talent focused on advancing AI techniques and technologies. You know, our little corner can benefit from it, right? These tools weren’t available even five years ago.

Sanders: What’s next for the human voice?

Samantha Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

Sanders: The Deep End is a production of Science News. It’s based on original reporting by me, Laura Sanders. This episode was produced and mixed by Ella Rowen. Our project manager is Ashley Yeager. Nancy Shute is our editor in chief. Our music is by Blue Dot Sessions. The podcast is made possible in part by the Burroughs Wellcome Fund with support from PRX.

#6280. The Universe Should Be Empty. A Single Trapped Antiparticle Might Finally Reveal Why It Isn’t.

Scientists chilled a single positron to its quantum ground state, chasing physics’ biggest mystery.

The conventional picture of Big Bang cosmology holds that 13.8 billion years ago, all mass and energy was packed into a singularity, a state that predated even atoms, protons, and quarks. Then, a lot happened in a very short time, including the rapid inflation of the universe and the creation of the fundamental building blocks of matter, which eventually coalesced into, well, everything.

Except that shouldn’t have happened at all, according to the Standard Model, otherwise known as Lambda-Cold Dark Matter, or ΛCDM model. During that immense Big Bang (which, of course, didn’t produce any “bang” at all), matter and antimatter created mere fractions of a second after the cosmic event should have annihilated one another in equal measure, leaving behind only a rapidly expanding void filled with radiation—no stars, no planets, no us. But, as evidenced by your eyeballs scanning these very words, that very much didn’t happen, and instead we live in a universe dominated by matter.

Our existence is the result of what scientists call the “matter-antimatter asymmetry”: for every billion matter-antimatter pairs created at the universe’s birth, one particle of matter somehow survived. That suggests that the Standard Model, our best theory of how the universe works, is incomplete. Now, a new study led by Northwestern University scientists details a promising technique that could help solve this cosmological conundrum.

In an article in the journal Physical Review Letters, the researchers explain how they essentially “trapped” an anti-electron, otherwise known as a positron, for months, creating what they call a “one-positron quantum cyclotron.” Antimatter annihilates on contact with ordinary matter, as it did in the first moments after the Big Bang, so holding even a single particle requires a nearly perfect trap.

“If we want to study antimatter, we must handle it carefully,” Northwestern physicist Gerald Gabrielse, senior author of the study, said in a press statement. “To be clear, it’s not dangerous. We don’t have enough antimatter to make an explosion.”

To capture the positron, researchers relied on radioactive decay from sodium-22, a rare isotope of sodium. Once the positrons emerged, the researchers guided a single one into the trap’s near-perfect vacuum, then cooled it to just 300 millikelvins above absolute zero. The whole process took less than 12 hours.

This process lowered the particle to its quantum ground state, and the scientists could then deliver energy via finely tuned microwaves to study the particle’s quantum transitions. The goal was to eventually gain a complete understanding of the particle’s magnetic properties and compare the results to the team’s previous work with a one-electron quantum cyclotron.

“Current theories suggest that there will be no difference in the two measurements,” Gabrielse said in a press statement. “If it turns out they are not equal, that would be the biggest discovery in physics in the last century.”

Paolo Crivelli, a physicist at Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (ETH) Zurich, who’s unaffiliated with the study, writes for Physics that this research is an “experimental breakthrough,” but it’s not enough on its own to provide high-precision measurements of a positron’s “g factor,” which describes the relationship between the particle’s magnetic moment and its angular momentum.

“Achieving such a measurement will require detailed spectroscopy and exquisite control of systematic effects,” Crivelli cautions.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6279. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column.

Wednesday, November 4Venus sits 2° south of Virgo’s brightest star, Spica, in the early-morning sky. The pair is joined by a lovely crescent Moon just over 20% lit, high above them in Leo.

Sunrise: 6:32 A.M.Sunset: 4:54 P.M.Moonrise: 1:44 A.M.Moonset: 2:30 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (17%)

Sunrise: 6:34 A.M.Sunset: 4:53 P.M.Moonrise: 2:50 A.M.Moonset: 2:53 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (10%)

Sunrise: 6:35 A.M.Sunset: 4:52 P.M.Moonrise: 3:56 A.M.Moonset: 3:16 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (5%)

Saturday, November 7This morning, the Moon passes 1.1° due south of Venus at 7 A.M. EST. You can spot the pair an hour before sunrise, some 6° high in the east and climbing as the sky begins to brighten. Magnitude –4.5 Venus blazes to the upper left of the delicate crescent Moon, whose western limb is just barely lit as the Sun sets across the lunar nearside. Look for earthshine on the already-shadowed portion of Luna’s face, as sunlight bouncing off Earth lights it up. Near Venus is another bright light: This is Spica, Virgo’s alpha star, shining at magnitude 1.0 and also lingering in the morning twilight.

Sunrise: 6:36 A.M.Sunset: 4:51 P.M.Moonrise: 5:01 A.M.Moonset: 3:40 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (1%)

Sunrise: 6:37 A.M.Sunset: 4:50 P.M.Moonrise: 6:07 A.M.Moonset: 4:08 P.M.Moon Phase: New

Monday, November 9New Moon occurs at 2:02 A.M. EST.

Sunrise: 6:38 A.M.Sunset: 4:49 P.M.Moonrise: 7:12 A.M.Moonset: 4:40 P.M.Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (1%)

Tuesday, November 10The waxing crescent Moon passes 0.3° south of Antares at midnight EST, although the pair is not visible at that time. You can catch our satellite setting in the west around sunset, although it will likely disappear before Antares pops out of the twilight only shortly before the star itself sets as well.

Friday, November 13The Moon reaches apogee, the farthest point from Earth in its orbit, at 12:50 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will be 252,040 miles (405,619 kilometers) from Earth.

Sunrise: 6:43 A.M.Sunset: 4:45 P.M.Moonrise: 10:54 A.M.Moonset: 7:55 P.M.Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (21%)

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.
